Description: THE DEPLOYMENT'S OWN SECRETS OBEY THE SAME RULE: SET, CHANGE, NEVER READ BACK. The platform settings surfaces hold real credentials -- the Vault token the secrets backend authenticates with, the KMS credential the encryption provider uses, an identity provider's client secret, the simple provider's JWT signing secret, the exchange spool's S3 secret key -- and every one of them was being handed back verbatim by the GET that renders its form. That is the leak REQ-1557 closed for org secrets and REQ-1574 closed for encryption keys, left open on the deployment's own. A field a registry marks ``secret: True`` is WRITE-ONLY from here on: the GET returns it as absent, never as its value and never as a mask that could be mistaken for one, and alongside it returns the single bit a form legitimately needs -- whether a value is stored -- so the UI can render "set, replace it?" rather than an empty box that lies about the state. A URL FIELD IS PASSWORD-BEARING AND IS TREATED AS ONE. A DSN carries its password in the userinfo, so a returned ``federation_engine_url`` leaks a warehouse credential while looking like an address. The password component is stripped on the way out and the rest of the URL -- scheme, user, host, port, path, the part an operator reads to know what they are pointed at -- is returned intact. On the way back IN, a submitted URL that is the same address with no password keeps the stored password, because the form posts back what it was given and would otherwise destroy the credential by saving an untouched page; a submitted password replaces it, and a CHANGED address does not inherit the old one. That password was issued for the old target and sending it to a new host is sending a credential somewhere it does not belong. WRITE SEMANTICS ARE ABSENT-MEANS-UNCHANGED, NOT EMPTY-MEANS-UNCHANGED. A secret field omitted from a PUT leaves the stored value alone, which is what lets a form that cannot read a value still save the rest of its page. A secret field present and empty is an explicit CLEAR, because an operator must retain a way to remove a credential and a rule that silently ignores the empty string takes it away.

THE DEPLOYMENT'S MAIL TRANSPORT IS SET FROM THE PLATFORM SETTINGS PAGE, NOT FROM A FILE ON THE NODE. Provisa sends mail on the platform's behalf -- today the org invitation (REQ-1330), tomorrow anything else the platform must say to a person -- and until now the only way to point it at a mail server was to edit ``mail:`` in provisa.yaml or set ``PROVISA_MAIL_PROVIDER``/``PROVISA_EMAIL_API_KEY`` and restart. That makes the one setting whose failure is invisible -- an invitation nobody receives looks exactly like an invitation never sent -- the one setting a platform_admin cannot see or fix from the product. It becomes a surface: ``platform_settings``, the same right that gates the secrets backend and the encryption provider, persisted to provisa.yaml and applied to the running process, so pointing the deployment at a mail server is a save rather than a redeploy. A TRANSPORT IS A REGISTRY ENTRY, NOT A BRANCH. REQ-1330 gave sending a port (``EmailSender``) and two adapters chosen by ``mail.provider``; both were spelled out in ``email_sender``'s dict and each carried its own switch flattened into one shared config block, which stops working the moment two providers want a field of the same name and different meaning. The transports are a REGISTRY of specs in the shape the secrets and encryption registries already use -- key, label, description, ``config_fields`` the form renders, an availability probe, and a builder over that provider's OWN config block -- and the config is nested per provider, so a deployment may keep an SMTP host on file while running Resend and switch back without retyping either. Selection is FAIL-CLOSED, as it is for secrets: an unknown provider, or one whose SDK is not installed, is refused at the point of saving with the distribution named, never quietly left on the previous transport. THE METHODS SUPPORTED ARE THE ONES DEPLOYMENTS ACTUALLY USE. Mail has no single popular protocol, so the registry ships the several that matter rather than electing one: SMTP for self-managed and corporate relays (host, port, credentials, STARTTLS or implicit TLS), and the HTTPS transactional APIs: Resend, SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Amazon SES, and Microsoft 365 via Graph ``sendMail`` for a tenant that already sends everything through Exchange Online. Each is one adapter over one HTTPS call or one SDK; the call sites keep depending on ``send()`` alone. THE CREDENTIAL OBEYS REQ-1575 WITHOUT EXCEPTION. An API key, an SMTP password, a Graph client secret is ``secret: True`` in the registry, and the GET that renders the form returns it as absent with a ``secret_set`` bit beside it. There is no show button and no mask. The write is absent-means-unchanged, present-and-empty-means-clear, so an operator can change the SMTP port without retyping the password and can still remove a credential outright. STATS ARE THE RECORD OF WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DELIVERED, NOT A GUESS FROM CONFIG. A configured transport tells an operator nothing about whether mail is arriving, and the failure that matters -- a rejected key, an expired relay credential, a bounced sender domain -- is visible only at send time. Every attempt is recorded in the registry: when, which provider, which kind of message, the recipient, whether it succeeded, and on failure the transport's own error text. The surface reports the basic counts a platform_admin needs to answer "is mail working": attempted, delivered and failed over the last day and week, the last successful send, the last failure with its message, and the most recent attempts in order. The record is written whether the send succeeded or failed, because a surface that shows only successes cannot show an outage. A SEND IS VERIFIED BY SENDING. The page can send a test message to an address the operator names, using the configuration as saved, and reports the transport's answer verbatim. It is the only check that proves the whole path -- credential, sender domain, relay, recipient -- and it lands in the same record as every other attempt rather than in a special case beside it. AN EMPTY SETTING IS NOT AN ABSENT ONE, AND THE LINK REFUSES TO BE BUILT WITHOUT ITS ORIGIN. ``${env:VAR:-default}`` resolves through ``os.environ.get(var, default)``, so a variable that is EXPORTED EMPTY resolves to the empty string and the default never applies, which is how a deployment reaches a running process with ``mail.base_url`` blank. The redemption link built from a blank origin is ``/?invite=<token>``, a relative path no mail client can open, so ``invite_redemption_url`` refuses it by name instead of emitting it. The refusal is reported where every other delivery failure is reported: composition sits inside the same boundary as the send, so the attempt is recorded and the creation response says ``failed: <reason>``, and the invitation row and its link survive to be distributed by hand.

Description: THE ORG IS NAMED IN THE FROM DISPLAY NAME AND THE INVITER ANSWERS THE REPLY. An invitation arrives from one deployment-wide address (REQ-1576 ``mail.from_address``), which is what keeps a single verified sending domain and a single warm reputation, but the invitee reads the sender column before they read anything else and "Provisa" alone does not tell them which organization is asking. The message therefore carries a DISPLAY NAME naming the org -- ``"Acme (via Provisa)" <invites@provisa.dev>`` -- so the org is visible in the inbox list while the address, the DKIM signature and the DMARC alignment stay on the one domain the deployment has verified. A REPLY GOES TO A PERSON, NOT TO A NOBODY. The invitee's first instinct on an unexpected invitation is to reply and ask. ``invites@`` is not a mailbox anyone reads, so the message sets REPLY-TO to the inviter's own authenticated email address and the answer reaches the human at the org who sent it. The inviter's address comes from the authenticated identity that created the invitation; when that identity carries no email address there is no Reply-To header at all, because a header pointing somewhere nobody reads is worse than its absence. THIS IS A PROPERTY OF THE MESSAGE, NOT OF THE TRANSPORT. ``MailMessage`` carries ``from_name`` and ``reply_to``, and every adapter in the registry honours both in the form its transport takes: an RFC 5322 display name for SMTP, a formatted from and a reply-to field for the HTTPS APIs, ``from``/``replyTo`` objects for Graph. A message that sets neither is delivered exactly as before, so nothing but the invitation changes shape. ONE TRANSPORT CANNOT CARRY THE DISPLAY NAME, AND THAT DECIDES WHICH TRANSPORT SHIPS. Exchange Online rewrites the sender of an app-only Graph send from the mailbox object itself, so ``microsoft365`` delivers the mailbox display name however the message was addressed; a live send verified this: the Reply-To arrived intact, the display name did not. The per-org name is the whole point of this requirement, so a deployment that wants it uses a transport that renders the ``From`` header verbatim (smtp, resend, sendgrid, mailgun, postmark, ses), and ``microsoft365`` remains a supported transport that delivers a fixed sender name. The adapter does not pretend otherwise and no substitute name is invented for it. THE ALTERNATIVE WAS REJECTED DELIBERATELY. Sending as ``invites@{org}.provisa.dev`` would put the org in the address itself, but DKIM has no wildcard: every org subdomain would need its own ESP domain registration, its own DNS records, its own verification state machine, and would start with no sending reputation at all. The display name and Reply-To buy the same recognition at no deliverability cost, which is what Slack, Notion and Linear send.

An org's LLM vendor API key may be the credential itself or a REFERENCE to one held in the deployment's secrets service. A ${secret:NAME} typed into the API key field on Admin / AI Models is stored verbatim, encrypted, and resolved against the org's vault on the way OUT, at the moment a call site builds an LLM client, not when the field is saved. An org that keeps every credential in one vault therefore keeps no second copy of its vendor key here, and rotating the vault entry rotates what the LLM client is handed with no visit to the AI Models page at all. Before this, the reference text was handed to the vendor as the key and the generators failed with the vendor's own authentication error, which names the header and not the reference. WHICH VAULT: the org running the request, resolved exactly as the per-request data plane resolves it: the bound org, or the boot org where none is bound. An environment resolves to its base org, because a branch is a copy of the model and not a second organization. The core layer cannot see the API layer's request context, so the API installs a resolver at import, the same seam the domain policy already uses. NO ACTING PERSON is bound, so ${user:NAME} in this field raises naming the scope. A vendor key is a credential the ORGANIZATION owns and no personal vault stands in for it. A reference naming nothing raises saying which name is unset, rather than reaching the vendor with unresolved text. A stored value carrying no reference is handed over untouched and never looked up.

The exclude-from-metadata-export control says which columns it is for. Some columns carry business data and some carry plumbing -- an ETL batch identifier, a row version, an ingestion timestamp -- and the term derived from a plumbing column has a real definition that is simply not business vocabulary. The help text under the control states the test (does the business speak this word, not is the definition good) and what exclusion does: the term and any relationship ending on it are withheld from the catalogs Provisa publishes to, while the columns themselves still export as assets. That last clause is the part readers get wrong: excluding a term does not hide the data.

A table name is cut at its connective when its concept is derived. An access-path name reaches ONE thing through a lookup key -- user_by_name is a user, orders_by_customer is an order -- so everything from the connective onward is the key, not the concept. Dropping only the connective token left the tail in place, so the surrogate key on user_by_name normalized to the phrase "user name" and collided with the genuine users.name attribute, putting a thing and one of its own fields on one term. The cut applies to table concepts only: in a column name the same token reads as a compound noun (pet_by_name and pet_name are one term, REQ-1387), and a connective with nothing before it names no concept to cut back to. This is what makes the REQ-1387 proxy-token rule land a key on the term for the thing it stands for.

A derived glossary term names the column's BUSINESS name: its alias where the modeller set one, its physical name where they did not. THE RECOMMENDATION THIS ENCODES: when a proposed term reads wrong, the name it was derived from is what reads wrong, and aliasing the column is the stronger correction than renaming the term. An alias travels with the data to every surface that reads it (SQL, GraphQL, the catalog, an agent's schema), so the model describes itself once; a term rename corrects one catalog entry and leaves the column still reading usr_nm to the next reader, human or agent. Poorly named physical fields mislead agents exactly as they mislead people, and a glossary layered over them is a second place to keep correct. So the proposed-term banner recommends the alias first and the rename only for the case it is actually for, where the column name is right and the vocabulary is not. FOLLOW-THROUGH: re-aliasing a column re-derives its term, so the glossary tracks the model rather than asking for the same correction twice, and the proposal it moves off is settled under the existing remove-or-deprecate rule. CURATION OUTRANKS IT: once the linked term carries a definition, a relationship, an expert, or a curator's retirement, an alias edit does not move the ref. That link is a person's judgement about which vocabulary this column belongs to, and a name change is not an instruction to discard it. The table's own alias already qualified TOO-GENERIC phrases (REQ-1387); this extends the same rule to the column itself.

The business glossary is queryable metadata: its terms, their physical refs, their relationships and their experts are registered in the built-in meta domain, the same surface that already carries the tag registry (REQ-1373/1377) and the derived tags (REQ-1443). THE REASON: governance reporting belongs in the governed pipeline, not in a bespoke endpoint. Until now the glossary was reachable only through the admin surface and the metadata export, so every question about vocabulary coverage had to be answered by hand. Registered in meta it is SQL, and it is audited, row- and column- governed and reachable from Cypher like every other meta table. WHAT IS EXPOSED: glossary_terms with a ref count, a rooted flag and a live flag computed by the same admission predicate the export uses, so a query can ask what actually publishes without reimplementing it; glossary_term_refs resolved to its address; glossary_term_edges with both endpoint names beside the ids; glossary_term_experts. THE JOIN IS THE POINT: a ref is a COLUMN identity, (table_id, column_name), deliberately not table_columns.id, which the table upsert replaces wholesale. The relationships table is single-column, so both the ref view and the table_columns view emit a synthesized column_key of table_id and column_name, and the edge is registered on that: stable in exactly the way the surrogate id is not. Through it a query reaches the column's alias, masking class and description, which is what makes coverage answerable: exported columns carrying no term, terms bound to masked columns, and a term whose name has drifted from the alias it was derived from (REQ-1581). FLAGS NOT FILTERS: retired and export_excluded are columns on the view, never predicates: meta is the internal surface and withholding is the export's job, so a meta view that filtered them would disagree with the admin surface it mirrors. user_id on the experts table is the only identity data in the set and is governed by the ordinary column visibility rule rather than omitted. All four tables carry tenant_id, so all four base tables take the tenant isolation policy; the views do not, as with roles_domain_access.

The tag graph is traversable in the meta domain: every tag table is joined to what it labels and to the tag registry itself. THE GAP: the tag tables were registered as meta TABLES (REQ-1373/1377/1443) but stood unconnected, so a governance query could list assignments and could list columns and had no edge to cross between them; each answer needed a hand-written join over surrogate ids the caller had to know. WHAT IS REGISTERED: tag_assignments to tags and back, to registered_tables and back, and to table_columns in both directions; tag_expiry, tag_param_values and derived_tags to tags; derived_tags to registered_tables and back. COLUMN-LEVEL TAGS JOIN ON column_key: the tag_assignments and tag_expiry views emit the same synthesized table_id-and-column_name key that table_columns and glossary_term_refs emit (REQ-1584), because relationships is single-column and table_columns.id is replaced wholesale by the table upsert. The key is null on a source-, relationship- or command-level assignment, which is precisely what makes the join select the column-level tags and nothing else. THE POINT OF THE SHARED KEY: it closes term to column to pii/deprecated in one traversal, so a business term reaches the governance labels on the columns it binds without any surface knowing about both vocabularies. Cardinality is one-to-many from the column side in both directions: a column carries many tags, and a column key may hold many refs.

A junction table is declarable as a first-class Cypher relationship, and its own columns are that relationship's attributes. THE GAP: relationships is a single column pair, so an associative table can only be modelled as two edges through a reified node: glossary_term_edges is registered as edges_from and edges_to, and a caller who wants "term A is a KIND_OF term B" must traverse (:GlossaryTerm)-[:EDGES_FROM]->(:GlossaryTermEdge)-[:EDGES_TO]->(:GlossaryTerm) and filter the middle node by rel_type. Variable-length traversal is then wrong by construction -- *1..3 counts half-hops -- and the middle node pollutes the graph schema with a label that is not a business entity. HOW A JUNCTION IS IDENTIFIED: by declaration on the relationship row, never by inference at query time. relationships gains six nullable columns: via_table_id (the junction, a registered table), via_source_column and via_target_column (its two foreign keys), and via_type_column with via_type_value (the discriminator, when one junction table carries several relationship types). A row with via_table_id null is an ordinary single-hop edge and is unchanged. Each end of the edge maps one or more junction columns, not exactly one: a junction whose foreign keys are composite is mapped by listing the columns of each end in order, and the two lists are paired positionally against the source and target keys. A single-column end is the same declaration with a list of one. The list is stored as a comma-separated ordered declaration on each of the four key columns, split by one shared parser on both sides of the wire, and the control plane refuses a save whose two lists do not pair. A mismatch is a malformed declaration, not something the compiler discovers at query time. One traversal cannot carry a composite end: the recursive path builder holds a single scalar end id per step and has nothing to pair the remaining columns against, so it refuses the pattern rather than matching on the first column alone. HOW THE EDGE IS NAMED: the exposed Cypher type is nominated, not guessed. via_label_source names one of exactly three sources: column, meaning the discriminator value this row is pinned to; table, meaning the junction table's own name; or fixed, meaning the cypher_alias declared on the row. Whichever is nominated is upper-snake-cased before it is exposed, so a junction edge is named the same way every other relationship type is. A CHECK constraint requires the nominated source to be present -- column without via_type_value, or fixed without cypher_alias, cannot be stored -- so nothing downstream has to invent a name when a nomination is missing. One row declares one exposed relationship type, so a discriminated junction is declared once per value and the Cypher schema stays static; nothing has to enumerate discriminator values at query time. Nothing is discovered: no sync, scan or heuristic ever proposes a junction, because whether an associative table is an edge or an entity is a modelling judgement and not a shape. A table of two foreign keys plus payload is just as often a fact table. A junction exists only where a steward declared one. WHAT THE JUNCTION TABLE STOPS BEING: once declared, it is not a node label in the Cypher schema; the reified pair it replaces is removed with it. Dropping the label drops it from every surface the schema drives: it is not a label a pattern can match, not a pill in the graph sidebar a user can drag onto the canvas, and not an entry under its domain's label list. Putting it back on any of those restores the reified-node modelling the declaration exists to replace. A domain or table grouping that held only the junction goes with it rather than rendering empty. It remains a registered table and is still queryable as a table in SQL and GraphQL. HOW IT IS EMITTED: as a real aliased join through the junction, not a semi-join, because the junction row must be projectable. A pattern crossing a declared junction emits two joins (source to junction, junction to target) with the discriminator as an additional predicate, and the junction's alias is carried on the relationship variable. ATTRIBUTES: every column of the junction table other than its two keys is an attribute of the relationship. They are returned in the edge object's properties rather than the empty object emitted today, and the edge object carries one meta field alongside its type naming the junction table it came through. It is present only on a junction-backed edge, and a sibling of properties rather than a member of them, so it cannot collide with a junction column of the same name. It is what lets an inspector say which table an edge's attributes were read from without re-deriving the mapping, they are readable as r.attr in RETURN and in expressions, and they are filterable: a WHERE on a relationship attribute compiles to a predicate on the junction alias, so it restricts the traversal rather than filtering assembled rows. A relationship with no junction has no attributes and its properties stay empty. An edge inside a returned path is the same edge: a step of a path carries the junction's columns and the junction's name exactly as a directly returned relationship does, so a surface that draws paths never shows an empty edge where a returned relationship would have shown attributes. HOW IT IS DECLARED IN THE UI: junction declaration is a rare act next to ordinary table registration, so it does not sit inline on the registration surface. Description: A GLOSSARY TERM IS SCOPED TO DOMAINS, AND ONE TERM MAY SPAN SEVERAL. A rooted term's domains are DERIVED -- the distinct ``registered_tables.domain_id`` of the tables its refs point at -- so nothing is declared and nothing can drift out of sync. An abstract term declares its domains explicitly, one or more, because it holds no refs to derive from. THE COMBINED MODEL: a term whose refs span two domains is ONE term scoped to both, not two terms. Cross-table merging is the mechanism the glossary is built on (``normalize_term`` sheds trailing proxy tokens so ``orders.id`` and every ``order_id`` foreign key land on one term), and a domain boundary is not a reason to stop it: if ``orders`` is in sales and ``order_id`` is in pet-store, "order" genuinely spans both. THE STAMP: a rooted term's domains become underivable the moment its last ref departs, so the departing refs' domains are recorded on the term at that moment; a deprecated or retired term stays curatable by exactly the people who owned it. The rule is one line: a term's domains are its refs' domains while it has refs, and its recorded domains otherwise. AUTHORITY IS ANY, NOT ALL: reading a term requires ANY of its domains to be within the caller's ``roles.domain_access``, and CURATING it requires the same. This deliberately breaks the symmetry with REQ-1531's ``require_domains``, which requires ALL: that rule guards acts reaching DATA in two domains, whereas a term definition is prose about a concept both domains already reference; editing it exposes and changes nothing in the other domain. Requiring all would leave a shared term curatable only by someone holding every domain it touches, an unsolvable deadlock manufactured by a name collision. THE ESCAPE HATCH: when two domains genuinely mean different things by one phrase, the answer is coordination, and failing that a SPLIT: create a term and move the refs to it with POST /admin/glossary/refs/move. That machinery already exists, and the split survives the next derivation because ``sync_table_refs`` leaves a held ref alone when its term is curated, so the new term must be given a definition, or the ref drifts back on the next registration. NO DOMAINS IS NOT NO ACCESS: a term with an empty domain set is UNSCOPED and reachable by any holder of the glossary rights; creating an abstract term in multi-domain mode therefore requires at least one domain, so an empty set cannot be minted as a way around the gate. THE NAVBAR FILTER IS A VIEW PREFERENCE, NOT AUTHORITY: the glossary list is filtered by the domains checked in the nav bar, passed as a ``domains`` query parameter, and that selection INTERSECTS with the caller's domain access and can never widen it: unchecking a box hides terms, checking every box does not reveal a term the role may not see, and the server answers 403 on a term outside the role's domains whatever the checkboxes say. SINGLE-DOMAIN MODE: where a domain gates nothing, this gate does nothing either, exactly as every other domain gate behaves.

Description: A GLOSSARY TERM IS OWNED, NOT MERELY REACHABLE. Domain reach alone made every curator a curator of every term they could see, so the terms that matter most -- the ones the whole org shares -- were the ones anybody could rewrite. Three rules replace that, over a new capability ``org_glossary_rw``. THE ORG'S GLOSSARY OWNER: ``org_glossary_rw`` curates ANY term in the org whatever its domains and whoever authored it, and is alone in being able to place a term in a domain it holds no other claim on. It is seeded to org_admin ALONE, not to modeler: modeler curates the model but does not override another curator's authorship. It widens what a curator may do rather than opening the surface, so a holder carries ``glossary_read`` and ``glossary_rw`` as well. THE ENTERPRISE SCOPE: a term may be scoped to ``"*"``, meaning the whole org: everyone holding ``glossary_read`` may READ it, and only ``org_glossary_rw`` may declare the scope, lift it, or change the term. ``"*"`` is EXCLUSIVE -- ``["*", "sales"]`` is refused 400, because a term is the whole org's or a named set of domains', never both -- and it is declarable on ABSTRACT terms only, since a rooted term derives its scope from its refs. THE AUTHOR LOCK: once a term has an AUTHOR, only that author or ``org_glossary_rw`` may change it. An EXPERT is a contact, not an owner: naming a colleague as someone to ask must never be a hostile act, so ``kind='expert'`` confers nothing and the lock keys on ``kind='author'`` alone. Adding or removing a steward of either kind is itself a curation act, gated the same way: a claim on a term is a privilege act, not a free one. WHERE A TERM MAY BE PLACED: a caller may declare only the domains in which they hold ``glossary_rw``, resolved PER CAPABILITY: an identity's domain_access is unioned over the roles that actually carry the named right, never over all its roles, or role A's right in one domain would compose with role B's domain into a grant nobody made. THE COST, ACCEPTED: a term whose authors have all left the org is frozen to everyone but ``org_glossary_rw``. That is what the override exists for. THE TWO STARS NEVER MEET: ``"*"`` on a role's domain_access is unlimited AUTHORITY; ``"*"`` as a term's scope is unlimited MEMBERSHIP. They are different tables and opposite directions and are never read across; creating a domain literally named ``"*"`` is refused so the two readings cannot collide. THE PICKER: an author or expert is CHOSEN from the org's roster, never typed. A mistyped user id would attribute the term to nobody and, for an author, lock every curator out of it.

Description: AN INVITATION ADMITS A NUMBER OF PEOPLE, NOT A PERSON. A "Try it Out" link on a public page is addressed to nobody and redeemed by everybody, and it is the SAME object as the addressed invitation -- an org, a role, an expiry, a creator to attribute it to, a revoke door -- differing only in how many redemptions it admits. So the count is a COLUMN and not a second feature: ``max_uses`` defaults to 1, which is exactly the invitation that already existed, and NULL means unlimited. ``uses`` counts what has been taken; ``used_at``/``used_by`` remain and now name the LAST redemption rather than the only one. WHERE THE CEILING IS ENFORCED: the claim is a single SQL statement that increments ``uses`` and repeats the ceiling in its own WHERE, returning the row it claimed. Two people clicking the same link at once both read ``uses`` before either wrote it, so an in-Python increment would let both through; a redemption whose claim returns no row lost the race and admits nobody, and anything it already provisioned is released. ONE PREDICATE: my-invites, the invite preview, both redemption paths and revoke all ask the same question and ask it through one clause, because five hand-written copies is how they stop agreeing. The two differ only in field values. WHICH ORG ISSUES THE PUBLIC LINK: the anonymous "Try it Out" link is minted by the org named ``sandbox``, an ordinary tenant org like any other. It is named rather than left to the operator because the org id is what every visitor's schema, Redis ACL and audit row is keyed by, and a demo issued from a customer-bearing org would seat strangers beside that customer's data. WHAT EACH POLICY REQUIRES: ``per_visitor`` without ``env_ttl_seconds`` would leave an environment nothing will ever reap, and ``shared`` without ``env_name`` seats nobody anywhere; both are refused by CheckConstraint, and mirrored app-side ONLY so the inviter gets a 400 naming the missing field instead of the 500 an integrity error becomes. ORDERING: the environment is minted BEFORE the membership names it, because a membership written first is unpinned for the length of provisioning and an unpinned member is served production. The price is that the loser of a race for the last redemption has already provisioned a schema, so it is retired again, branch and all. A ``shared`` environment is NEVER retired by a failed redemption: the org published it and other people are working in it. ONE PROVISIONING SEQUENCE: reserve, provision, deploy the model, start the branch, roll every part of it back on any failure. It is shared with the admin endpoint rather than re-derived, because the ordering is the part that must not diverge. The GUARD is not shared: the endpoint requires a right in the org, while the invitation IS the authorization, granted when the org minted the link.

That link sits on the sign-in page of every hosted deployment, so an org a person remembered to create by hand is an org some deployment is missing, and a redemption that arrives at a missing org fails in front of the stranger the invite was for. It is therefore seeded the way the bootstrap org is: by the lifespan, idempotently, on every boot. ORDINARY IN EVERY OTHER RESPECT. It gets the same ``provision_org`` build a self-service org gets, the demo data set seeded into it (an empty sandbox is nothing to try), the shared engine lane, and the Starter plan's ceilings: what a visitor tries is the plan the platform sells. WHAT IT IS NOT IS SOLD. Nobody buys the sandbox, so the checkout gate a commercial deployment puts in front of org creation (REQ-1476) is not in this path. Routing it through that gate would leave it parked at ``awaiting_checkout`` waiting for a subscription webhook that never comes. For the same reason its plan cannot be set by a subscription, and the ``trial`` an org row opens at would EXPIRE the one org that must never stop answering; a commerce seam puts it on Starter directly and leaves ``subscription_status`` NULL, because there is no commercial relationship to describe and the query path caps off the plan alone. ANY UNFINISHED STATE IS REBUILT. A row at ``provisioning`` is a build that died with its process, and one at ``failed`` or ``awaiting_checkout`` is an org the platform still owes its visitors. All three are taken back to ``provisioning`` and rebuilt, and only ``ready`` is left alone. The build is spawned as the create path's own background task rather than awaited, so a boot does not block for the minute a cold shard takes to wake; ``provisioning_state`` is where its progress is read. OWNERLESS BY CONSTRUCTION. ``created_by`` is NULL because there is no account to grant org_admin to: its members arrive by redeeming the open invite, and the role that invite carries is ``sandbox`` (REQ-1597). THE SWITCH IS THE COMMERCE SEAM, not an environment variable of its own. The sandbox exists to hand a stranger the product the platform SELLS, so the deployments that need one are exactly the deployments that sell it, and a self-hosted install has no public sign-in page, no open invite on it, and no reason to carry a spare org's schema.

THE DEPLOYMENT'S ADMINISTRATORS MAY USE THE SANDBOX ORG. The sandbox (REQ-1598) is a tenant org like any other, and platform_admin confers NOTHING inside a tenant org. It is stripped from the resolved assignment set there (REQ-1297), and everyone, operators included, is confined to the orgs they are a member of (REQ-1327). An operator answering for what the public "Try it Out" link shows a stranger would therefore be unable to open the org it admits them to. So they are seated in it THE ORDINARY WAY, exactly as the platform-admin claimant is seated in the bootstrap org (REQ-1296): a membership on the admin plane and a role assignment inside the sandbox's own schema. THE ROLE IS org_admin, NOT sandbox: an operator has to reach the environments, the members and the settings a visitor's role deliberately withholds (REQ-1597). THE MEMBERSHIP IS UNPINNED: the env pin (REQ-1596) is what confines a stranger to the environment minted for them, and an operator is not a stranger. RECONCILED FROM BOTH ENDS, so no boot leaves an administrator outside the org. The list of administrators is read from the ROOT org's schema, which is the whole list; platform_admin is only ever conferred there. Seating runs when the sandbox's build finishes (the moment its schema exists), on every later boot that finds the org ready, and on every conferral of a role thereafter: the super-admin claim and either invitation path. The conferral hook does not ask WHICH role was granted: a gate on a role name is exactly what REQ-1337 forbids, and the answer is already in the assignments the seating reads. It is a no-op, never an error, for a deployment with no sandbox org and for one whose sandbox is still building.

AN ENVIRONMENT MAY BE GIVEN AWAY FOR A SPAN OF USE RATHER THAN A SPAN OF TIME. REQ-1523's expires_at is a FIXED deadline: it stands where it was written and nothing moves it, which is right for a branch cut for a named piece of work. It is wrong for an environment handed to a visitor by an invitation, where the promise is "yours until you walk away". An hour of work must not end it, and an hour of quiet must. So an environment carries an OPTIONAL idle_ttl_seconds, and a value there makes its expiry SLIDING: the serving path pushes the deadline out by that many seconds each time the environment actually serves a request, which is the last point at which the routing knows the environment was reached. NULL is REQ-1523's fixed deadline, unchanged; being used is no argument against it. THE RENEWAL IS BOUNDED, not per request: it writes only when less than half the TTL remains, which holds the writes to one per half-TTL and still leaves the environment at least that long to be used again. A row written per request would put an UPDATE on the serving path for no further guarantee. THE REFUSAL COMES FIRST: an environment already past its deadline is refused rather than renewed, because otherwise the request that arrived one second late would be the one that moved the deadline and it could never arrive. The reaper (REQ-1523) drops the environment on its next sweep either way. A per_visitor invitation (REQ-1595) passes its env_ttl_seconds through as the idle allowance, so the hour it names is an hour of DISUSE.

EVERY ORG_ADMIN MAY MINT AN ENVIRONMENT-PROVISIONING INVITATION FROM THEIR OWN TEAM PAGE. The open link (REQ-1594) and the per-visitor environment (REQ-1595) are not a sandbox arrangement (REQ-1598). The sandbox is only the first user of a feature every org_admin has: hand someone a link that seats them in a private environment deployed from production, so they see the real model without being able to reach the org, and lose it again once they stop using it. The org_admin's own invite surface (REQ-1266) therefore carries three further controls: WHO THE LINK ADMITS (a single invitee, or anyone holding it, an unlimited ceiling), WHAT THE REDEEMER WORKS IN (the org itself, or a fresh environment of their own), and HOW LONG AN UNUSED ENVIRONMENT SURVIVES (a span of DISUSE, REQ-1600, defaulting to one hour). The TTL control appears only for the per-visitor policy, which is the only policy it means anything under. THE INVITE LIST REPORTS WHAT EACH LINK IS: its redemptions against its ceiling, and what it hands its redeemer. AN INVITATION IS SPENT WHEN IT HAS NO REDEMPTIONS LEFT: "used_at is set" stopped describing that the moment a link could admit more than one person, so copy and revoke are offered against the ceiling and not against the first redemption. Nothing here is gated on which org the org_admin administers: the server scopes create, list and revoke to the caller's active org already.

A ROLE MAY BE SHOWN A RIGHT IT DOES NOT HOLD. Alongside its capabilities, a role carries a DEMONSTRATED list: rights it is deliberately denied whose surfaces are still rendered, labelled as part of the production system rather than removed from the page. The sandbox role (REQ-1597) is the first holder: it is org_admin minus four rights, and a visitor holding it is being shown the product, so deleting those four surfaces would advertise a smaller product than the one being sold. The two lists are disjoint by construction -- a right the role holds is used, never explained -- and the client unions them across the acting roles the same way it unions capabilities, subtracting everything actually held. THE DEMONSTRATION IS REACHABLE, NOT A DEAD BADGE: a nav entry into a demonstrated region stays clickable, the route resolves, and the PAGE carries a banner saying what it is while its contents render inert (aria-disabled, dimmed, keyboard- and pointer-refused by the browser itself). An inline control demonstrates in place instead: greyed, badged, and explained on hover. NOTHING HERE IS AN AUTHORIZATION CHANGE: the server refuses every call behind a demonstrated surface exactly as it refuses a denied one, and the client reads a rights list off the role, never a role id (REQ-1337).

Description: SIGNING OUT ENDS THE SESSION WHERE THE SESSION LIVES. An org subdomain holds no session of its own (REQ-1348). It borrows the bearer from the control plane through the relay iframe, and the identity-provider session that mints that bearer is stored in the control-plane origin, which no script on the org origin can reach. A sign-out performed locally therefore ended nothing: it cleared this origin, reloaded, and the boot borrowed the same live session straight back, so the user stayed signed in. The org host instead clears its own borrowed state and hands the browser to the control plane's /logout, which is an ENTRY POINT rather than a route. The boot answers it before React mounts, so no signed-in query is issued during the sign-out it exists to perform. There the identity session is settled first and only then torn down: on a cold document load no user has been read back out of browser storage yet, and a sign-out issued before that lands on nobody. What is cleared is unchanged (REQ-1326): token, org, role and the persisted snapshot.

AN INVITE LISTING IS SCOPED TO THE ACTIVE ORG, FOR EVERY CALLER. An invitation token is a live credential: it hands whoever holds it an account and a role in the org that issued it. Listing and revoking are therefore bounded by the org the request is bound to -- the org named by the Host or the org header -- and not by how much authority the caller has. cross_org (REQ-1337) is the right to act in any org one at a time, never a right to read every org's invitations at once; read that way it put one tenant's live tokens on the page of the tenant the operator had selected. A caller bound to no org at all (the platform plane, before an org is chosen) is scoped to nothing rather than to everything, and a caller without user_management is refused as before.

PLATFORM_ADMIN MAY ACT ACROSS ORGS BUT MAY NOT READ AN ORG'S DATA AT REST WITHOUT ITS OWN MEMBERSHIP THERE. cross_org (REQ-1337) is authority to act in any org for support and recovery: issue an invite, add or remove a member, reset a policy. It is not a grant to browse who is in an org, its join policy, its branding, or its full config export; those are that org's data, and platform_admin sees them only where it also holds a real org-scoped assignment in that org (seeded, the sandbox org, or a REQ-1303 recovery grant taken there), the same gate every other caller already passes. Reading them via the bare cross_org right, with no membership anywhere in the target org, is refused.

redeem_env resolves a per_visitor environment before it mints one. An invitation token is written to localStorage the moment the login page first sees it in the address bar, and redeemed from that memory rather than from the tab's query string. OnboardOrgPage - where the membership gate routes an account belonging to no org - spends a still-unredeemed invitation on arrival, once, opening in join mode with the token in the field so a server-side refusal leaves it in front of the person holding it. The redemption is dropped only when it succeeds, or when /register redeemed it server-side.

The environment switcher reports the membership's pinned environment (REQ-1596) rather than the name this browser stored, and offers a confined membership no other row. A pinned membership is served from its own environment whatever the request names, and naming any other - prod included - is refused with env.switch_forbidden. Reading "the stored selection, or prod" made the header name prod over a sandbox visitor who was being served their ephemeral branch all along, while the menu beside it listed other visitors' ephemeral branches - names one visitor should not be told and rows that answer 403 if chosen. The control plane is never auto-selected into a sandbox visitor's ephemeral environment. The sandbox auto-select (REQ-1602) derives an environment from the caller's user id, and a platform administrator is not a visitor - they hold an assignment in the org's prod schema and nothing at all in a visitor's branch, so being served one leaves them with an empty capability set and every admin surface in their own deployment refuses them. The fact cannot be recovered where the selection happens - identity.roles is a list of claim STRINGS, so probing each for a capabilities attribute answered "not the control plane" for every caller alive, and the acting capability set cannot answer either because inside a tenant org the control-plane roles have already been stripped out of it (REQ-1327). AuthMiddleware, the one place that reads the platform plane, settles it and publishes it on the request; both the role read and the request binding pass it in explicitly, so the two can never disagree about who is being served what.

An environment that expires owns its own copies of every file-backed source it was given. A source's identity is the same in every environment - copy_model carries the row across with its id intact, and registered tables, lineage, policies and the materialized table name all key off that id - so an environment created with its bindings carried points at the very file prod points at, and a write through it is a write to prod's data. Creating an environment that carries an expiry therefore forks each file-backed source into a directory the environment owns and rebinds the copy, so a visitor may write freely and nothing outside the environment moves. Retiring the environment discards the directory through the one retire door, before the registry row that names the environment is forgotten. Environments without an expiry are untouched by this - an environment is a first-class place and is free to point at any source, prod's included; it is expiry, not the environment, that says the data is disposable.

An environment that expires withholds the administrator's mutation bypass. Within its own semantic layer a visitor holding org_admin may do anything - drop sources, drop tables, change roles, issue further invitations - because all of it is contained by the environment and goes away with it. What must not travel is a write that reaches through to the source: a GraphQL mutation or an UPDATE/DELETE that lands in a system the environment merely points at. The administrator's bypass exists so an org_admin is not stopped by a table's write policy; in an environment carrying an expiry, that bypass is not granted, so a mutation is authorized by the table's declared write rights alone and an unwritable table stays unwritable no matter who is asking. The runtime decides this once, when it is built, from the environment's expiry, and exposes it read-only so no request can change it; AppState routes the flag to the active runtime so every mutation door reads the same answer.

Where an environment's data lands is part of its address, and what it owns alone is removed when it retires. A landed replica is named from the source id, which every environment shares, so an unqualified materialization store has every environment writing the same table - and the store is a different DSN from the tenant pool, so dropping an environment's tenant schemas never reached it. Two things close that. First, ${scope:ENV} and ${scope:ORG} join the existing ${provider:reference} grammar as a scope provider, answering where a resolution is happening rather than what a secret is; the provider is named scope and not env because ${env:...} already means the deployment's process environment. It is expanded over a source's row when the runtime is built, where the environment is known, and only the scope half is expanded so a credential in the same string still resolves at its own use point. Second, every non-prod environment lands its replicas in a namespace of its own - mat_env_<name> - unless the store's own address already names the environment, in which case the store is the author's and its default schema is right. A schema-less store (sqlite) whose address does not name the environment is refused rather than silently shared, and the error names the template as the fix. Retiring an environment drops the schema its existence created; a schema this rule did not name - prod's mat, an author's templated store - is out of reach from that path by construction.

The federation lineage graph (REQ-1161) is read through a role. The role is an analytic lens, not a redaction - an analyst holding several roles switches between them to see where each role's data comes from. The columns the selected roles can query seed the graph; the walk from those seeds runs upstream and unrestricted, so every ancestor of a seed is shown in full whether or not the role could query it. What is reachable only downstream of the seeds belongs to another role's perspective and is cut. The domain filter restricts which relations may seed, never which may be an ancestor, so a chain crossing an unchecked domain is not severed.

Complete lineage covers every relation the platform can reach, not only those with a derivation in front of them. A registered table that nothing selects from and that selects from nothing still appears, as an isolated source node per column - its absence reads as "not reachable" rather than "not derived". Registered relations are also supplied to the parser as known relations so a bare table reference a view parse yields is stitched to the registered relation rather than standing as a second node for the same data; a bare name matching more than one registered relation is left unstitched rather than guessed.

A federation-wide graph carries more nodes than a column-per-node render can show, so it arrives collapsed - one node per relation, labelled with its column count - and expands per relation on click, with expand-all and collapse-all for the whole graph. Edges between two collapsed relations roll up into one edge carrying the count of columns it stands for. The same graph opens in a near-fullscreen modal, sharing the collapse state with the inline panel so opening it continues the trace rather than restarting it.

The role the lineage is read through is picked on the lineage form itself, not taken from the NavBar role picker. The two answer different questions - the NavBar picks which of the user's own roles they act as, the lineage picker picks whose data is being analysed - and the analytic use requires naming ANY role in the org, including roles the analyst does not hold. Because reading the federation through an arbitrary role discloses which columns that role can query, the perspective is gated by view_governance, the same right the visible_to / masking / grant columns carry. The gate is enforced on GET /admin/lineage/federation and the picker and Complete Lineage control are absent without it. No selection means every role.

Every row of a registered table is traceable in the graph to its table and domain. Each registered table outside the meta domain has a HAS_TABLE relationship to the node that represents it among the meta domain's registered tables, and a row's table and domain are read by following that relationship. HAS_TABLE is left out of variable-length paths unless the query names it.

The admin GraphQL allRelationships resolver synthesizes virtual HAS_TABLE relationship rows — one per non-meta registered table — linking each data-instance row to its registered_tables meta-definition row. These rows are computed at query time without schema migration, enabling the graph explorer's drag-and-drop feature to discover and wire HAS_TABLE relationships.

Boot-time eager landing for MATERIALIZED sources must create schema-only (zero-row) replica tables, not full data copies. Before creating a replica, check whether a matching replica with identical column metadata already exists in the target federation engine's store. If so, skip creation (idempotent no-op). Only when no existing matching replica is found should a DDL-only CREATE TABLE be issued. Actual row population remains under the existing poll/push refresh cadence, not boot. Applies uniformly to any federation engine (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Postgres, DuckDB, etc.). The fix belongs in the engine-agnostic boot_create()/ land_source_table() path, not in per-engine connector code, since Strategy.MATERIALIZED resolution and boot-time landing are already engine-agnostic. Post-boot column edits must reconcile the same way: editing a registered table's columns is saved as one whole-table metadata write (update_table), which already triggers reconcile_landed_tables() -> reconcile_duckdb_native() synchronously before the mutation returns (provisa/api/app.py:_rebuild_schemas -> app.py:1691). The reconciler always receives the complete new column list in a single call, never a per-column diff, and on drift RECREATES the landed table (DDL only, zero rows) rather than re-inserting data; data reland remains the refresh cadence's job, not the edit's.

A landed replica's shape includes its PRIMARY KEY. A SQLite file source's key columns are resolved from the file's own PRAGMA table_info at seed time (PRAGMA pk order), and the landing reconcile treats a difference between the store table's PRIMARY KEY and the registered key as drift, recreating the table, so a replica created before its key was known does not stay key-less for good.

A landed replica carries the landed model's keys, converged by the landing reconcile with the tables themselves and for every landed table regardless of Data Product membership: its declared PRIMARY KEY, and a FOREIGN KEY for each approved relationship whose two ends are landed and whose referenced columns are the referenced table's PRIMARY KEY (many-to-one on the source, one-to-many on the target, a junction relationship as one key per hop). Applied only on stores that hold constraints as informational metadata (Snowflake; Databricks and BigQuery when their terminals implement the hook); an enforcing store gets no FOREIGN KEY, since a REPLACE land would violate it. Idempotent: a matching PRIMARY KEY is left alone, a differing one replaced, an existing FOREIGN KEY of the same name skipped, and a provisa_fk_* constraint no relationship declares is withdrawn. A key the store cannot hold is withheld and logged with its reason, never emitted. Where the compiler's physical name is a VIEW over the replica, the view mirrors the keys as PRIMARY_KEY (1-based key position) and FOREIGN_KEY (referenced physical column) column TAGs, with stale key tags unset. The metadata export publishes no constraints.

The Snowflake federation engine owns its landing terminal: a non-attachable source's rows land in the engine URL's database under the store schema (mat for prod) as "<source>__<schema>__<table>", and the compiler's physical name for the source is a SECURE VIEW over that replica. The eager reconcile converges the replica's columns and PRIMARY KEY (drift on either recreates it) and creates the view when absent, replacing it only after a recreate; the per-fire land is REPLACE (delete + insert) or APPEND, CDC being refused. An MV's own store table converges and persists through the same terminal (replace, append, or upsert by MERGE). The engine's default materialization store is the engine URL itself, never the platform database.

A landed table's description and its columns' descriptions travel with the landed model: the landing reconcile writes them as COMMENTs onto the replica and onto the view that backs the compiler's physical name, for every landed table, and onto an MV's store table when that table is converged. A comment that already begins with the description is left standing (another writer may have extended it), and an empty description never erases one.

The stewards' tag assignments on tables and columns travel with the landed model as native TAGs in the PROVISA_GOVERNANCE namespace (value = the assignment's reason, else the tag id), set by the landing reconcile on every replica and its backing view and on an MV's store table when it is converged. A tag the model defines that sits on an object but is no longer assigned there is withdrawn; a tag of any other origin is never touched. The snowflake_horizon export no longer publishes model tags.

A Snowflake Horizon organization listing's data dictionary covers every member of the Data Product and every column: the dictionary is generated from the share, so membership is the share's SELECT grants, reconciled on each publish (a former member's grant is revoked). The manifest features the first five members in the share's primary database (Snowflake's cap, one database), each with its real object kind, and declares the data preview's has_pii and pii_columns from the masking rules on member columns. Provisa owns the manifest: after the CREATE, the live manifest is read back and replaced with ALTER LISTING when it differs, so an edit made in Snowsight does not survive the next publish.

On a Databricks engine the landed model's keys, descriptions and tags converge with the landed Delta tables in the landing reconcile and on MV refresh, as on Snowflake (REQ-1652, REQ-1654, REQ-1655): the registration's PRIMARY KEY is declared inline (key columns NOT NULL, which Unity Catalog requires), relationship FOREIGN KEYs are added as informational constraints, descriptions are COMMENTs, and tag assignments are Unity Catalog tags keyed provisa_governance:<tag id>. A drifted key recreates the table; a withdrawn relationship or assignment drops its constraint or tag; keys and tags of any other origin are never touched. No view layer exists on Databricks, so the landed table itself carries everything.

BigQuery gains the eager landing terminal the other native stores have: the landing reconcile converges each landed table (DDL only, with its PRIMARY KEY NOT ENFORCED) at boot and on registration, and materialize_source converges before it loads. The landed model's metadata then follows REQ-1652/1654/1655: FOREIGN KEYs as NOT ENFORCED constraints, descriptions on the table and its columns through the client API, table tag assignments as labels keyed provisa_governance_<tag id> with the value folded to the label alphabet. A column tag has no BigQuery counterpart and is reported withheld. With the terminal in place the Analytics Hub data-product export, which requires it, runs for BigQuery.

The registration-time migration into the control-plane Postgres, its mtime stale loop and the remigrate mutation are removed: they were the eager copy of an older design, wrote to one store regardless of the engine, and on a self-only warehouse left the landed replica empty while the event loop read the source through the engine.

Description: A source node whose produce raises for any reason (an adapter whose endpoint refuses the connection, a store that rejects the land) is that node's outage, not the event loop's: the processor logs the traceback and records it exactly as an ABORT is recorded, an error event fanned to dependents, an ok=False stamp and the claim completed, and the tick goes on to the next node. A Great Expectations check can be extended with a Python function registered through the Commands surface under a new implementation kind (gx_check), bound the way a python command is (module:attr callable, or inline source under the MV preprocess sandbox). The function takes the check's arguments and returns the SQL predicate selecting the UNEXPECTED rows; at scan time the worker resolves the contract's type to that function, calls it with the expectation's kwargs and emits GX's UnexpectedRowsExpectation, so results land in the shipped envelope unchanged. The check catalog derives the builder's CheckKind from the function's signature — a `column` parameter means column scope, the remaining parameters become params typed from their annotations and defaults — so the panel offers the new type and its args with no UI change. A gx_check is never exposed as a GraphQL mutation or query; function dispatch refuses it. Row-level checks only; aggregate checks (a scalar expression plus a comparator) are a later shape.

The lineage DAG draws a relation as ONE box whose rows are its columns, the shape the SQL canvas (ERD) uses, with edges running row to row and labelled by the transform. Only the boxes are laid out (ELK layered, left to right); rows are pinned inside their box in a stable order and follow it when dragged. Intermediate computations are boxes too: a CTE or subquery keeps the relation name the lineage already gives it, and the statement's final projection lands in a "result" box, or the view/MV it defines when one is named. A collapsed relation shows its header only and its edges fold onto the box with a count. Columns no edge touches are not drawn; the box footer counts them ("+N unused"), so a wide table referenced by two columns stays two rows tall.

A data product's detail lineage is scoped to the product's member tables, their full upstream ancestry, and the tables one hop downstream of them. Data-quality results tables are not part of it even though they are members by inheritance (REQ-1443 clause 10). Every column of a member table is an output of the graph: columns the federation lineage never mentions are added as rows of their table, and all member columns ring as outputs.

A data product's detail lineage is drawn in swimlanes by distance from the product's member tables: "Output Ports" (the members, lane 0), "-1", "-2"… for contributors by longest upstream path (a lane exists only when a box occupies it), and "+1" for direct consumers. Lanes are ELK partitions, so boxes never cross them; dotted vertical rules and lane titles are part of the canvas and pan, zoom and export with it. A member table no edge touches still sits in lane 0. The panel shows the colour legend and a hover button opens the same graph in a 90% modal sharing the inline collapse state.

A `neo4j` source registers as a persisted query-API source. In the config file a `neo4j` source names host, port and database; each table under it carries `query_template` (the Cypher that produces its rows) and typed columns; `query_template` is forbidden under any other source type. Config load persists the source as an `api_sources` row (type `neo4j`) and each table as an `api_endpoints` row carrying `body_encoding`, `query_template` and `response_normalizer` (new columns), keyed by table name; the admin REST router (`POST /admin/sources/neo4j`, `POST /admin/sources/neo4j/{id}/tables`) persists the same rows instead of process-lifetime dicts. The startup loader restores those three columns, and the event loop lands a neo4j table through the same fetch chain as openapi. Endpoint shape: POST of the transaction-API envelope `{"statements": [{"statement": cypher}]}` to `/db/<database>/tx/commit` (body_encoding `neo4j_tx`), flattened by the `neo4j_tabular` normalizer, which refuses a response carrying errors. The control-plane metadata (`schema_org`) admits `neo4j` in the `api_sources` type check. The SQLite control plane is built from it, and a refused insert must surface: the shared upsert re-raises an INSERT the store refused when its fallback UPDATE matches no row, instead of treating every IntegrityError as a lost insert race.

Role inheritance is one parent per role (`parent_role_id`), resolved by walking the chain from the child up, and it covers the whole permission surface, not only capabilities and domain_access (REQ-215). Grants are unioned up the chain: a column's visible_to, writable_by and unmasked_to, and a metric's, function's or webhook's visible_to, hold for a role when they name it or any ancestor. RLS resolves per table with the child taking precedence: the nearest role in the chain that has a rule for the table (its own table rule, else its domain rule) supplies the one predicate that runs; an ancestor's rule is never ANDed or ORed with it. A masked column is masked for a role unless the role or an ancestor is in unmasked_to. rate_limit is inherited when the child sets none. The chain is materialized once per runtime build so every lookup stays keyed by the acting role id. A parent must be an existing role in the same org, may not be the role itself, and may not close a cycle; each is refused at save with the reason. `parent_role_id` is exposed on the admin GraphQL role type and input, on the roles REST router, and on the Security page's role form as "Inherits from". Deleting a role that other roles inherit from is refused naming them.

The reference is what the admin API may expose; the credential is not, and nothing reads it back by name.

THE GROUP-BY NODES PROJECTION'S ``?include=`` RESOLVES A DOT-PATH AT ANY DEPTH, NOT JUST ONE RELATIONSHIP HOP. ``assignment.employee.id`` (a relationship, then its own relationship, then a column) previously 400'd with "Unknown field 'employee.id' on relationship 'assignment'". The handler split only the first dot and looked the remainder up as a single column name of the immediate relation, which a nested relationship's own field never is. It now recurses through relationships exactly as far as the path goes, translating each physical segment (REQ-1417) to the schema's GQL spelling at that depth, mirroring the recursion gRPC's ``include`` (query_ir::_insert_include_path, REQ-1405/REQ-1408) already does; one plan drives every surface. The JSON:API Explorer's Include picker offers two levels of relationship (a table's direct relationships, plus theirs) so the common case is checkboxes rather than a hand-typed path; a path past what the picker offers is still accepted by the backend.

THE EXPLORE/SQL PAGE'S METRICS/FACTS/DIMENSIONS GROUPS HONOR THE SAME CHECKED-DOMAINS FILTER THE SCHEMA TREE DOES. The SchemaBrowser sidebar's SCHEMA section already filtered its table tree by the domain checkboxes at the top of the page, but the Metrics/Facts/Dimensions groups above it read the unfiltered table and metric lists straight from the hooks. Unchecking a domain hid its tables from one panel while its facts, dimensions, and derived metrics kept showing in the other. A metric attributes to the fact table it was derived from (``Metric.fromFact``); a hand-authored metric (``fromFact`` null, no ``FROM`` a fact metric reads from) has no domain to filter by and stays visible under every selection, the same way a table with no ``domainId`` does.

THE GRAPH EXPLORER'S CANVAS TRACKS ITS CONTAINER'S SIZE, NOT JUST ITS SIZE AT MOUNT. The `.gf-canvas` element is `width/height:100%` — the CSS layout is already responsive — but Cytoscape reads its own canvas pixel dimensions once when the instance is created and never again on its own. Without something to tell it otherwise, the rendered graph keeps whatever size it was born with as the browser window resizes or the surrounding panel reflows, clipping or floating in dead space. A `ResizeObserver` on the canvas container calls `cy.resize()` on every size change, the same pattern the lineage DAG (REQ-1401 area) already used and the Graph/Cypher explorer never had.

KafkaNotificationProvider, WebSocketNotificationProvider, and subscriptions.cdc_landing.consume_cdc_into_store all existed and were individually unit-tested, but no boot-time code ever built a real provider and started the drain loop, so a registered kafka/websocket source landed nothing, forever, with one buried log line. `provisa/events/push_wiring.py`'s `wire_push_listeners` (called from app.py's lifespan alongside `wire_event_loop`, and `shutdown_push_listeners` on app shutdown) closes it: for every registered table on a kafka/websocket source, it resolves the landing target (`engine.backend.landing_target`), requires a primary key (CDC upsert/delete needs one to identify rows), builds the right `NotificationProvider` via the existing `subscriptions.registry.get_provider` factory (kafka: bootstrap_servers from `Source.host`, topic from `Table.live.kafka.topic`; websocket: `Source.base_url` when set, else derived `ws://host:port` — the same override-else-derive shape REQ-1730's DuckDBAirportConnector/neo4j_config_from_source already use), and starts `consume_cdc_into_store` as its own asyncio task, independent of the poll/MV tick loop (CDC upsert/delete-by-PK is not expressible through the generic `land_source_table` write face — store_writer.py's own docstring: "Hard-delete CDC is the separate streaming path"). Idempotent re-wire (a node already running is skipped); best-effort per table (one misconfigured push table is logged and skipped, never aborts wiring for every other one). Folded into the same pass: an optional DEBOUNCE on `consume_cdc_into_store` (`debounce_quiet`/`debounce_max_delay`, the identical deadline formula REQ-963 already uses for live-MV recompute — `min(last_event + quiet, first_event + max_delay)` — but an independent knob on the CDC streaming path, not the poll/MV tick loop), plus the operator-facing UI surface for the latency/throughput tradeoff: two new NumberInputs (`push-debounce-quiet`/`push-debounce-max-delay`) in `LiveDeliveryFieldset.tsx`, shown whenever the effective change signal is a push signal (kafka/debezium/native), mirroring `MaterializedViewPanels`' existing `mvDebounceQuiet`/`mvDebounceMaxDelay` UI pattern exactly. Two new `Table`/`TableInput` fields, `push_debounce_quiet`/`push_debounce_max_delay` (server_default 0/5, additive columns; REQ-1338/1339's `add_missing_columns` reconciles them into any pre-existing database at next boot, no migration needed). A background task pumps `provider.watch()` into a BOUNDED internal queue (`queue_maxsize`, default 10,000) rather than wrapping the async generator's `__anext__()` directly in `asyncio.wait_for`. A timed-out `wait_for` on the generator itself injects `CancelledError` into whatever the generator was awaiting, permanently killing the stream after the first debounce timeout (found and fixed via a live regression test before this shipped). The queue bound IS the backpressure mechanism: once full, the pump's `queue.put()` blocks until a flush drains it, stalling `provider.watch()` itself. For Kafka this stalls aiokafka's own internal fetch behind the unconsumed `async for`; for WebSocket it stops reading the socket, ordinary TCP flow control back to the sender. The auto-commit/crash-window limitation originally documented here is closed by REQ-1734: KafkaNotificationProvider now runs with auto-commit off and only advances its offset via `provider.ack()`, called from `cdc_landing._flush()` after a batch is durably landed.

Description: Closes the auto-commit crash-window limitation REQ-1733 documented (and deliberately did not silently claim solved): KafkaNotificationProvider previously ran with aiokafka's default auto-commit, a 5s timer gated on "yielded to the app," not "landed." REQ-1733's debounce/backpressure buffering widens the window between a message being yielded and actually durably applied, so a crash in that window could lose a message the consumer group had already advanced past on restart. `NotificationProvider` (subscriptions/base.py) gains `ChangeEvent.ack_token` (opaque, provider-specific position identity — Kafka: `(topic, partition, offset)`; `None` for providers with no offset concept — websocket, mongo, postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY) and an `ack(events)` method, no-op by default. `KafkaNotificationProvider` now constructs its `AIOKafkaConsumer` with `enable_auto_commit=False`, stamps `ack_token` on every yielded event, and implements `ack()` to commit each `(topic, partition)`'s HIGHEST offset among the given events (+1, the Kafka commit convention), never "wherever the consumer currently is," which could be past other events still sitting unflushed in a caller's debounce buffer. `subscriptions/cdc_landing.py`'s `_flush()` calls `await provider.ack(buffer)` immediately after `apply_cdc` durably lands that buffer, with exactly that flush's events, so the offset only ever advances past a message once it is actually in the store.

Closes the top-priority findings of a full Add-Source/Register-Table UI audit across all 54 SourceTypes (5 parallel agent audits, one per source-type family): `federation_hints_json` — the designated channel for warehouse extras a source's host/port/database/username/password can't carry (Snowflake account/warehouse/role, Databricks http_path, BigQuery service-account credentials) — was captured into `SourceFormFields.tsx`'s `authFields` React state but never included in `SourcesPage.tsx`'s submit payload, and had no counterpart on the READ side at all (`SourceType`, the GraphQL object type, had no `federation_hints_json` field), so even a correct fix would silently lose those extras the moment a source was reopened for editing. Concretely: Databricks (http_path is hard-required by DatabricksDriver) was entirely unusable; Snowflake's password-auth mode never submitted username/password at all (AuthUserPass binds to authFields, not `form`, outside the SIMPLE_RDBMS family); Snowflake's "Warehouse/Database" field was a single combined text input with no code ever splitting it; BigQuery's service-account key path was collected but dropped, silently falling back to Application Default Credentials. Also closes a related, structurally identical bug for delta_lake/iceberg: their "Warehouse Path" field wrote to `form.database`, but `source.path` (the only field their DuckDB connectors actually read) was only ever submitted for `FILE_SOURCES = {sqlite, csv, parquet}`, so `source.path` was always submitted `null` for these two types regardless of what was typed. Compounding it, their S3 storage credentials were written into `mappingJson`, while the only code that turns credentials into a DuckDB SECRET (`_s3_secret_ddl`) reads `source.federation_hints`, a second, independent field-routing mismatch. And a THIRD bug, found only by reading the connectors themselves: `DuckDBDeltaConnector`/`DuckDBIcebergConnector` never called `_s3_secret_ddl` in the first place (only `DuckDBParquetConnector` did), so even with both routing bugs fixed, no SECRET DDL would ever have been emitted for an S3-backed delta_lake/iceberg source. Fix, backend: `DuckDBDeltaConnector.details()`/`DuckDBIcebergConnector.details()` now call `_s3_secret_ddl(source)` and include `secret_ddl` in their returned dict when the source has S3 credentials, mirroring the existing `DuckDBParquetConnector` pattern exactly. `SourceType` (the GraphQL read type) gained `federation_hints_json: str = "{}"`, populated in `_source_from_row` from the `sources.federation_hints` JSONB column (which already existed; the write side always persisted it, only the read side never exposed it back). Fix, frontend: `SourcesPage.tsx`'s submit path now builds a `federationHints` object per type (Snowflake: warehouse/schema/role; Databricks: http_path; BigQuery: credentials_path; delta_lake/ iceberg: access_key_id/secret_access_key/endpoint when storage-auth is "aws") and includes it as `federationHintsJson` in the mutation payload, and merges Snowflake password-mode / Databricks token-mode `authFields` into the payload's `username`/`password`. The edit-load path (opening an existing source for editing) now parses `federationHintsJson` back into `authFields`/ `authType` for these five types, so editing a source no longer wipes its own extras on save, the same round-trip `mappingJson` already had for hive/google_sheets/sharepoint/splunk. `SourceFormFields.tsx`'s Snowflake "Warehouse/Database" combined field is split into separate Database/Warehouse/Schema/Role inputs; Databricks gained a required "SQL Warehouse HTTP Path" field it previously had no input for at all; delta_lake/iceberg's "Warehouse Path" field now writes to `form.path` instead of `form.database`. Explicitly NOT fixed (no backend driver support exists for these auth modes; wiring them would not make them functional, only hide that they don't work): Snowflake key-pair/OAuth auth (SnowflakeDriver only implements plain password auth) and Databricks OAuth2 M2M (DatabricksDriver only implements personal-access-token auth via the `password` slot). These UI options remain present but non-functional, tracked as a follow-up requiring new backend auth support, not a wiring fix.
