The first demo to use it is weblogs (demo/named/weblogs/): a web shop behind nginx with its Postgres, nginx's JSON access log and the database's jsonlog read as Logs sources and joined to the shop's tables and to each other by the request id nginx generates.

MongoDB sources can optionally use MongoDB's native change streams ($changeStream) to achieve near-real-time freshness for materialized and cached data, instead of relying solely on TTL-based polling refresh. (Amended 2026-09-24, DEPLOYMENT PATH CONFIRMED:) Change streams require Mongo to run as a replica set; a bare standalone instance cannot serve them. Confirmed workable as a single-node replica set (no extra containers): `command: ["mongod", "--replSet", "rs0", "--bind_ip_all"]` plus a self-initiating healthcheck (`rs.status()`, falling back to `rs.initiate()` on first run); see demo/named/perf/docker-compose.yml's mongodb service, now our standard approach for every Mongo service in a named demo, not just this one. One real gotcha: the replica-set member is registered under a hostname only resolvable on the same Docker network (the Compose service name), so any consumer connecting from outside it (a host-machine driver via the published port, or Provisa's own connector under --native) must set directConnection=true to skip topology discovery; see generate_mongo.py's MongoClient call for the pattern. Whether Provisa's own mongodb connector needs the same directConnection flag to reach a replica-set-backed source is unverified. Flag it if sources register but queries against them fail to connect (see fragment.yaml's bench-mongodb comment).

pgwire SQL compiler recognizes and handles textual SQL `DECLARE CURSOR ... FOR <query>`, `FETCH FORWARD N FROM <cursor>`, and `CLOSE <cursor>` statements, translating them into the same portal-based streaming mechanism that the extended-query protocol (Bind/Execute/PortalSuspend) already provides internally. Clients relying on textual cursor SQL syntax — including psycopg2's named/server-side cursor feature (`conn.cursor(name="...")`) and some BI tools — receive true streaming without protocol-level fallback or failure. (Amended 2026-09-25, IMPLEMENTED — DIFFERENT MECHANISM THAN PROPOSED:) Built as its own SQL-text dispatch in ProvisaHandler._process_query_stmts (alongside the existing COPY/CTAS/DDL keyword regexes covering DECLARE/FETCH/MOVE/CLOSE, not just FETCH FORWARD), NOT by routing through the extended-query protocol's Bind/Execute/PortalSuspend machinery — that mechanism is keyed by wire portal name and driven by the binary Execute message's row-limit field, which a simple-protocol FETCH statement has no way to supply. Instead, DECLARE's inner SELECT runs through the normal governed pipeline (ctx.execute_sql -> ProvisaSession.execute_sql), and its row generator (ProvisaQueryResult.rows()) is drained lazily. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1862, 2026-09-25 -- rows were unconditionally buffered forever on the session's per-cursor _CursorState regardless of SCROLL, which OOMs a forward-only FETCH through a large result. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] and buffered on the session's per-cursor _CursorState as it's read (_cursor_move), which is what lets FETCH support PRIOR/BACKWARD/ABSOLUTE/RELATIVE/FIRST/LAST — not just FORWARD N — without a rewindable engine cursor underneath. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] pgwire has no BEGIN/COMMIT state machine (ProvisaSession.in_transaction() is hardcoded False), so every DECLAREd cursor behaves as if WITH HOLD: it lives on the connection's ProvisaSession until CLOSE/CLOSE ALL or disconnect (session.close() releases every still-open cursor's underlying stream via a new ProvisaQueryResult.close()). (Amended 2026-09-25, MEMORY-BOUNDED NO-SCROLL CURSORS:) The unconditional buffering above was a live OOM bug: a plain forward-only FETCH through a large result (e.g. an 80M-row table) accumulated every row ever pulled into _CursorState.buffer, unboundedly, in Python-object memory, the same failure class as a 31GB-RSS oom-killer case found in a separate benchmark harness this session. Fixed by threading real PostgreSQL SCROLL semantics through the cursor: _DECLARE_CURSOR_RE now captures a named "scroll" group for SCROLL / NO SCROLL, and _handle_declare_cursor sets _CursorState.scrollable from it (default False, i.e. NO SCROLL, the same as PostgreSQL's own default when neither keyword is given). A SCROLL cursor keeps the full buffer as before, accepting that memory cost as the correct price of explicit backward/ absolute navigation. A NO SCROLL cursor only allows "forward" and "relative" with a non-negative count; _cursor_move trims cs.buffer[:cs.pos] and resets cs.pos to 0 after every forward step, so memory stays bounded to roughly one FETCH batch instead of the whole result. PRIOR/BACKWARD/ABSOLUTE/FIRST/LAST/negative-RELATIVE against a NO SCROLL cursor now raise _CursorNotScrollableError, sent to the client as SQLSTATE 55000 (object_not_in_prerequisite_state), matching real PostgreSQL's own rejection of backward FETCH on a NO SCROLL cursor, rather than silently returning wrong or truncated results.

When routing a pgwire DIRECT-route query to a PostgreSQL source, avoid decode/re-encode overhead by forwarding raw DataRow wire messages directly to the downstream client, exploiting the fact that masking/RLS is always pre-applied in the compiled SQL.  (Amended 2026-09-29, uvloop incompatibility:) Live-confirmed the raw-socket-driving technique (open_raw_connection's transport.pause_reading() + .dup() + manual loop.sock_sendall/sock_recv) does not work under uvloop: the dup'd socket is still a uvloop.loop.PseudoSocket, whose .send() is a deliberate stub that unconditionally raises TypeError: transport sockets do not support send() method. It is 100% reproducible on every passthrough-eligible query when the process event loop is uvloop. This violated the "falls back on any error" guarantee below: the exception propagated from deep inside the streaming generator (provisa/federation/runtime.py's _pg_passthrough_stream), past the ONE call site in provisa/pgwire/server.py that catches PassthroughError (which only wraps the initial open_passthrough() call, not the ongoing fetch loop), and killed the downstream client connection with zero visible signal outside ~/pgwire_debug.log's separate buenavista/provisa.pgwire file handler, silently breaking every SQL-transport query under a live server for an entire benchmark session before being traced. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1863, 2026-09-30 -- the passthrough now works under uvloop; declining there disabled it on every deployed server. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Fixed by detecting uvloop in open_raw_connection and raising PassthroughError immediately, before ever attempting the incompatible technique -- restores the documented fallback guarantee rather than changing it. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK]  (Amended 2026-09-30, works under uvloop; applicability vs failure:) main.py installs uvloop on every non-Windows deployment (REQ-1867), so the 2026-09-29 uvloop refusal meant the passthrough never engaged on any deployed server, only on asyncio's own loops (tests). [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1863, 2026-10-01 -- the passthrough no longer opens connections of its own; it reads on one connection borrowed from the destination's existing pool. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] open_raw_connection now builds a genuine socket.socket over os.dup() of the transport socket's fileno(): both loops' wrappers (asyncio's TransportSocket, uvloop's PseudoSocket) refuse send()/recv() but expose fileno(), and a real socket over a dup of that descriptor drives loop.sock_sendall/sock_recv under either loop while the original transport stays paused. The raw connection identifies itself to the source as application_name "provisa-pgwire-passthrough" (pg_stat_activity, the source's logs). [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] PassthroughError now means only "does not apply" -- a result column whose advertised wire type lacks the source type's exact byte layout -- and by design that statement takes the decode/re-encode path. A passthrough that applies but cannot open or read (no connect parameters, no transport socket, a source ErrorResponse, a closed connection, a column-count mismatch) raises PassthroughFailure, which no caller catches: the request fails with that error and never falls back to decode/re-encode. (Amended 2026-10-01, one pooled connection, no per-query connect:) The passthrough opens no connection. It borrows ONE connection from the destination's existing pool for the query's duration -- the DIRECT source driver's own pool (`PostgreSQLDriver.borrow_raw`), or the Postgres engine runtime's read pool (`PgFederationRuntime.borrow_raw`) -- and drives the extended-query exchange on that connection's socket as blocking I/O on the request's own thread (a socket built over a dup of the connection's descriptor, which keeps the non-blocking mode its driver relies on): Parse + Describe(Statement) + Flush reads the source's own RowDescription; Bind + Execute(n) + Flush fetches up to n DataRows and is repeated for the next batch (nothing is Synced, so the portal stays open without a transaction bracket); Sync ends the exchange. The connection's driver never sees the exchange and is idle before and after it, so a connection whose exchange completed returns to its pool, and one whose exchange did not (closed, reset, silent past its bound) is closed and the pool replaces it. Whether the passthrough APPLIES is decided from the source's RowDescription before anything executes: every source column must have exactly the wire layout the client was told at Describe (the described type OIDs; the text family counts as one layout), or -- for a statement that was never described -- a type pgwire advertises under its own OID. When it does not apply (PassthroughError) the connection is back in its pool and the statement is decoded; a TLS-encrypted pooled connection also does not apply, because its socket carries TLS records. The request deadline cancels the statement in flight on the borrowed connection. A PgBouncer source and an engine without a pooled Postgres connection never take the passthrough. [AMENDED 2026-10-01 (2): the statement is prepared under a name on the borrowed pooled connection and remembered with that connection (name + RowDescription, at most 100 per connection); every later run of the same statement text on it is Bind + Execute + Sync — one round trip — with the DataRows read off the socket a batch at a time. A result abandoned mid-stream discards its connection; an error whose SQLSTATE invalidates the prepared statement (26000, 0A000) forgets it.]

Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] each cached row carries its own _row_cached_at/_row_expires_at freshness clock, independent of every other row's, driven by that same cache_ttl duration [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK]. A query whose predicate does not resolve to a bounded PK set [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1915, 2026-10-01 -- a row-level table has no whole-table fallback; an unfiltered read is refused at planning and a filtered read replicates the rows its filter matches. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] falls back to the table's ordinary whole-table materialize/live resolution unchanged. That parse, validation and compile are kept through the same mechanism under a stage of their own, `generated-graphql` (`provisa/api/generated_plan.py`), keyed like every stage (generation, role, person) and anchored to the role's schema object as well as its governance objects. ONE plan is kept per request SHAPE — the synthesized text with its values taken out — and a request binds its own values into the kept statement's parameter list, so N point lookups on N ids, or N pages of one list, compile once. No value is part of a key and no value is written into a statement; bound parameters stay bound end to end. A value is taken out of the shape only when its reading cannot depend on its content (a 32-bit integer, a float, a string with no quote, backslash or newline); a larger integer and a string the compiler writes as a TIMESTAMP literal stay in the shape and are validated and compiled for themselves. A shape is kept as one plan only after it is proven value-independent: compiled a second time with a different value in every position, the two results must be the same statement with each value at the same parameter position; a shape that fails the proof (a filter on a virtual column, which is decided at compile time) is kept per request text instead. Governance of the compiled SQL stays the compiled stage's own kept plan, keyed on that one parameterized statement. Only text the schema rejects is answered 400; nothing rejected or empty is kept. Measured locally with rotating ids over 200 requests, the REST front end went from one parse and validation per request (2.5 ms of CPU each) to none.  (Amended 2026-10-01, gRPC bound filter values:) The gRPC lowering (provisa/grpc/query_ir.py grpc_table_to_semantic_sql, shared by the native server and the HTTP gRPC proxy) returns the statement and its bound values: a filter value is a $N placeholder in the statement and the value travels in exec_params, never as text in the statement. The statement is therefore the request shape - table, masked columns, filtered fields, limit - so requests that differ only in their filter values reuse one kept compiled plan, and the response-cache key, which includes the bound values, keeps one entry per value. A value that arrives as text for a typed column (the proto filter field of a timestamp, date, time or uuid column is string) is bound and cast to the column type in the statement (CAST($N AS TIMESTAMP) and so on), so it compares on every engine dialect - a bound text value has no implicit comparison with a timestamp on Trino; an ISO T separator in a timestamp value is normalized to a space. Numeric and boolean values bind as their own type. The native ENGINE streaming terminal passes the plan bound values to the engine (it passed none before, which was harmless only while nothing was bound). The row limit is bound the same way, after the filter values, as the GraphQL compiler binds its own, so the request shape is the table, the masked columns, the filtered fields and whether the request is limited. Measured locally on a real server with 200 requests over rotating and never-seen filter values: from 8 to 9 SQL tokenizations and 7 expression-tree copies for each new value, to none.  (Amended 2026-10-01, kept-plan store: no time expiry, least-recently-used bound, person out of the key.) The 60 s lifetime did not protect the inputs the key and anchors cover; it was the only bound on two settings governance reads outside the schema generation, and it rebuilt every kept plan once a minute per key per worker (8-12 ms each). (1) The kept-plan store (`OrgRuntime.compiled_query_cache`, `CompiledQueryCache(expires=False)`) has no time expiry. A kept plan answers while its generation and anchors hold, and the anchors now include everything governance reads beyond the statement, the role and the session variables: by identity - the role's compilation context, RLS context and role record, the masking rules, the registered tables, the relationships, the metrics, the source types and the bound engine; by value (`governed_plan.governance_settings`) - the resolved default row limit and the security mode. A changed setting therefore misses at once instead of within the old lifetime. The routing cache keeps its lifetime. (2) The store is bounded at 4,096 entries per org and evicts the least recently used entry (a read refreshes an entry). (3) The acting person is no longer part of a kept plan's key: governance reads nothing from the person, and a per-person value reaches it as a session variable, which is in the key - so one role's users share a plan (proved by test: a statement governed for one person is served to another with identical governed SQL, governed once; a different per-person RLS session value is a different plan). The validate-outcome key (`compiled_query_cache_key`) keeps the person. (4) Both keys carry the set of roles the caller is acting as when there is more than one (REQ-1620, `governed_plan.acting_role_set`): domain access is the union over that set, so a statement admitted under a wider set is governed again, and refused, for a narrower one.

(2) Range comparisons <, <=, >, >= against a literal propagate like =, IN and BETWEEN (a = b and a >= 1 imply b >= 1; the GraphQL compiler emits a range as separate >= / <= conjuncts). Trino's ClickHouse JDBC connector maps ClickHouse's LowCardinality(String) column type to varbinary instead of varchar. The JDBC driver's type metadata doesn't unwrap the LowCardinality dictionary-encoding wrapper, so Trino sees raw dictionary-encoded bytes with no declared string type. A query selecting such a column returns garbage (hex-looking byte sequences) unless the caller manually CAST(col AS varchar), which most callers won't know to do since the column looks like a normal string column everywhere else (ClickHouse itself, postgres_fdw analogues, application code). (Amended 2026-09-28, ROOT CAUSE:) Confirmed by inspecting Trino's own io.trino_trino-clickhouse-481.jar bytecode: ClickHouseClient.class contains zero references to "LowCardinality" anywhere; the connector has no type-mapping logic for the wrapper at all. The clickhouse-jdbc driver (0.9.8, the new client-v2 codebase) itself reports these columns with JDBC SQL type VARBINARY directly, not as an "unrecognized type" Trino falls back on. This was confirmed by setting unsupported-type-handling=CONVERT_TO_VARCHAR on the catalog, which had zero effect (column stayed varbinary), because that setting only intercepts types the driver can't classify at all, and this one is misclassified, not unclassified. Root cause sits in the clickhouse-jdbc driver's own type metadata, upstream of Trino's connector. CAST(col AS varchar) does NOT work as the workaround (Trino raises "Cannot cast varbinary to varchar"; varbinary/varchar aren't cast-compatible in Trino's type system); the real, verified workaround is from_utf8(col), which correctly decodes the dictionary-encoded bytes back to text (confirmed live: from_utf8(event_type) returned "shipped"/"delivered"/"returned" correctly). Any query plan reading a ClickHouse LowCardinality(String) column through Trino must wrap it in from_utf8(...), not CAST, until this is fixed upstream (or Provisa's own trino_connectors.py TrinoClickhouseConnector, if one is ever specialized beyond the current generic JDBC passthrough, could inject this wrap automatically per column based on the source schema's declared LowCardinality types). (Amended 2026-09-28, IMPLEMENTED:) The automatic from_utf8() injection sketched above is built, not just proposed. Detection needed no upstream fix: introspect.py's native_columns clickhouse branch (system.columns) already stores ClickHouse's raw type string verbatim (e.g. "LowCardinality(String)"), and schema_query.py's native-columns path only .lower()s it before it reaches Column.data_type -- the LowCardinality wrapper was never normalized away. provisa/compiler/sql_rewrite.py's new is_clickhouse_lowcardinality_string() matches LowCardinality(String) and LowCardinality(Nullable(String)) (whitespace/case-insensitive), defaulting False for anything else or missing data_type -- a missed wrap is visible, debuggable garbage; a wrong wrap risks an error or corrupting correct data, so unmatched/unknown never wraps. wrap_lowcardinality_columns() (leaf module, sqlglot-only) wraps every value-context exp.Column reference (SELECT list, WHERE/HAVING, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, function args, JOIN ON) in from_utf8(...), resolving each column to its nearest enclosing SELECT so nested-subquery aliases are never confused with an outer query's; idempotent against a reference already wrapped by an earlier pass or by the caller's own SQL. Wired into provisa/pgwire/_pipeline.py's _govern_and_route_planned, Route.ENGINE branch, immediately after REQ-1880's join-predicate-propagation step and before fold_catalog_into_schema/transpile_physical, gated strictly on state.federation_engine.dialect == "trino" AND the referenced table's own registered source type == "clickhouse" AND the column's data_type matching the LowCardinality(String) family; never applied to any other engine or source type. Runs unconditionally (no join required, unlike REQ-1880) since a bare SELECT of an affected column needs the same wrap. Live-verified against the real perf-bench Trino coordinator (104.196.4.57, trino-bench container, bench_clickhouse catalog): DESCRIBE order_events confirmed event_type/channel/device/browser/os/geo_country still report varbinary; running the rewrite's exact generated SQL shape (multi-column SELECT list + WHERE + ORDER BY, all wrapped) directly against that coordinator returned correctly decoded text ("shipped"/"marketplace"/ "desktop", etc.) for every wrapped reference. This was a direct Trino-CLI SQL-text verification, not a full Provisa pgwire round-trip. The unit test suite (tests/unit/test_sql_rewrite_lowcardinality.py) covers the rewrite logic itself, including the ineligible-source, non-matching-type, and idempotency cases.

A single expensive concurrent query (e.g. a full-table GROUP BY aggregation) serializes and blocks ALL OTHER concurrent query processing across every governed transport (Flight SQL, gRPC, Bolt/Cypher, pgwire) for its entire duration, including trivially cheap, table-disjoint point lookups submitted on entirely separate client connections. Live-verified on the perf-bench VM (2026-09-28): a single-row PK lookup (perf_bench.orders WHERE order_id = 12345, normally ~120ms) took 12.1s when submitted 0.5s after a concurrent GROUP BY aggregation over the same table (11.3s of its own), and returned to its normal ~120ms latency for every subsequent call once the aggregation completed. A 50-way-concurrent A/B test with 200 Flight SQL requests further showed IDENTICAL median/p99 latency whether the client used one shared `pyarrow.flight.FlightClient` or a pool of 8, which rules out client-side FlightClient thread-safety as a cause. `pg_stat_activity` on the embedded control-plane Postgres during the same load showed only 1 active query and 12 idle connections (max_connections=100), which rules out Postgres connection/resource exhaustion as a cause. The most likely mechanism, based on a live py-spy dump of the running server during concurrent load, is `_run_on_loop` (provisa/api/flight/server.py:212-234): every governed query's plan/residency work (govern_batch_final_plan, ensure_rows_resident, pushdown_row_materialize, ensure_resident) is dispatched via `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(..., self._main_loop).result()` onto ONE shared asyncio event loop, and the py-spy dump caught that single MainThread synchronously executing SQL tokenization (sqlglot), a synchronous DB catalog fetch (fetch_tables -> registered_tables -> row_materialized_tables_by_name), and SQL-rewrite regex work in-line, i.e. doing blocking, non-yielding work directly on the one loop thread every other concurrent request's governance step must also pass through. This is NOT fully isolated to the governance phase alone: the observed 12.1s block on the small query tracked the heavy query's own ~11.3s total duration closely enough that residency/pushdown logic that re-runs all or part of a query during governance (see pushdown_row_materialize's "run the query, AS WRITTEN, through the engine once" mechanism) has not been ruled out as a contributing factor. This is a real server-side concurrency ceiling, not a benchmark harness artifact: the perf-bench saturation ramp's collapse (demo/named/perf/bench/run_benchmark.py's run_saturation) for the `flight` transport, and the gRPC transport's total 0-completions result at every rate including rate=1, are both consistent with this mechanism once a 30%-weighted heavy aggregation enters the concurrent mix. gRPC is hit even harder by a compounding, separate cost multiplier in its GroupBy aggregate-function selection, now fixed and tracked as its own entry; see REQ-1883. (Amended 2026-09-28:) An earlier draft of this description measured gRPC's single_source_aggregation call with `funcs=[]` (empty) and reported 23.4s. That number did NOT reflect the real benchmark spec, which already sets `funcs=["count","sum"]` (demo/named/perf/bench/queries.py); re-measured with the actual spec, the call takes 4.24s, not 23.4s. The 23.4s figure was a measurement artifact of an isolated test script using the wrong request shape, not a live benchmark result; it is corrected here so it is not misattributed/reused elsewhere. REQ-1883 covers the real residual gap (4.24s vs ~2.3s for the equivalent SQL/GraphQL/Flight query) and its fix. Extends REQ-1884's gRPC-serialization investigation: `provisa/federation/runtime_support.py`'s `_STREAM_BATCH_ROWS` (the `fetchmany` batch granularity for row-cursor streaming) was 1000, vs the Arrow-native streaming path's `_ARROW_STREAM_BATCH_ROWS` of 65,536, a 65x difference. Read fully before changing: `_STREAM_BATCH_ROWS` is NOT gRPC-specific. It is shared by every row-cursor streaming consumer in the codebase: `runtime_support.stream_from_dbapi` (DuckDB's non-Arrow ROWS path, `run_sync`), `pg_runtime.py`'s named-cursor `itersize`/`fetchmany` (DIRECT PG streaming), `sqlalchemy_runtime.py`'s `yield_per`/`fetchmany`, and `runtime.py`'s `execute_native_stream` / `_pg_passthrough_stream` (the DIRECT-route stream shared by pgwire AND Flight SQL, driven via `run_coroutine_threadsafe` per batch, an even costlier per-batch hop than gRPC's `run_in_executor`). gRPC's ENGINE-route reaches this constant through `execute_engine_sync` -> backend `execute_sync` -> `run_sync`, then pulls each batch via `await loop.run_in_executor(None, next, batch_iter, None)` (`provisa/grpc/server.py` line ~501), one thread-pool round trip per batch, so at 1000 rows/batch a 2,000,000-row scan costs ~2,000 executor hops. The docstring's REQ-028 guarantee is "peak memory bounded to one batch, not the whole result", not a specific batch size. A row-cursor batch holds plain Python tuples/objects (or, for gRPC, is converted into protobuf messages downstream), a costlier per-row representation than Arrow's packed columnar buffers, so the two constants were not assumed interchangeable without checking. `tests/integration/test_streaming_memory_bounded_e2e.py` (REQ-1220's memory-bound proof suite) measures this concretely: a 3-column row (bigint, bigint, char(40)) over 5,000,000 rows totals ~1 GiB materialized (~215 bytes/row including Python object overhead), against a 400 MiB RLIMIT_AS headroom and 500 MiB peak-RSS ceiling for the streaming variants. At that per-row cost a 65,536-row batch is ~10-20 MiB, trivial against either ceiling, with no test in that suite asserting on a specific batch size (only on `_STREAM_BATCH_ROWS` symbolically in `tests/unit/test_duckdb_stream_terminal.py`). No consumer's correctness or memory-bound guarantee depends on the batch staying near 1000. `_STREAM_BATCH_ROWS` raised from 1000 to 65,536, matching `_ARROW_STREAM_BATCH_ROWS` exactly. That cuts gRPC's executor-hop count for the benchmarked 2,000,000-row `large_scan` from ~2,000 to ~31 (~65x), and equivalently reducing `run_coroutine_threadsafe` hop counts for the DIRECT-route pgwire/Flight-SQL stream and network round trips for `pg_runtime`'s named-cursor `itersize`.

The Bolt protocol's row-streaming path does two unconditional WARNING-level log calls plus a metering call PER ROW, with no log-level gate. `provisa/bolt/session.py`'s `send_record` (near line 96-98) logs `[BOLT] send tag=...` via `logging.getLogger("uvicorn.error").warning(...)` unconditionally on every framed write, and the `PULL` handler (near line 568) logs a second `[BOLT] PULL sending record row=%r` warning for every row before calling `send_record`, plus a `report(...)` metering call per row. None of these are gated behind a log-level check (e.g. `if log.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)`). They format and emit unconditionally regardless of the configured log level, incurring string-formatting + I/O cost on every single row of every Cypher result set streamed over Bolt. (Implemented 2026-09-28.) `_send` now takes `meter: bool = True` and gates its log call behind `log.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)`, downgraded from `.warning(...)` to `.debug(...)`. `send_record` gained the same `meter` passthrough and now returns the byte count `_send` reports. `handle_pull`'s per-row `[BOLT] PULL sending record row=%r` line is gated the same way and downgraded to DEBUG. The per-row `report(...)` metering call is batched: the PULL loop calls `send_record(row, meter=False)`, sums the returned byte counts, and reports the batch total once via a single `report(self.org_id, batch_bytes)` in a `finally` block (so bytes for rows already written are still reported if a later row in the batch raises, matching the prior report-immediately-per-row behavior on partial failure). Granularity check (per REQ-1452 / REQ-1455): `provisa/core/egress.py`'s `report()` only accumulates `n_bytes` into an in-memory per-org dict (`_PENDING[org_id] += n_bytes`), drained periodically by `drain()` into `meter_egress`; REQ-1455 confirms billing reads a summed `org_usage_hour.egress_bytes` counter with no per-row audit requirement. Per-row and per-PULL-batch totals are identical, so batching is correct and removes N lock acquisitions per PULL down to 1. `send_success`/`send_failure`/`send_ignored` are unaffected (they still meter individually; each is one message, not a loop).

provisa/compiler/prepared.py's REQ-1866 pre-governance cache is keyed on SQL SHAPE (a literal-blanked digest computed directly from the tree the mandatory per-call parse already produces, algorithm-equivalent to compiled_query_cache.sql_shape_digest but never a second parse of the same text) instead of raw text, role_id, and schema generation, so a repeated query differing only in a literal value (e.g. a point lookup with a different id each call) now actually hits. `raw_sql` is still parsed exactly once per call, hit or miss. This is a hard ceiling, not an oversight: Provisa's pgwire bind path inlines $1/$2 into literal SQL text (_substitute_params/_execute_sql_bound, provisa/pgwire/server.py) before this stage ever sees it, so there is no bind-parameter list to read a shape from without parsing; genuinely avoiding that parse needs a real Parse/Bind/Execute wire protocol, separate larger work, not done here. What a hit skips is the structural work after the parse: the REQ-1159 localize-check re-walk (skipped entirely on a hit, since a cache entry only exists for shapes that never localize a command, and command detection is literal-independent by callee name), and for a REQ-1317 metric-expanded shape, the dimension-resolution/join-plan rebuild, cached as a template tree and spliced with the CURRENT call's own WHERE/LIMIT/ORDER literal nodes (the only literal-bearing parts expand_metric_query passes through from the caller) rather than ever replaying a prior call's literal values, which would be a silent wrong-answer bug. A literal-count mismatch between template and current call raises loudly rather than substituting a partial/best-guess splice. The UI-sampling wrapper shape (`SELECT * FROM (<inner>) _sample LIMIT n`) is excluded from templating (its literal positions span two recursive expansion levels) and reruns expand_metric_query fresh on every hit instead. A statement that localizes an inline command is still never cached, for either raw_sql or its normalized/metric-expanded form (unchanged from REQ-1866).

`PgFederationRuntime.run_sync` (`provisa/federation/pg_runtime.py`) opened a brand-new `psycopg2.connect(self._engine_dsn)` on every single call — confirmed by reading the method before this change — and `run_arrow`/`run_arrow_stream` did the same via `adbc_driver_postgresql.dbapi.connect`. Bind params were already correct end-to-end (`$N` placeholders preserved through `provisa/compiler/pk_bounds.py` and `provisa/pgwire/_pipeline.py`, `cur.execute(sql, params)` throughout); the defect was purely connection lifecycle. A fresh connection per call means a fresh backend Postgres session per call, which pays a full TCP+auth handshake every time and never lets Postgres's own server-side generic-plan-after-5-executions optimization engage for a repeated-shape query (that optimization is scoped to one session). Specific to the pg engine (`PROVISA_ENGINE=pg`). The duckdb engine already reuses one persistent connection (`provisa/federation/duckdb_runtime.py`), no equivalent gap there; clickhouse/sqlalchemy runtimes were not investigated and are out of scope. Fixed by adding a per-instance connection pool: `self._read_pool`, a `psycopg2.pool.ThreadedConnectionPool(minconn=1, maxconn=10)`, created in `__init__` and scoped to the owning `PgFederationRuntime` instance (never a process-global singleton; the same per-instance reasoning `registered_tables_cache.py` documents: two unrelated runtime instances must never share pooled connections). `run_sync` borrows a connection with `getconn()` and returns it with `putconn()` in the stream's `on_close`, or `putconn(..., close=True)` to discard it if the borrow's own setup (`cursor()`/`execute()`) raises before `on_close` exists to release it normally. `psycopg2.pool`'s own `putconn` already checks `transaction_status` and discards a connection whose backend session is gone (`TRANSACTION_STATUS_UNKNOWN`) rather than returning it for reuse. A dead pooled connection surfaces as a real error on its next borrow, never silently retried. `run_arrow`/`run_arrow_stream` get the equivalent fix via a new hand-rolled `_AdbcConnectionPool` (same file): `psycopg2.pool` only pools psycopg2 DBAPI connections, and `adbc_driver_postgresql` has no pool of its own, so a new pooling *dependency* was avoided by writing a minimal bounded pool (list + `threading.Condition`, same min=1/max=10 bounds) instead, matching the "prefer what's already a dependency" constraint. Lazily created on first `run_arrow`/`run_arrow_stream` call, since `adbc_driver_postgresql` is already an optional, lazily-imported dependency in this file. `close()` drains and closes both pools alongside the existing `self._con.close()`.

`provisa/cache/middleware.py`'s `store_result` encoded response-cache values with `json.dumps(result_data, default=str)`, which is lossy: a `Decimal` became a string (precision only recoverable if the reader remembers to re-parse it), `bytes` became its `repr()` (unrecoverable), and integer width/type identity was not preserved as a distinct wire concept. This was tolerable while GraphQL's `Route.CACHE` was the only reader of its own writes, but REQ-1897 makes the response cache shared across every query transport (Flight SQL, gRPC, Bolt, HTTP-Cypher, pgwire). A value one transport writes must be readable, byte-for-byte, by any other, and JSON's lossy defaults silently break that for exactly the value types query results are full of. Fixed with a new `provisa/cache/codec.py`: `encode_cache_payload`/`decode_cache_payload` msgpack-encode an arbitrary JSON-like payload dict, with `Decimal`/`datetime`/`date`/`time` preserved via msgpack ext types (`bytes` is msgpack's native bin type already); an unsupported type raises `TypeError` rather than silently stringifying. This is an internal-only wire format for cache values this process itself wrote, never exposed to untrusted deserialization. `store_result` gained a `column_types` parameter (the result's real column types, stored alongside the row data) so a transport serving a cache HIT in its own native wire shape (Arrow/protobuf/COPY-binary) can rebuild it without re-deriving types from the row values. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] `decode_cached_result` is the paired read helper GraphQL's own cache-hit path (`provisa/api/data/endpoint.py`) and the shared `check_response_cache` helper (REQ-1897) both use. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK]  (Amended 2026-10-04, ONE READER:) `decode_cached_result` is the read helper of the one pipeline's cache (`_read_response_cache`, REQ-1897); GraphQL reads through the pipeline and has no cache path of its own.

That is correct and fast for the point lookup REQ-1891 targeted, but a real scaling defect for a large DIRECT scan. Live-caught on the perf-bench VM (2026-09-28): `large_scan` (2,000,000 rows, `perf_bench.order_items` via `bench-postgresql`) via grpc took 190,697ms for a single iteration — ~9.4x Flight SQL's ~20,200ms for the byte-identical query against the same source, because Flight's DIRECT path already streams (`execute_native_stream`) while gRPC's did not. gRPC's DIRECT branch could not simply reuse `execute_native_stream`: that terminal is documented SYNCHRONOUS-for-a-worker-thread (drives itself via `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(...).result()`), and `_handle_query_bound` already runs natively on the event loop — calling it there would deadlock (the same reasoning REQ-1891's own comment already recorded for why `execute_native`, not `execute_native_stream`, was chosen). Fixed by using `SourcePool.open_stream`/`DirectResultStream.fetch` (REQ-1190) instead, a genuinely ASYNC-NATIVE primitive (plain `await`s, no executor or `run_coroutine_threadsafe` hop), safe to drive directly from this event-loop-resident async generator. When `state.source_pools.supports_stream(plan.source_id)` is true (postgresql today), the DIRECT branch now pulls bounded batches via `fetch(_STREAM_BATCH_ROWS)` and yields rows as each batch arrives, exactly matching the ENGINE route's own streaming shape just above it in the same file. A source whose driver has no streaming support (`supports_stream` false) is unchanged; it is still served via the buffered `execute_native` path, so no existing DIRECT-route behavior regresses for those. (Amended 2026-09-28, verified NOT the root cause of the latency gap:) Live-reverified after deploying this fix: `large_scan` via grpc still measured 188,804ms/189,077ms, statistically unchanged from the pre-fix 190,697ms, with the new streaming branch CONFIRMED taken (a temporary debug marker proved `open_stream`/`fetch` executed, not `execute_native`). A local micro-benchmark of the row->kwargs->message-construction loop alone (2,000,000 iterations, 17 columns) completed in 2.65s, which rules out per-row Python/message-construction cost too. Root cause is architectural, not a fetch-strategy bug: `provisa/grpc/proto_gen.py:403` generates `rpc Query{Type}({Type}Request) returns (stream {Type})`: ONE PROTOBUF MESSAGE PER ROW. A 2,000,000-row scan is 2,000,000 individual gRPC stream sends, each paying full per-message framing/serialization/flow-control cost, vs. Flight SQL's ~31 large columnar Arrow RecordBatches for the identical data. This streaming-fetch fix stands on its own merits (bounded memory, matches the ENGINE-route/Flight pattern, avoids buffering the whole result before the first byte) but does NOT close the `large_scan`-scale latency gap. That would require batching multiple rows into one streamed message (e.g. a `{Type}Batch` message with a `repeated {Type} rows` field), a wire-contract/proto-schema change affecting every existing gRPC client, not something to do unilaterally without the maintainer's decision. Tracked as an open follow-up, not implemented here.

Every existing gRPC client (internal or external) keeps working exactly as before, with zero behavior change, since nothing about the original RPC's generation or handling was touched. Description: Direct follow-up to REQ-1900: the embedded-DuckDB materialize store (REQ-989, the fully- embedded zero-config dev-desktop tier) crashes a second uvicorn `--workers N` process's readiness probe outright (`duckdb.IOException: Conflicting lock is held ...`) because DuckDB enforces a single writer connection per file. First design tried — a bounded POOL of separate materialize files, one claimed per worker (write), every other pool member cross-ATTACHed READ_ONLY (mesh) for visibility — was EMPIRICALLY DISPROVEN across three isolated topologies: full mesh, hub-and-spoke, and a plain two-process writer/reader pair. Confirmed live: DuckDB's file lock is a plain EXCLUSIVE lock regardless of the requested access mode: whichever connection opens the file FIRST, in ANY mode (including READ_ONLY), blocks every OTHER connection from opening it in ANY mode for as long as the first stays open. Since each worker's write connection stays open for the whole server lifetime, peer READ_ONLY attaches would essentially always fail in real deployment, reducing the mesh design to "independent per-worker files, zero cross-worker visibility", the exact outcome it was meant to avoid. Hub-and-spoke has the identical constraint (confirmed by directly testing that exact writer+reader shape); it is not topology-dependent. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1901's 2026-09-29 "SIMPLER FINAL DESIGN" amendment below -- kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Final design: exactly ONE process ever opens the file. A singleton broker (`provisa/federation/ materialize_broker.py`), elected by "first process to bind a local Unix-domain-socket address wins" (the same pattern REQ-1900 uses for the Flight port pool), owns the one real DuckDB connection with the store ATTACHed, and serves every operation against it — reads AND writes — over `multiprocessing.managers.BaseManager`. A worker process, including the elected one, never opens the file itself; `DuckDBFederationRuntime.ensure_materialize_attached()` never ATTACHes `mat_store` on its own connection for a `duckdb`-scheme store at all — it resolves `self._store_broker = get_broker(path)` instead, and every duckdb-store call site (materialize_source/attach_landed_source/land_table/apply_cdc_events/reconcile_mv_table/ persist_mv_table) calls the broker's corresponding method. Applied uniformly regardless of worker count (no worker-count detection) — a single-worker deployment just pays one local loopback IPC hop per operation instead of a direct call, keeping one code path correct in both cases; this store's tier (dev-desktop, REQ-989) has no performance requirement that hop would violate. The production multi-worker target (Trino/PG materialize store) has no analogous lock at all and never goes through this module. Reads had to be proxied too, not just writes: DuckDB's exclusive lock blocks concurrent READS from other connections exactly as hard as writes (see above), so a worker's own connection can never hold `mat_store` attached even read-only. `_expose_landed` therefore does not create a DuckDB VIEW for a duckdb-scheme store; it records the physical-name -> (schema, table) mapping in `_store_relations`, and a new `_refresh_store_relations(duck_sql)` — called at the top of `run`/`run_sync`/`run_arrow`/`run_arrow_stream` — [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1901, 2026-09-30 -- the copy now happens only when the store's write generation changed since the last copy, not before every query; see the generation-gated copy amendment below. Description: A real 3-way federated join under the PG engine (Postgres orders JOIN ClickHouse order_events JOIN MongoDB order_docs, each reached via a Foreign Data Wrapper — postgres_fdw/clickhouse_fdw/ Supabase `mongodb_wrapper`), filtered to a 1M-row range on each side, took 13+ minutes and hash-joined with repeated disk spill (`wait_event=IO/BufFileRead`) — for a query the benchmark expected to complete in seconds. Root-caused by comparing `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` against the query's own literal filters (never assumed): `IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA`/`CREATE FOREIGN TABLE` (`pg_runtime.py`'s `attach_source`) creates the foreign table with NO statistics populated. A foreign table is never touched by autovacuum, so `pg_statistic` stays empty until something explicitly runs `ANALYZE`. Every foreign scan the planner considered was therefore costed against the FDW's hardcoded PLACEHOLDER default (`rows=1000` for clickhouse_fdw, `rows=1` for `mongodb_wrapper`), not the query's real match count. For the actual ~1,000,000-row range, that misestimate led the planner to size a hash join for a tiny result and spill to disk repeatedly under the true row count. A parallel investigation into whether `mongodb_wrapper`'s predicate pushdown itself was at fault (it does NOT support range operators, only literal equality) was DISPROVEN empirically: `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` on the isolated MongoDB view showed the wrapper's own `Wrappers: quals = [...]` diagnostic correctly capturing BOTH `"="` and `">="`/`"<="` operators as pushdown-eligible, confirming that the wrapper pushes down range predicates exactly like equality ones. The apparent "hang" on isolated single-table test queries during this investigation was a SEPARATE artifact: an unrelated, still-running long query (before this fix) held the whole Postgres instance in a state where even planning an unrelated query blocked on a `transactionid` wait; killing that backend immediately unblocked normal planning, and the isolated pushdown tests then confirmed instantly. Neither the "pushdown doesn't work" nor the "backend is stuck" leads were the real cause; the missing `ANALYZE` was. Fixed by calling `ANALYZE` on each foreign table immediately after `attach_source` imports/creates it (both the `IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA` branch, for postgres_fdw/clickhouse_fdw/mongodb_wrapper, and the `CREATE FOREIGN TABLE` branch, for file_fdw/csv), guarded by the same `source.id not in self._raw_attached` per-source-once gate the DDL itself already uses. Runs once per source at attach time, not per query.

A read-only audit of `provisa/grpc/server.py`/`proto_gen.py` found `generate_proto` (`proto_gen.py`) assigned every message's field numbers via `enumerate(sorted_cols, start=1)` freshly on EVERY schema regeneration, with no `reserved` tracking. Since protobuf field identity on the wire is the NUMBER, not the name, this is silent data corruption waiting to happen: a client holding an older-generation stub (downloaded from `GET /data/proto/{role}`) decodes a later generation's bytes using the OLD number->field mapping. Any change that shifts the sort order for a table — a column added, renamed, or (for relation fields) a relationship added — reassigns every subsequent field's number, and the client reads the wrong column's bytes into the wrong field. No error on either side; just wrong data. Traced the actual regeneration lifecycle before designing the fix: `state.wire_proto` (the UNION of every role's visible columns, `app_loaders._build_and_register_schemas`) is compiled ONCE into the served `_pb2`/`_pb2_grpc` modules at process startup (`app_startup._start_servers` -> `compile_proto` -> `start_grpc_server`). There is no live-hot-reload path that recompiles and re-registers the running gRPC service. But `_build_and_register_schemas` itself (and thus `generate_proto`) DOES re-run on every schema rebuild (`build_org_runtime`, config reload), which regenerates BOTH `state.wire_proto` (compiled into the next process restart's served descriptor) and each role's downloadable `.proto` (`GET /data/proto/{role}`, read live by any client that redownloads it), so the instability is real across restarts/rebuilds even within one long-lived deployment, not just a theoretical multi-version concern. Fixed with a persisted, monotonic field-number allocator (`provisa/grpc/field_numbering.py`, `FieldNumberAllocator`): a number is assigned once per `(table_id, namespace, field_name)` — `namespace` separates the independent field-number spaces of `{Type}` (row + relation fields), `{Type}Filter`, `{Type}Input`, and the aggregate `SumFields`/`AvgFields`/`.../MinFields`/ `MaxFields` sub-messages, since each is its own protobuf message with its own numbering — and never reassigned. A new field gets `max(every number this (table_id, namespace) has ever used, including retired ones) + 1`, so a retired number is never handed to a differently-named field later (the `reserved` guarantee, enforced at generation time instead of in a static `.proto`). Persisted in a `grpc_field_numbers` table in the org's own tenant-DB schema (same `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` bootstrap convention `init_audit_schema` uses for `query_audit_log`, in the same `org_<id>` schema; table_id is only unique within one org's `registered_tables`, so the registry is scoped per org like the audit log is). Postgres-only, matching `init_audit_schema`'s own restriction (the upsert uses `ON CONFLICT`); a non-Postgres tenant DB gets an allocator with nothing persisted, so `generate_proto` calls there fall back to the pre-fix fresh-enumerate behavior for that backend rather than a partially-persisted, inconsistent one. `generate_proto(si, field_numbers=None, authoritative=False)`: the SAME allocator instance is threaded through every `generate_proto` call in one schema build (every role's proto plus the union/wire proto), loaded once (`load_field_number_allocator`) before the role loop in `app.py`'s schema-rebuild path and flushed once (`persist_field_numbers`) after. This is required for correctness, not just for stability across restarts: the server's wire bytes are always decoded against a ROLE's own downloaded `.proto`, so a role's proto and the wire/union proto must agree on the field number for the same column, which only holds if they share one allocator per build. `authoritative=True` (passed only for the union/wire call, the only call that sees a table's FULL column set: every column, `visible_to=[]`) is the only point allowed to retire a field number (`reconcile_removed`); a role-scoped call seeing fewer columns than the union is a normal permission restriction, never evidence a column was dropped from the table. `field_numbers=None` (the default) preserves the pre-fix fresh-enumerate behavior. It is used only by `provisa/api/data/endpoint_dev.py`'s design-time proto preview, which is never decoded by a real cached client stub, so stability doesn't apply there and requiring DB access at that call site would be scope creep unrelated to the served wire schema.

Remaining findings from the same read-only gRPC audit (REQ-1903 covers the field-number correctness finding), all in `provisa/grpc/server.py` unless noted: 1. Mid-stream error status codes: `_handle_query_bound`'s three ENGINE/DIRECT streaming terminals caught `Exception`, finalized the audit row, then bare-`raise`d, surfacing as opaque `UNKNOWN` on the wire, unlike the request-validation paths in the same file which already use `context.abort(StatusCode.X, ...)`. Added `_status_for_exception(exc)`, mapping `TimeoutError`->`DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, `PermissionError`->`PERMISSION_DENIED`, `(ConnectionError, OSError)`->`UNAVAILABLE`, `ValueError`->`INVALID_ARGUMENT`, else `INTERNAL`; each site now calls `await context.abort(_status_for_exception(exc), str(exc))` after `finalize_audit`, preserving the audit-finalization behavior. 2. No concurrency ceiling: `grpc.aio.server(...)` had no `maximum_concurrent_rpcs`, so an overloaded server queued RPCs indefinitely instead of fast-failing with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`. Added `maximum_concurrent_rpcs=200` (env `GRPC_MAX_CONCURRENT_RPCS` / `server_cfg ["grpc_max_concurrent_rpcs"]`, same override pattern as the existing `grpc_max_message_bytes`). This is a per-PROCESS ceiling (this deployment runs `--workers N`, each its own process/server), distinct from REQ-369's `max_flight_streams`, a per-ROLE fair-share limit enforced by the rate limiter, not a server-wide gRPC construction option. 200 is sized well above the default DB pool (`pool_size=5` per worker, `core/database.py`) since most RPCs stream rather than hold one connection for their whole lifetime. 3. No keepalive tuning: added `grpc.keepalive_time_ms=60_000`, `grpc.keepalive_timeout_ms=20_000`, `grpc.keepalive_permit_without_calls=1`, `grpc.http2.min_ping_interval_without_data_ms=10_000`, `grpc.http2.max_ping_strikes=2`. A dead peer's call slot is now reclaimed within ~80s instead of held forever, and a normally-configured client's between-call keepalive pings aren't penalized as abusive. 4. No `grpc.max_connection_age_ms`: added (30 minutes, `grpc_connection_age_grace_ms=30_000`), in preparation for a future L4 load balancer (none confirmed in front of this deployment today) so a long-lived connection eventually recycles instead of pinning one client to one backend process forever. 5. No real gRPC health check: registered the standard `grpc.health.v1` `HealthServicer` (`grpcio-health-checking`, added to `pyproject.toml`) alongside the generated service, set SERVING for `""` and every registered service name. `AuthInterceptor.intercept_service` (`provisa/grpc/auth.py`) now exempts `/grpc.health.v1.Health/*` from both the high-security KMS-key check and the bearer-credential check. That mirrors the HTTP surface's own unauthenticated `/health`/`/live`/`/ready` (`provisa/api/app.py`), since a health probe returns no row data or schema and an orchestrator that can't reach it without a bearer credential could kill a live pod over an unrelated auth outage. 6. Reflection gated unconditionally: `enable_reflection(...)` ran regardless of whether auth was configured. That is safe when auth IS active (`AuthInterceptor` covers reflection too, REQ-273/REQ-1263), but an unsecured/dev-parity deployment left the whole service surface enumerable with no explicit decision behind it. Gated behind `auth_active(state) or grpc_allow_unsecured_reflection` (env `GRPC_ALLOW_UNSECURED_REFLECTION` / `server_cfg`), the latter a documented, explicit opt-in for a deployment that wants reflection's discovery convenience despite having no auth. `auth_active` raising `RuntimeError` (a misconfigured, supposedly-active auth middleware) is NOT caught here — that must fail server startup loudly, not be silently read as "reflection off". 7. upb protobuf backend verification: added a startup check in `app_startup._start_servers` (`google.protobuf.internal.api_implementation.Type() == "upb"`) that raises loudly if the pure-Python/cpp backend is active instead — a silent multi-x serialization slowdown with nothing in a passing test to reveal it, matching this repo's fail-closed convention (CLAUDE.md).

Configurable via `FLIGHT_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` env var or `server_cfg["flight_max_concurrent_streams"]`, defaulting to one-third of the shared asyncio default executor's size (`min(32, cpu_count()+4)`, floor 2). Checked and acquired before, and released after, the existing per-role `max_flight_streams` gate in `do_get` (provisa/api/flight/server.py). [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] (Amended 2026-09-29, per-connection-thread execution, REQ-1882:) Flight RPCs no longer run on the shared asyncio default executor: each RPC runs on its own handler thread and loop, whose default executor runs inline on that thread. The ceiling therefore now bounds concurrent Flight executions against the engine and sources the other transports share with Flight, not a shared executor; its configuration and default formula are unchanged. (Amended 2026-10-01, A STREAM OVER THE LIMIT WAITS:) the limit rejected the moment it was reached, so any client concurrency above it became errors instead of queueing (perf VM, Flight SQL: 237 req/s at 1 client, then 3,118 / 8,892 / 5,933 errors at 16 / 64 / 256 clients; local single process, limit 5: 20,134 errors at 16 clients and 28,014 at 64, none after this change with 1,367 req/s and 822 req/s served). A query stream over the limit now WAITS for a slot, the same model as the other bounded pools (`_WaitingThreadedPool`): the limit is a semaphore (`provisa/api/flight/stream_slots.py`), the wait is bounded by the request's remaining deadline (`provisa/core/request_deadline.py`), or by the server's `request_timeout` when the caller has bound none, and only when no slot frees in that time is the stream refused, with an error that names the limit (`max concurrent Arrow Flight streams reached (server-wide): all N stream slots of this worker (flight_max_concurrent_streams=N) stayed busy for the Ts this request could wait`). [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1905 (amendment THE SLOT IS TAKEN AT THE ENGINE AND HELD FOR THE STREAM), 2026-10-01 -- the slot is no longer taken at the top of do_get nor released when do_get returns. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] The slot is held for the execution window, as before, and is taken before the per-role `max_flight_streams` gate (REQ-369), which is unchanged and still rejects. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] The limit is PER WORKER PROCESS. What it protects is the capacity the other transports share with Flight inside one process, and since every worker serves the advertised Flight port (REQ-1900) a deployment-wide count would need a shared-store round trip per stream and could not be waited on without polling. `FLIGHT_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` / `flight_max_concurrent_streams` therefore name one worker's slots; a deployment of N workers runs up to N times that. The DEFAULT is the host's budget — one-third of `min(32, cpu_count()+4)`, the figure a single process has always defaulted to — divided among the launch's workers (`PROVISA_WORKERS`), floor 2 per worker: 6 for one process on a 16-core host, 2 per worker (32 in all) for 16 workers on it. The limit is no longer kept in Redis and no `rl:flight:global` key exists. (Amended 2026-10-01, ONE DEADLINE FOR THE WHOLE TICKET:) a Flight query ticket had no request deadline: only its wait for a slot was bounded, and its execution and its stream then ran for as long as they took, so a ticket that waited 50 s of a 60 s budget still ran in full. The wait, the execution and the stream now share ONE deadline, bound around the whole `do_get` with the existing mechanism (`provisa/core/request_deadline.py`, its statement-cancel registration included; `provisa/api/flight/deadline.py`): `server.limits.request_timeout` (`PROVISA_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, default 60 s), the same budget a request on every other transport has, or a tighter deadline the caller already bound. A result is often a lazy stream pyarrow pulls after `do_get` returns, so the deadline is carried through the pull: it is rebound around each batch and, once passed, the stream ends with `Arrow Flight request exceeded its Ns request deadline (server.limits.request_timeout)`. Every lazy stream `do_get` returns is under it (the SQL engine and direct-source streams, and the GraphQL engine stream). CONSEQUENCE: a legitimate extract that streams for longer than `request_timeout` is now cut off; the config offers no Flight-specific timeout (`engine_query_timeout` bounds the engine's own statement, not the request), so the only way to allow it is to raise `request_timeout`, which raises it for every transport. (Amended 2026-10-01, THE PER-ROLE LIMIT STILL REJECTS, DELIBERATELY:) `max_flight_streams` (REQ-369) is a QUOTA on a role, not a capacity limit: a role over its quota is refused at once, by design, and does not queue behind its own streams. Only the server-wide limit waits. (Amended 2026-10-01, THE SLOT IS TAKEN AT THE ENGINE AND HELD FOR THE STREAM:) the slot was taken at the top of `do_get` and given back when `do_get` returned. Two things followed: a response-cache HIT, which never reaches the engine, took a slot; and a lazy Arrow stream — which pyarrow pulls AFTER `do_get` returns — held its slot for none of the time it actually occupied the engine, so the limit bounded nothing for the scans it exists to bound. The slot is now taken where a ticket reaches the engine or a source (`_acquire_stream_slot`): after the response-cache check on the engine stream, when the direct-source cursor is opened, in the direct buffered read the cache runs only on a miss, and around the Cypher engine read. A lazy stream HOLDS its slot until it is drained, fails, or is dropped by the client (`stream_slots.SlotHeldBatches`). The role quota is checked first, at the top of `do_get`. Two places take the slot before a cache lookup they cannot see into: the Cypher pipeline terminal (the lookup is inside the shared pipeline call) holds one for that call, and residency preparation of a materialized source runs before the slot, in the same loop dispatch as the cache check. (Amended 2026-10-01, THE REQUEST TIMEOUT IS SET PER TRANSPORT:) Different transports carry different workloads, and which workloads a deployment allows is the customer's decision (one customer allows large GraphQL queries, another does not), so the request timeout is an operator setting per transport. `server.limits.request_timeout` stays as the default, and `server.limits.request_timeouts` holds an optional value per transport: graphql, rest, jsonapi, sql_http, cypher_http, pgwire, flight, bolt, grpc, mcp, and scheduler, a scheduled trigger's run (REQ-2001). A transport with no value of its own uses the default, with two exceptions shipped in the product: Flight is expected to carry large data transfers, so its shipped value is 3600 seconds, and pgwire carries a lot of BI workloads (dashboards and ad-hoc analytical SQL, mixed medium to small), so its shipped value is 300 seconds; every other transport ships on the 60-second default. An operator can change or clear either like any other. The deadline bound around a request (REQ-1882) is the one of the transport the request arrived on. For Flight it covers the whole ticket as described above, so a deployment that serves long extracts raises the Flight value alone and no longer has to raise it for every transport. A per-request timeout hint may only shorten the deadline of its transport, never lengthen it. The values reach every worker and instance like any other operator setting, and the error a timed-out request gets names the transport and the setting. Like every operator setting, these have a UI surface: the admin settings page shows the default and one value per transport next to the other server limits, reads and saves them through the settings API (`limits.request_timeout`, `limits.request_timeouts`), shows which transports are using the default, and refuses a value that is not a positive number.

Per-user-class staleness tolerance as a table attribute. A table carries a keyed list of role to TTL in seconds, set by the operator in the table's config (for example `role_ttl: {trader: 0, analyst: 360}`). It is a table attribute, not a role attribute, because freshness needs and upstream cost differ per table. The role_ttl lookup defaults to cache_ttl: role_ttl(role) returns the listed entry, or cache_ttl when the role is not listed. A reader's effective TTL on a table is always max(cache_ttl, role_ttl(role)), where cache_ttl is the table's resolved TTL (table, else source, else global) and is the operator's floor. A per-request hint (GraphQL `@cached(ttl:)`, SQL comment `-- @provisa cache_ttl=N`) may only loosen the reader's tolerance; it can never tighten it below the table's role_ttl entry or below the floor. A query that reads several tables applies each table's effective tolerance to that table. A read refreshes a landed replica only when the replica's age exceeds the reader's effective tolerance on that table, so readers with a larger tolerance serve the existing replica and never start a refresh. Concurrent reads that need the same refresh share one in-flight refresh per table and wait for it within their own request deadline. Response-cache entries are stored with their creation time and kept up to the operator's maximum; each reader accepts an entry only when its age is within that reader's smallest effective tolerance across the tables the entry read, so one entry serves every class. Every response reports the actual age of the data it served. Responsibilities: the upstream ideally manages its own backpressure; the operator owns platform backpressure, and upstream backpressure when the upstream cannot, and sets each table's role_ttl list; Provisa enforces only the floor, so how many roles receive a tolerance of 0 is the operator's decision. UI: the table edit form (provisa-ui/src/pages/tables/TableEditForm.tsx), next to the existing Cache TTL field, shows a Role TTL list: one row per role with a role picker (existing roles only, no duplicates) and a TTL in seconds (integer >= 0), with add and remove. Beside each row it shows the effective TTL, max(cache_ttl, role_ttl(role)), so the operator sees when an entry below cache_ttl has no effect. Roles not listed are shown as using cache_ttl. Saving writes role_ttl through the same admin path as cache_ttl, and every label is translated in all shipped locales.

Temporal fields -- date, time, time with time zone (timetz), timestamp, timestamp with time zone (timestamptz) and interval -- surface in GraphQL as ISO 8601 text in every output and accept ISO 8601 text in every input, whatever the column's physical storage. Outputs: a date/time value is never a number in a GraphQL response. Driver values render with isoformat() (Date and DateTime scalars; a T separator, never str()'s space); an interval is its ISO 8601 duration (P3DT4.000005S) through a GraphQL Interval scalar with an ordered IntervalFilter, and the same duration text on JSON results and gRPC string fields (ir_types.iso8601_duration). A column registered as temporal whose values are physically stored as numbers (e.g. an epoch integer) is translated to the temporal type in the SQL the compiler emits, so the value reaches the response as a temporal and renders as ISO text; the scalars refuse a raw number rather than pass or stringify it. Inputs: every argument and filter operand on a temporal field (eq, neq, in, gt, gte, lt, lte, mutation values) accepts ISO 8601 text, and for a number-stored column the emitted SQL translates the ISO operand to the physical representation (or the column to the temporal) so the comparison is exact. INTERVAL is an IR type (ir_types, SQLAlchemy Interval); timetz and timestamptz resolve on the IR, GraphQL and proto faces. A raw bytea value in a JSON result renders as Postgres's own hex text (\x0001ff, ir_types.bytea_hex) instead of failing the response; bytea stays String-typed.  (Amended 2026-09-30, epoch-stored temporals as built:) A column declares its epoch storage with Column.epoch_unit ("s" | "ms" | "us"; persisted in table_columns, round-tripped by the admin API), valid only on a timestamp, timestamptz or date data_type, never inferred, since seconds and milliseconds overlap for plausible values. build_context records every such column by physical (schema, table) under both its physical and SQL-exposed names, for all registered tables regardless of the role's visibility (RLS may read a column the role cannot select). Both physical rewrites (rewrite_semantic_to_physical and rewrite_semantic_to_catalog_physical), which every surface passes through, and compile_mutation (whose SQL is physical as built) call sql_rewrite.translate_epoch_temporal_columns, one idempotent AST pass. A read yields the temporal (UnixToTime, transpiled per engine; timestamp -> AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', date -> CAST AS DATE), aliased to the column's own name in a select list or RETURNING. A comparison, IN or BETWEEN against only ISO literals (including the GraphQL filter's TIMESTAMP '<date> <time> UTC' form) folds each literal to its exact epoch number at compile time and keeps the column bare, so a source index applies. A bound value is cast to the registered temporal and compared with the column read as the temporal (a SQL-side epoch conversion loses the offset on Trino). ORDER BY, GROUP BY and IS NULL keep the bare column (monotonic, one-to-one). INSERT/UPDATE store an ISO value as its epoch number. ISO text without an offset is read as UTC (epoch storage is a UTC instant; reads render in UTC); a value finer than the unit is refused, never truncated. Scope: live reads and writes. Landing such a table is refused in residency.resolve_landing_args, the step every landing path shares, naming the column, since no landing path converts values; converting at landing is not built.

Description: Lean tracing by default, detailed tracing in a debug mode. Every request is still traced (this is not sampling), but in normal mode a request produces ONE span: the request span, carrying what the child spans carry today as attributes: transport, role, org, route (cache, direct, engine), engine, source ids, cache hit or miss, row count, status, and the duration of each pipeline stage (governance, compile, route, execute, encode). Normal mode creates no child span for a pipeline stage, a Redis command, an ASGI receive or send, an outbound HTTP call or a source or engine statement, and it records no SQL text or plan. Debug mode produces today's full detail: a span per stage and per Redis, source, engine and outbound call, with SQL text, plan and row counts. Debug mode is scoped and temporary: the operator turns it on for an org, a role or a source for a stated time window, after which it turns itself off; and a single request can ask for a debug trace with a per-request hint that the operator permits per role, since a debug trace adds platform load and operator settings are the floor (REQ-030). The auto-instrumentation that creates per-command and per-message spans (FastAPI ASGI receive and send, Redis, httpx, database drivers) is active only in debug mode; instrumentation for a driver the code no longer uses is removed. Metrics (request counters and latency histograms per transport, route and engine) stay on for every request in both modes, so dashboards and alerts do not depend on the trace detail level. The first deliverable is a measurement: the number of spans and the tracing CPU per request on the cached GraphQL path and the pgwire point-lookup path before the change, recorded in this requirement, and the same two numbers after it. (Amended 2026-10-01, one record per request in the trace database:) The built-in trace database (the otlp2sql collector's traces table) always holds exactly one record per request: the request span with its attributes. The collector filters to request (root) spans in both modes, so the table's size and write load follow the request count, not the span count. The child spans that debug mode produces are written to a separate debug-detail table keyed by trace id, with a short retention, and are still forwarded to any external OTLP endpoint the operator configured. (Amended 2026-10-01, existing reporting is the contract:) The single request record must carry every piece of information the existing trace-based reporting reads today. Before the span reduction, every consumer of trace data is inventoried — the ops-schema views (provisa/observability/ops_schema.py), the seeded reports and dashboards (provisa/api/startup_seed.py), the UI Observability tab and trace-detail views, lineage, and the catalog descriptions — with the span names, attributes and columns each one uses. Each of those values is then present on the request record (as a column or attribute), each report is repointed to it, and each report returns the same results in normal mode as it did when every span was stored. A report that needs per-statement or per-stage rows that one record cannot express is listed explicitly with how it is served (attributes holding the list, or the debug-detail table), never silently degraded. (Amended 2026-10-05, A PRE-READ BODY'S RECEIVE SPAN:) An HTTP request's debug-trace window is resolved in the org-routing middleware, and a small request body is read before that, on the accepting loop (REQ-1882). That read opens no span: its start time, end time and body size travel with the hand-off to the request thread, and once the window is resolved the "<request span> http receive" span is recorded with those measured times, as a child of the request span, when the request's detail is debug; in normal detail nothing is recorded for it. A body too large to read up front, or chunked, and every later receive on the request (a disconnect watch, a WebSocket frame) keep a live receive span opened when the read happens. The ASGI instrumentation's own receive span is turned off; these are the request's receive spans.
