Description: Write-surface isolation. Everything Provisa writes into an engine store is written to a schema (or equivalent write surface) that holds nothing else. Materialized views are written to a write surface of their own. Replicas are written to a write surface of their own. Neither shares a schema, or a relation name within a schema, with each other, with the live attach of a source (the views or foreign tables through which the engine reads a source live), or with any object of a source. A statement that creates, refreshes, truncates, deletes from, inserts into, reconciles or drops a materialized view or a replica addresses only its own write surface, and before it writes it verifies that the target is an ordinary table that Provisa owns in that surface; a target that is a view, a foreign table, or anything outside the surface is refused with an error naming it. A read is served from a replica or a materialized view by addressing it where it lives, never by replacing a live object with a written one at the same name. This holds on every engine. It exists because a replica that shared its name with the live view of its source was refreshed through that view into the source database. (Amended 2026-10-01, approved design:) Each store has one schema that holds only replicas and one that holds only materialized views. A replica is named by one rule on every engine (source, schema and table joined into one name in the replicas schema); the per-engine exceptions that placed a replica at the registered address of its table are removed. Where a statement's tables are turned into engine names, a table served from its replica is addressed in the replicas schema and a live table at its live attach; a source that is always replicated has no live attach or connector registered at all. The write check verifies the schema as well as the kind of the target. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1912 amendment, 2026-10-01 -- there are no existing installs to convert, so no cleanup of replicas at old addresses is built. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Replicas written at the old addresses before this layout are removed by a one-off cleanup at first boot on the new layout: it drops only ordinary tables at the old replica addresses that Provisa can show it wrote, logs each one, and leaves and reports anything else. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] (Amended 2026-10-01, no conversion:) This is a new product with no installs to convert. The layout is defined for a fresh install only; nothing is built to find, move or drop replicas written under an earlier layout.

Every operator setting has a UI surface. Any value an operator can set to change how a deployment behaves (a config key, an environment variable, a server limit) is readable and editable in the admin settings pages through the settings API, not only in a config file or the environment. That covers, at least, the default row limit, the request timeout and its per-transport values (REQ-1905), the engine query timeout, the retry budget, the Flight stream limit, the gRPC concurrent-call limit, the request threads per worker, the background workers, the worker count, foreign-key auto-tracking, the engine settings, the security mode, the server hostname, the persisted-query cache TTL, the MCP row limit, the UI proxy timeout, and the listener, TLS, Redis and trace settings. Every one is editable. A setting that takes effect only after a restart is marked "restart required" next to its field, and after it is saved the page shows that a restart is pending and which settings are waiting for it. A setting that takes effect at once reaches every worker and instance (REQ-1900). A value saved in the UI is stored in the control plane and takes precedence over the environment and the config file; the page shows where the effective value comes from when it is not the stored one. Secrets are write-only in the UI (shown as set or not set, never echoed). Each field is validated in the UI and by the API, which refuses a bad value with an error naming the field. A new setting is not complete until it has this surface. (Amended 2026-10-01, design decisions:) Settings are declared once in one registry (key, type, range, default, live or restart-required, secret) and resolved in one order: stored value, then environment, then config, then the declared default; a value that cannot be parsed is an error naming the setting and its source. The catalog is served by its own route beside the existing settings endpoint. Worker count, the HTTP port and the HTTP TLS pair are consumed before the server process starts, so the launch goes through one Python entry point that reads the control plane, resolves them and starts the server; the launcher script and the compose file call it. The one class that is not editable is the bootstrap settings that locate the control plane itself (its address, pool sizes, config path, data directory); they are shown read-only with the reason. Deployment settings are edited by platform_admin only, in every deployment, including single-tenant ones where org_admin otherwise holds the platform-settings right. On a deployment with no auth provider, the guarded settings (security mode, superuser, listener ports, TLS, and those that widen exposure) are refused for the anonymous caller with an authentication-required error; other settings stay editable. Guarded settings also need an explicit confirmation, and a change that would lock out the admin making it is refused. A launch can be told, by an explicit environment flag, to ignore stored settings and start on environment and config only; it logs every stored setting it ignores. That flag is an operator override for recovering from a stored value that stops the server booting, and it applies only when set. (Amended 2026-10-01, who holds platform_admin, and telemetry:) In a single-tenant deployment the bootstrap administrator is seeded with platform_admin as well as org_admin, so the platform_admin-only rule does not leave a default install with nobody able to edit deployment settings. The other deployment-wide admin endpoints (federation engine, cache storage, encryption, secrets service, auth, config file, query engine) use the same platform_admin gate. The telemetry exporter settings (endpoint, protocol, service name, sample rate, log level, support endpoint) take effect at once on every worker and instance: each process re-attaches its exporters when the stored setting changes, through the change propagation of REQ-1914; they are not restart-required. The same propagation carries the naming and remote-GraphQL settings, which are build inputs of the model.

A model or governance change reaches every worker and every instance. A change made through any admin surface (registering or changing a source, table, column, relationship or materialized view; a role, a column-visibility rule, a row-level-security rule, a masking rule; any other input the governed model is built from) takes effect in every worker process of every instance that shares the control plane, not only in the process that served the change. The control plane holds a model generation that every such change advances in the same transaction as the change. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1914 amendment, 2026-10-01 -- the mechanism is a version stamp that every process monitors; a notification is an optional accelerator, not the mechanism. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] On a Postgres control plane the change also sends a notification, and every process listening rebuilds its model at once; every process also compares its own generation with the control plane's on a short interval, as the backstop for a missed notification and as the only path where the control plane cannot notify. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] A process that is behind rebuilds before it serves its next request on the changed model, and its per-process caches (kept plans, compiled queries, routing, registered-table views) are keyed on the shared generation so nothing built under an older generation is served. The interval is an operator setting with a UI surface (REQ-1913). The health endpoint reports each worker's generation and the control plane's, so a worker that is behind is visible. (Amended 2026-10-01, a version stamp every process monitors -) The mechanism is one stamp held in the control plane for the model and its governance. Every change writes a new stamp in the same transaction as the change, and the value is assigned by the control plane itself, so it is one stored value that every process reads. No process compares it with its own clock, and nothing depends on the clocks of different machines agreeing. Every process that holds the model (each query node worker, the coordinator, anything else that builds from it) remembers the stamp it loaded, reads the stored stamp on a short interval, and when the two differ reloads before it serves on the changed model. A request reads nothing from the control plane for this; it runs against what its process has loaded. The interval is an operator setting. The same pattern, with its own stamp, carries the other things a process must reapply when they change -- operator settings applied live in each worker, the telemetry exporters, the naming and remote-GraphQL settings -- so a change of one kind does not reload another. A push notification from the control plane may be added later to shorten the wait; it is not required and the stamp must be correct without it. (Amended 2026-10-01, updates carry a concurrency check -) Every update to configuration (the model, governance rules, operator settings, the config file, anything the stamp covers) is checked against what it was based on. The editor, whether a person in the UI, an API client or an automated process, sends with the update the version of the thing it read before changing it. The control plane compares that with the stored version inside the same transaction that would apply the update, and applies it only when they match. When they do not match, somebody else changed it in the meantime, so the update is refused with a conflict error that names what changed, and nothing is written; it is never applied over the newer state and never merged silently. An update that sends no version is refused. The UI then shows the current state so the editor can reapply the change on top of it. The two are separate and neither is used for the job of the other. The config stamp is used strictly for reloading: any update advances it, and its only purpose is to tell every process that it must reload. Concurrency is checked at the level of the object. Each object that can be edited (a source, a table, a role, a rule, a setting, and so on) carries its own version or timestamp, the editor sends the one it read, and the update is compared against that. The config stamp is never what an update is checked against, so two editors changing unrelated objects do not block each other. (Amended 2026-10-03, A NAMED BOOT ORG RELOADS UNDER ITS OWN ID:) A boot org named by `ORG_ID` is reloaded under that id. Before 2026-10-03 a watcher reload of a boot org not named `default` reloaded nothing. The multi-worker sync tests cover a named boot org.

Replication is bounded, single and survivable. Replicating a table never holds the table in a worker's memory: where the engine can reach the source, the copy runs inside the engine and no row passes through the server process; otherwise rows move from a cursor on the source into the store in bounded batches. Memory used by a replication does not grow with the size of the table. A refresh writes into a fresh table and swaps it in only when complete, so a reader never sees an empty or half-filled replica and a process that dies mid-copy leaves the previous replica intact. At most one copy of a table runs at a time across every worker and instance, coordinated by a lock the store or control plane guarantees. A copy is started by the read that finds no usable replica, and it continues after that request ends. The request waits for it up to its own deadline; if the replica is not ready by then the request fails with an error that names the table, says its replica is still being built, and gives the progress so far. Later requests join the copy that is running and never start another. Progress (rows copied) is recorded per table. A statement that reads a table replicated row by row without binding its key, on an engine that cannot attach the source, is refused at planning with an error naming the table and its key, on every surface alike; it is never answered from whatever rows happen to be replicated, and it never triggers a copy of the whole table. Before this requirement a whole-table copy was read into the worker three times over and written one row at a time, each worker started its own copy, and some surfaces answered an unfiltered read of a row-level table from a partial replica. (Amended 2026-10-01, replicas are built eagerly, not on the first query:) A replica starts building when the decision to replicate takes effect, in the background, without waiting for a read. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1915 amendment, 2026-10-03 -- there are no save triggers; one convergence step at the end of every model build requests and retires builds. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Three things start it: an operator saving a table or source as always replicated or load-protected; a boot that finds a table set to always replicated with no replica; and a table crossing its Hot threshold, where the promotion itself is the trigger. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] It is the same single copy job described above, run under the single scheduler holder. While a replica is being built, a table under a Hot threshold is read live and switches to the replica when it is ready, so no read waits and none fails; a table that is always replicated or load-protected may not be read live, so a read waits up to its deadline and then gets the still-being-built error with the progress. A replica is also refreshed ahead of time: the scheduler starts the refresh when the TTL passes (REQ-1907), so a read waits for a refresh only when the replica is older than its maximum age. A read that finds no replica and no build in progress still starts one; that is the backstop for a failed build or a wiped store, not the normal path. The Load Management and Timeliness panel shows the state of the replica of a table: not built, building with the rows copied so far, ready with its age, or failed with the error, and lets the operator start a build or refresh. (Amended 2026-10-01, central state and central scheduling:) The state of every replica is held in one place, the control plane: for each replicated table, whether it is not built, building, ready or failed, the rows copied so far, when it was last completed, when its next refresh is due, the last error, and which process holds the build. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1661, 2026-10-03 -- REQ-1661 (amended 2026-10-01, staleness decided in memory) gives each process a copy of the record: provisa/federation/replica_state_view.py:10-25, read first at provisa/federation/query_residency.py:381-384. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Every worker and instance reads that one record; none keeps its own view of whether a replica exists or is fresh. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] The triggers are managed centrally as well: the single scheduler holder decides, from that record and the operator settings, when a build or a refresh starts, and it is the only thing that starts one, including the builds requested by a saved setting, a boot, a Hot threshold crossing, an operator action or the read backstop, which all enqueue a request in the central record and do not copy anything themselves. Row-level replication does not use this path: a table replicated row by row is filled by the keyed reads that ask for its rows, on the request that needs them, and has no whole-table build, schedule or build state. (Amended 2026-10-01, guidance for large tables:) A whole-table replica is the wrong tool for a large table. The recommendation, stated in the operator documentation, in the sizing and tuning guide (REQ-1911) and in the Load Management and Timeliness panel, is to use row-level replication, so only the rows that are asked for are copied, and/or scheduled materialized views that hold the enriched or aggregated subset that is actually queried, refreshed on a schedule. When an operator sets a table to always replicated and its size is above the automatic-promotion size guard, the panel says so and names these two alternatives; it does not refuse, because an explicit Always is the operator's decision. (Amended 2026-10-01, replication always streams:) Replication is always a stream. No replication path, whole-table or refresh, on any engine or store, reads a result into memory and then writes it. Where rows pass through the server process they move in bounded batches from the source's streaming read to the store's bulk write: ideally as Arrow record batches, the same buffers the Flight path carries, and otherwise through a cursor on the source that is fetched a bounded batch at a time. Either way the whole result is never held, and rows are never written one statement at a time. A source driver that offers neither an Arrow stream nor a cursor is given one before it may be replicated from; a store that cannot take a bulk write of a batch is given one. A copy that runs inside the engine (the engine reading the source and writing the replica itself) is a stream by construction and is preferred where the engine can reach the source. (Amended 2026-10-01, the engine always performs the copy:) The engine always performs the copy and the coordinator (REQ-1916) only orchestrates it: it submits the work to the engine, records the engine's job or statement identifier in the central record, follows its status, and updates the record. When the engine can reach the source, the copy is a job or statement on the engine (an asynchronous job where the engine has a job service, otherwise a statement the coordinator runs on it) and no row passes through any Provisa process. The single exception is a source the engine cannot reach: the coordinator extracts it as a stream (Arrow batches or a cursor, as above) into the engine's own bulk loader, or to a stage the engine can read from which the engine then loads, so the engine still performs the write and Provisa is only the extract. No Provisa process writes replica rows into a store itself. The schedule stays with Provisa: the coordinator triggers every build and refresh from the central record and the operator settings; an engine-owned schedule (an object the engine refreshes by itself) is not used unless an operator chooses it explicitly for a table. Each engine backend declares what it offers (an asynchronous job service, a statement-level copy, a bulk loader, a stage), and the coordinator uses the first of those that applies. A coordinator that restarts or takes over resumes following a recorded job; it does not start another. Row-level replication is the one exception to all of this paragraph: a table replicated row by row is not copied by the engine and has no job. The request that needs a row fetches it from the source by key and writes it into the row-level replica itself, in the query node, as part of answering that request, and only for the keys the request binds. (Amended 2026-10-01, the data replicator:) Every whole-table copy is produced by one component, the data replicator. It takes the capabilities of the three parties (what the source can do: be reached by the engine, stream Arrow batches, be read through a cursor, export to a stage; what the target store can do: take a statement-level copy, a bulk load of a stream, a load from a stage, an atomic swap of a finished table; what the engine can do: reach this source, run an asynchronous job, run a statement-level copy) and produces the correct job for that combination: an engine job, an engine statement, a streamed extract into the bulk loader, or an extract to a stage followed by an engine load. The choice is a pure decision from declared capabilities, so it is testable as a table of every source, store and engine combination without running any of them, and the same table is the documentation of what a replica of a given source on a given engine costs and how it is built. A combination for which no job can be produced is refused at config validation, naming what is missing. Each kind of job has one executor, which the coordinator runs and follows. Capabilities are declared by each source driver, store and engine backend in one place each; nothing else in the code decides how a copy is made. Replica builds and refreshes use this tool, and so does every other whole-table write Provisa makes into a store. Row-level replication does not. (Amended 2026-10-01, what counts as binding the key:) The refusal is decided once, where the pipeline resolves key bounds, before the response cache is read and before a route is chosen, so every surface refuses the same statements and a cached answer never stands in for it. It is decided per reference to the table, not per statement. A reference is bound when the SELECT that names it carries, as a top-level AND term of its own WHERE or of one of its JOIN ON conditions, a predicate that gives concrete values for the primary key. That is key equals value, key IN a list of values, or an OR made only of such equalities on the one key column, each value a literal or a bound parameter. A composite key needs exactly one value per column. A reference is also bound when a join pushes the key down, which holds when the statement is a SELECT, the reference is the target of a JOIN, that JOIN is the only one naming the table, its ON condition is a single equality between one column of the table and a column of another relation, and the primary key is a single column. Nothing else binds it. No predicate, a predicate on another column, a range on the key, a key predicate in an enclosing or nested query, a second join to the same table and a join inside a UNION are all refused. The table an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE writes is not a read of it. The error is HTTP 400 with code data.row_level_key_required and params table and key, and the wire protocols report the same message as text. The whole-table path for a row-level table is removed from the read path. A source whose tables are all row-level is never landed by a read. (Amended 2026-10-01, a row-level table needs a filter, not a key:) Requiring a read by key is too limiting. The rule for a table replicated row by row, on an engine that cannot attach its source, is that the statement must FILTER that table: any predicate on its columns, or a join that supplies its key, counts. A statement that reads it with no filter at all is still refused at planning, and the error says why: the table is replicated row by row because it is large, so it is not read whole; add a filter. For a filtered read the request pushes the filter to the source, fetches the rows that match in bounded batches and within its deadline, writes them into the row-level replica, and is answered from it; the filter and the time it was fetched are recorded, so the same filter is served from the replica until its TTL passes, as the parameter sets of an API source already are. A key filter stays the cheapest case and keeps its per-row freshness. A filter can be written to match most of a table, and that is accepted. It is bounded in memory and by the request deadline like any other read, and it is the choice of whoever wrote it. Until this is built the earlier rule stands in the code -- a read is accepted only when it binds the key or a join supplies it -- and the block above describing what binds a key describes that interim behaviour. (Amended 2026-10-03, ATOMIC REPLACE, IDENTITY KEPT:) A reader sees the whole old copy or the whole new copy, and the replica keeps its key, its grants and its comment across a rebuild. The swap is a rename only where the store keeps identity across it (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, the MySQL and MariaDB paired rename, DuckDB, ClickHouse EXCHANGE). Snowflake and Databricks use INSERT OVERWRITE, BigQuery one MERGE, and Fabric and any other transactional dialect DELETE followed by INSERT ... SELECT in one transaction. A store that offers neither is refused. (Amended 2026-10-03, THE LOAD METHOD IS A DECLARED CAPABILITY OF THE STORE:) Each store declares whether it is loaded by bulk stream or by row copy. SQL Server, MySQL and MariaDB stores use row copy, which works within limits and is not suited to very large datasets; this is guidance and no build is refused for size. Oracle uses direct path load and PostgreSQL uses COPY. (Amended 2026-10-03, A SOURCE THAT CANNOT BE READ BY ROW IS SPOOLED:) A source that cannot be read by row or by cursor (the single-document kinds) is spooled to a temporary file while it is replicated, always, for the kinds that can be. The spool is bounded by `replication.spool_max_bytes` (2 GiB, node-wide); a build that would exceed it fails with an error naming the limit. Spooling is marked as not optimal. Provisa writes no other data files to its own disk. (Amended 2026-10-03, CONVERGENCE REPLACES TRIGGERS:) There are no save triggers and no delete calls. One step at the end of every model build, on every coordinator-capable node, compares the model with replica state: it requests a build for each replica that is missing or whose definition changed, and retires each replica whose table is gone or no longer replicated. A retired replica is dropped after the grace period, and a node drops one only when the model stamp it has loaded is at least the stamp on the retirement record. A failed build is retried after `replication.retry_interval`. (Amended 2026-10-03, A REPLICA IS NEVER CUT SHORT:) A build that reaches an API endpoint's `max_pages`, or a GraphQL connection's `max_rows`, while the remote still has more, fails with an error naming the limit (`replication.page_limit_reached`, `replication.row_limit_reached`). A replica never holds a truncated copy. (Amended 2026-10-03, NO WHOLE COPY, NO WHOLE BUILD:) A table that has no whole copy (parameterized or row-level) is never built whole, by convergence, by the runner or by the read backstop. Its parameter-set fills live in the store's API cache schema, not in the control plane, and call the remote through `call_api`. (Amended 2026-10-05, ANY FILTER) A read of a table replicated row by row (row_materialize, on an engine that cannot attach its source) that the engine federates must filter it: a key bound (=, IN, or an OR of key equalities), a key a join supplies, or any predicate on the table's own columns with literals or bound parameters (= <> < <= > >= IN BETWEEN LIKE, IS [NOT] NULL, AND/OR/NOT); with none it is refused at planning, data.row_level_filter_required naming the table. The filter is translated into the source's own query and pushed down; matching rows are streamed and replace that filter's rows in the copy in one transaction; each fetch is recorded by the filter's exact hash and served from the copy within the reader's TTL. A filter a source type cannot evaluate natively is refused by name, data.row_level_filter_not_pushable naming the table, source type and reason, and is never answered by a whole fetch. (Amended 2026-10-15, lead ruling: scope of the pushdown) The filter is pushed down for a source read through a SQL direct driver, as a WHERE in the source's dialect, with the region's row rule pushed beside it where it reads only the table's columns. Every other source type is refused by name for a filter, data.row_level_filter_not_pushable (its key still reads it); per-type translations (bool queries, find filters, CQL restrictions, label matchers and the like) are not part of this requirement. This requirement is complete for that scope. Registration refuses row_materialize on API sources (filtered by their own parameters), on govdata (read live) and on types no connector reaches. A single-source read through the source's own driver (DIRECT, maintainer 2026-10-05) reads the source live, with no filter required and nothing fetched into the copy; the copy serves only federated reads, and a statement that filters such a table neither way is never answered from the response cache.

Process roles. A deployment runs the same code in two roles, chosen when a process is started. A query node serves requests on every transport and does nothing else: it never runs a replication copy, a scheduled refresh or any other background job. A coordinator serves no data requests and does the central work: it holds the central replica record and decides and runs every replica build and refresh (REQ-1915), and it runs the scheduled and single-holder background work (materialized view refresh and cleanup, hot-table refresh, scheduled triggers, and the like) that query nodes used to elect one of themselves to run. Query nodes enqueue requests in the central record and read state from it; the coordinator is the only thing that acts on them. Both roles are the same image and the same entry point with a role argument, read the same control plane, and are told of changes by the same propagation (REQ-1914). [SUPERSEDED by the 2026-10-02 amendment below -- the default is now the every mode, one process doing both. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] By default the launcher starts one coordinator on the same host next to the query nodes, so a small install needs no extra setup; [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] a larger deployment runs the coordinator on its own server with its own memory and network budget, close to the store and the sources. [SUPERSEDED by the 2026-10-02 amendment below -- several coordinators work at once, each on different jobs. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] More than one coordinator may run for availability, and a lock the control plane guarantees lets exactly one of them act at a time, with another taking over when it stops. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] The health endpoint and the admin pages show the coordinator, whether it is running, and what it is doing, because when no coordinator runs nothing is replicated or refreshed; a query node reports that state on reads that need a replica instead of doing the work itself. The role is a launch setting shown in the deployment settings (REQ-1913). (Amended 2026-10-02, THREE MODES:) A process starts in one of three modes -- every, query or coordinator. every is the default and needs no flag -- the process serves requests on every transport and also does the coordinator work, so a small install is one kind of process with nothing to choose. query and coordinator are chosen by a startup command-line flag. A query process serves requests and runs no replica build, view refresh or other background job. A coordinator process serves no data requests and does the background work. The mode is fixed for the life of the process and is shown read-only with the other launch settings. (Amended 2026-10-02, EVERY COORDINATOR BUILDS:) Background capacity grows by adding processes that do coordinator work (coordinator or every mode). Each such process claims requested replica builds, and later view refreshes, one job at a time per claim. A lock the control plane guarantees per replica or view keeps each job to one builder, so several coordinators work at once on different jobs. Three operator limits bound the total: builds per node, background jobs per engine across all nodes, and reads per source (REQ-1915, REQ-1909). Work that must fire exactly once per deployment, such as deciding that a refresh is due or running a scheduled trigger, still goes to one holder at a time, taken over by another when it stops. (Amended 2026-10-02, SCALING AND MEMBERSHIP:) Capacity is added in either of two ways, and the operator chooses by workload. The simple way is to add more every-mode nodes; each adds request capacity and background capacity together. The designed way is to run some number of query nodes and some number of coordinator nodes, sized separately for request load and for replication and refresh load. Both may be mixed in one cluster. A cluster is the set of processes started against one control plane. A node joins by starting against that control plane and leaves by stopping. No other node is restarted or reconfigured, and nothing is registered by hand, so capacity is added and removed while the cluster serves. A joining node loads the current configuration (REQ-1914) and must hold the deployment encryption key (REQ-684) before it serves. A leaving query node finishes or times out the requests it holds. A leaving coordinator releases the jobs it holds: the control plane frees its locks when its session ends, and another node claims and restarts those jobs (REQ-1915). The admin pages and the health endpoint list the nodes now in the cluster with each one mode, so an operator sees what capacity is present and whether any node is doing coordinator work. (Amended 2026-10-03, THE NODE LIST LIVES IN THE PLATFORM STATE STORE:) The node heartbeat and the cluster node list are held in the platform state store (REQ-1932).

A domain is deleted only when nothing refers to it, and the operator is shown everything that does. Asking to delete a domain returns its complete impact list -- the registered tables and their columns, relationships, row filters, masking rules, metrics, materialized views and plain views, commands and webhooks, data products, glossary links, tag assignments, the roles and role assignments that name the domain, the sources that list it as an allowed domain, and the replicas and view storage held for its tables -- each kind with a count and the names, and each item linked to where the operator removes or moves it. While that list is not empty the deletion is refused and nothing is removed. The operator is responsible for the cleanup. Each item is removed or moved through its own existing action, under the right that action already requires and with its own audit record. When the list is empty the deletion succeeds and removes only the domain itself. No deletion of a domain removes any other object. The control plane does not cascade from a domain, and the rule is checked in code so that it holds the same on every control plane. A role that lists the domain is on the impact list like anything else. The operator edits the role, and a data role cannot be left with no domain (a role always lists one or more domains or all of them). Removing an individual object cleans up after itself -- removing a table removes its replica, its rules and its place in relationships, or is itself refused while something reads it -- so that emptying a domain leaves nothing behind. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1918, 2026-10-02 -- deletion follows the general rule there. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] A bulk removal built on the same list may be added later; it is not part of this requirement. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] (Amended 2026-10-02, GENERAL RULE) Domain deletion follows the general deletion rule of REQ-1918: one object at a time, refused while anything depends on it. There is no bulk removal of a domain's contents.

One rule governs the deletion of every kind of object. An object has parts and dependents. Its parts are the things that exist only as part of it -- a table and its columns, the row filters defined on it, its replica, its cache entries -- and they are removed with it. Its dependents are other objects that refer to it -- a view that reads a table, a relationship that joins it, a role that lists a domain, a grant that names a role -- and a dependent blocks the deletion. A deletion names one object. While anything depends on it the deletion is refused, nothing is removed, and the operator is shown every dependent, named and linked to where it is removed or moved; the operator is responsible for that cleanup, through each object's own action. A reference from an object to itself never blocks it. Dependents are chosen so that there is always something that can be deleted first. A relationship stands on its own and is removed before the tables it joins, so two tables related to each other are not a circle. The one way objects could block each other in a circle is views that read each other, and that is refused when a view is saved, since such views cannot be evaluated. So no legitimate circle exists and there is no deletion of several objects at once. If a damaged control plane nevertheless holds a circle, the deletion is refused and the members are named, so the operator can edit one of them. The parts and dependents of each kind are as follows: a source is blocked by its registered tables; a table or view is blocked by every relationship it takes part in and by the views, metrics and commands that read it, and takes its columns, its row filters, its tags and its data with it; a role is blocked by anyone who holds it and by every grant that names it, each listed with an action that removes the role from that grant; a data product is blocked by its members; a tag takes its assignments with it; an org secret is blocked by any source or configuration that names it; a domain is blocked by everything that refers to it (REQ-1917). Data held for a removed object is removed by background jobs. One function answers what depends on an object, and every deletion path and the refusal shown in the admin pages use it. The rule is checked in the model store (REQ-1919) and holds the same on every control plane; no deletion relies on a database cascade. Each deletion is recorded in the audit trail. Deleting several objects in one request is a possible future feature and is not part of this requirement. (History, 2026-10-02: earlier wordings of this requirement, written the same day and never built, let the operator name a set of objects, and then let a circle be removed whole on the operator's approval. The maintainer replaced both with the rule above.) (Amended 2026-10-03, RULINGS PER KIND:) Every command and every webhook sits in a domain. A deletion of any kind goes through the guard. A row filter that names a column blocks dropping that column. An org secret is deleted only when no stored value names it; the encrypted authentication columns are searched in memory to answer that. An environment is retired only when nothing refers to it; a visitor's `ephemeral_*` or `sandbox_*` environment takes its pinned accounts with it. The domain-policy switch is refused while a catalog exists.

The model store. The model -- sources, tables and columns, relationships, roles and their assignments, row filters and masks, metrics, views, commands and webhooks, data products, domains, tags, glossary terms and the other objects held in the control plane -- is created, read, changed and deleted in one place, the model store, and nowhere else. The model store is the control plane's create, read, update and delete for every kind of object, and it carries four things with every change. Dependency guards: a deletion or a change of domain is refused while something depends on the object, under the rule of REQ-1918 and REQ-1917. Versioning: each object carries its own version, and an update made against a stale or missing version is refused (REQ-1914). Syncing: every change advances the stamp that tells every process to reload, in the same transaction as the change (REQ-1914). One transaction: a change that touches several rows is applied whole or not at all, so no other process ever reloads a half-made change. A change is also recorded in the audit trail. The admin API, the configuration loader, the startup seed and every other caller change the model only by calling the model store; no other code writes a model table, and a test fails the build when one does. The model store behaves the same on every control plane and relies on no database cascade. It is built from the existing repository layer made complete, kind by kind -- deletion and domain change first, then creation and update -- and the test that forbids writes from elsewhere grows with each kind converted. The term is model store; it replaces maintenance module and repository layer in documents and, at the terminology pass, in code. (Amended 2026-10-03, EVERY OBJECT RECORDS ITS ORIGIN, AND A LOAD MANAGES ONLY WHAT A CONFIG DECLARED:) Every model object records its origin: config, admin or seed. A configuration load adds and updates what the file declares and removes only config-origin objects the file no longer declares. Removal happens at the end of the primary's load and through the guard (REQ-1918); it is refused, with the full list, when something that is not also being removed depends on them. A load never touches an object an admin made. A secondary's load only upserts (REQ-1229). A config-origin row filter the file drops is removed, and the removal is logged loudly. A seeded object that a file redefined reverts to the seed's definition when the file stops declaring it. An admin import (Hasura) records admin origin and removes nothing. Replace mode (`PROVISA_CONFIG_REPLACE`) is removed. An admin may edit or delete a config-origin object; the admin pages show it as declared in config, with a warning. (Amended 2026-10-06, A CONFIG IS A ONE-TIME SEED) [SUPERSEDES EVERY OBJECT RECORDS ITS ORIGIN, AND A LOAD MANAGES ONLY WHAT A CONFIG DECLARED, and every sentence making a configuration load re-assert itself.] A configuration file seeds the model once -- at a deployment's first start, into an empty model store -- and from then on the model store alone owns the model; restarting, redeploying or reloading never reapplies the file, and nothing an admin changed is ever overwritten by it. A configuration can be written from the UI -- the model as it stands, or a chosen part of it, exported as a configuration file -- and an admin can apply a configuration again, as an explicit one-time seed, which adds and updates what the file declares through the model store, guards and versions included, and removes nothing. Objects carry no visible mark of having been seeded; the UI shows no origin, and people need not know an object came from a seed. (Amended 2026-10-06, DEMO ORGANISATIONS ARE THEIR CONFIG) A demo organisation is defined by its demo configuration, and every build of its runtime loads that configuration again, so a demo always starts as its configuration says; what is changed in a demo organisation lasts until its next build. The one-time seed applies to every other organisation.

The state store. Provisa keeps three kinds of data in its control plane and treats each differently. The model is what the operator declares, and it lives in the model store (REQ-1919). State is what the runtime works out while making the estate match the model -- the build state of each replica and whether a table is promoted as hot, the freshness of each table and view, the status and log of each view refresh, queued events and the outcome of each job, cached source catalogs and file timestamps, and the like -- and it lives in the state store. The record is the audit trail and usage history, which says what happened and is kept apart from both. State is never declared. No operator and no configuration file writes it; only the runtime does, the coordinator for most of it. State is derived: it can be discarded and rebuilt from the model and the estate, and losing it costs work but no information. A change to state never causes a model reload; where other processes must learn of it, state has its own stamp, separate from the model stamp, whose reload reads only that state (REQ-1914). The state store is the one place that reads and writes state, as the model store is for the model. Other code asks it, and a test fails the build when state is written from elsewhere. State is not part of a configuration export and is not copied when the model is copied to another environment. State held outside the control plane for speed -- kept plans, the response cache, per-interval read counts -- follows the same rule of being derived and discardable, and is keyed to the model it was derived under so that it cannot outlive a change to that model. The record is not state: it cannot be rebuilt, it is append-only, and nothing in the state store may be relied on as the record. The replica state built for the data replicator (REQ-1915) is the first resident of the state store. (Amended 2026-10-02, WHAT EACH IS FOR) The three fit together. The model says what should be true. The state store is the sink the runtime uses to keep track of what it has done about it: when a view was last refreshed, whether a replica is built, what a job did last time. The record proves that the state matched the model: that what was served, copied or refused was what the model in force at that moment required. For the record to prove that, each entry names the model it was made under (the model stamp in force, REQ-1914) and what was applied -- the role acted as, the row filters and masks enforced, the route taken, the replica or view read and how old it was -- so that an entry can be checked against the declaration of that moment without trusting the runtime's present state. (Amended 2026-10-03, WHAT EACH RECORD ENTRY CARRIES:) Each served answer records `model_stamp` always. It records `model_commit` only when the environment's deployed stamp equals the model stamp and the environment is not drifted; otherwise `model_commit` is null and the entry carries the visible columns of each table read. It records `enforced` (row filters, with session variables by name only; masks by rule; row caps; and for a write the table and columns written), `route_reason`, `sources`, and `data_age` (the cache age, the as-of time, or each replica's build completion; null for a live read). Where the model declares regions (REQ-1922) it also records `region` and, for a read served across regions, `replica_region`.

Data residency (the rule in force is the SIMPLE RULE amendment at the end). [SUPERSEDED by the SIMPLE RULE amendment below, 2026-10-02 -- the maintainer reduced residency to regions, the row and column rules, and a region on a table for whole-table copies. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] A source, or a single table of it, can be declared resident -- its data is subject to rules about where it may be held. Two things then hold. First, a reader gets only what the rules allow -- row filters and column rules written on user attributes, such as the country a user is in, decide what each request may see, exactly as for any other table, and the statement sent to the source already carries them, so nothing a reader may not see is read. Second, a resident table takes no part in anything that keeps a copy automatically -- it is never replicated, whatever the replicate setting says (REQ-826); a response read from it is never kept in the response cache, even when the request asks for caching (REQ-544); it is never kept as a hot table; and no per-request cache table is kept for it. It is always read live. A setting that would require a copy of a resident table -- replicate Always or a hot threshold, load protection -- is refused when saved, naming the conflict, and an engine that cannot read the source in place cannot serve the table at all rather than copying it. Readers outside the country are served the same way, live, and receive what the rules allow them. Where live reads are not fast enough, the operator builds a materialized view over the resident table that holds only what may be kept where the view is stored -- that view is a deliberate declaration in the model, its compliance is the operator's responsibility, and it is the only way a copy of resident data comes to exist. The declaration is inherited by a table from its source unless the table says otherwise, is shown in the admin pages beside the replicate setting, and the record of each request notes that resident data was read (REQ-1920). [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1922, 2026-10-02 -- regions are separate clusters on one shared model. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Further steps -- nodes, stores and caches that declare the region they are in, so that a copy may be kept where a reader in that place could see it, and traffic directed to an in-country address -- are possible later and are not part of this requirement. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] (Amended 2026-10-02, HOME REGION) Where a deployment runs more than one cluster on one shared model (REQ-1922), a resident table names the region that is its home. In the cluster of its home region it behaves as any other table. It may be replicated, cached and kept hot, because that cluster's engine, storage and cache are in the region. In every other cluster the rule above applies: it is read live, readers get what the rules allow, and no copy is kept there unless the operator declares a materialized view for the purpose. In a deployment with a single cluster the rule above applies as written. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] (Amended 2026-10-02, SIMPLE RULE) Residency is three things and no more. First, regions (REQ-1922): one shared model store, and every other store (engine, replica and view storage, cache, state store, record) belongs to a region; a node is launched in a region by a command line flag. Second, the row and column rules keep data where it is. Rules written on user attributes decide what each reader gets, the statement sent to the source already carries them, so a response, and anything kept from a response such as a response-cache entry, holds only what that reader was allowed. There is no separate resident declaration and no restriction on the response cache. Third, whole-table copies: a replica or a hot table is a copy of the table itself, made before any reader's rules apply, so the operator controls it in two ways. The operator may disallow it, with the replicate setting Never (REQ-826). [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1921 amendment, 2026-10-04 -- a source's region is the default for its new tables, not a region its tables take at run time. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Or a table, or its source for all its tables, may name a region, and whole-table copies of it are then allowed only in that region [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] -- the cluster of that region builds and refreshes the replica and may keep the table hot, and no other cluster builds one. A reader who connects through another region is served from the home region's replica. The other region's engine reads it in place, at the address the model gives (the home region's replica storage, REQ-1922, and the replica's name, REQ-1912), with the reader's row and column rules in the statement, so the filtering is done in the home region and only what the reader is allowed crosses. The source itself is not read from outside the table's region, so a source that is replicated to protect it stays protected. When the replica has not been built or the home region cannot be reached, the request is refused, naming the home region; the source is not read live in its place. A table that names a region and is not replicated (replicate Never, or a setting that calls for no copy yet) is read live from its source by every region, as any unreplicated table is. A table that names no region is replicated, when its replicate setting calls for it, in the region of the node the reader connected to, like any other table. No setting is ever satisfied by building a copy outside the table's region. A materialized view is built in every region, and each region's copy is right for that region. Each region's coordinator builds and refreshes its own copy in its own view storage, on the view's schedule, and the statement that builds it is governed. It is run under the identity of the organisation's administrator, and an identity processing within a node carries that node's region as its region attribute, so the same row and column rules apply to the build as to any request from that region. The build may reach sources and copies in any region, as any node may (REQ-1922); what it cannot do is land data that people in its own region are not allowed to see. So a copy holds exactly what an administrator in that region may see: the copy in a country's region includes what may be held in the country, and the copy elsewhere leaves it out. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1921 amendment, 2026-10-04 -- a view may name a region. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] No view declares a region and none is inferred from its tables; a copy resides in the view storage of the region that built it, and what it holds follows from the rules. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] A reader is served from the copy in the region they connected to, with their own rules applied on top. A view whose definition aggregates therefore gives each region the aggregate over what that region may hold, and the same view can return different figures in different regions. That is the rule working, and the admin pages say which region's copy a figure came from. (Amended 2026-10-02, ROW-LEVEL REPLICATION) Row-level replication follows the same rule as a materialized view. The rows a request causes to be fetched from a source and kept are moved by the organisation's administrator taken to be in the region of the node doing the fetch, so the fetch carries that region's row and column rules and only what the region may hold is kept there. The kept rows are one shared copy per region, not a copy per role; each reader's own rules are applied afterwards, when the statement runs over the kept rows, as they are today. So a reader outside a country cannot cause a row that must stay in the country to be kept in their region. (Amended 2026-10-03, HOT COUNTS ARE THE HOME REGION'S:) A table's Hot count (REQ-239) is the traffic of its home region only. (Amended 2026-10-03, A TABLE'S REGION IS ONE OF ITS ORG'S REGIONS:) The region a table or source names as its home must be one of the regions its org has selected (REQ-1922). Any other is refused at save and at load, with an error naming the org's regions. (Amended 2026-10-04, A VIEW MAY NAME A REGION:) A materialized view may name a region, one of its org's regions. A view that names a region is built and refreshed only by that region, governed as the organisation's administrator with that region as its region attribute, and kept in that region's view storage. A reader who connects through another region is served from that copy, read in place at the address the model gives with the reader's row and column rules on the view in the statement, exactly as a table that names a region is served from its home region's replica; when the copy has not been built or its region cannot be reached, the request is refused naming the region. The copy holds what an administrator in its region may see, so what other regions read from it, including aggregates over rows their own rules would exclude, is the operator's decision; keeping the view's rules consistent with the rules on its tables is the operator's responsibility, as the choice to name a region is. A view that names no region is built in every region as above. The record of each request names the region whose copy served it. (Amended 2026-10-04, A TABLE CARRIES ITS OWN REGION; A SOURCE'S REGION IS ITS DEFAULT:) The region that decides where a table's whole-table copies may be kept is the region stored on the table, and only that. A source's region is a convenience for setting it -- the region a new table of the source starts with -- not a region its tables take at run time, so changing a source's region later moves none of its existing tables. When a table is registered through the admin, its region starts as its source's region, or, when the source names none, as the region the operator is connected to; the operator may change it, and a table has no region only when the operator removes it explicitly. A configuration file is explicit: a table it declares with no region has no region, whatever its source names, and copies of it may be kept in every region; a source's region in a file is a default only for tables later registered through the admin. A materialized view created through the admin starts with the region the operator is connected to, and is otherwise the same: stored on the view, changed or removed only by the operator. When a table's or view's region changes, every region that is no longer allowed a copy of it removes the copy it holds. None of this applies when the platform declares no regions (REQ-1922). (Amended 2026-10-04, A REGION GOVERNS WHERE DATA MAY BE, A DOMAIN GOVERNS WHO OWNS IT:) The two are kept apart. A domain is ownership -- who may change a table, its row and column rules, its masks and grants, a relationship (both stewards agreeing), a glossary term or any other object -- and every question of who may edit an object is answered by domain reach and the domain's stewards, wherever the object's data lives. A region is cross-border data movement and nothing else: where whole-table copies and view copies may be kept, where another region reads them from, and, through the row and column rules, what crosses. A region confers no right and is not a dimension of access or of administration; an organisation that wants a region's tables administered by that region's people gives them domains owned by those people. They meet at one point only. Setting, changing or removing the region of a table, a source or a materialized view is a decision about where data may physically go, so it requires the right data_residency in addition to owning the object through its domain; an organisation can give that right to its compliance function alone, and a domain steward without it manages everything else about the object but cannot move its data across a border. A save that sets, changes or removes a region without data_residency is refused, naming the right. The right exists only when the platform declares regions. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1921 amendment NO REGION IS A REGION A GRANT NAMES, 2026-10-04 -- no region is now one of the values a grant covers, and a move between regions is made through draft. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] (Amended 2026-10-04, DATA_RESIDENCY NAMES ITS REGIONS:) A grant of data_residency names the regions of the organisation it covers. Setting a region on an object that has none requires covering that region; removing an object's region requires covering the region removed; changing it from one region to another requires covering both. No region is no one's jurisdiction and needs nothing. So an object moves from one region to another either by one holder who covers both, or by agreement between two -- the holder for the first region removes its region and the holder for the second sets theirs. While the object has no region, whole-table copies of it are allowed in every region, as for any object with none; the holder who removes a region accepts that, and can keep it from happening by setting replicate Never first. A save outside the grant is refused, naming the region it does not cover. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1921 amendment DRAFT IS ITS OWN SETTING, 2026-10-04 -- draft is a setting of its own on a table or view, not a region value. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] (Amended 2026-10-04, DRAFT:) Besides the org's regions and no region, an object's region may be draft. A draft table, source or materialized view is out of service -- it is neither readable nor writable on any surface, no data surface offers it in its schema or catalog, and a statement that names it is refused, naming it as draft; no region builds a copy of it, and every copy that exists is removed. It stays fully editable in the admin by its domain's owners. Like no region, draft is no one's jurisdiction, so a holder of data_residency for region A may set an object from A to draft and a holder for region B may set it from draft to B -- a move between regions passes through draft and no data is held or read anywhere in between. Draft exists only when the platform declares regions. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] (Amended 2026-10-04, DRAFT IS ITS OWN SETTING:) Draft is a setting of a table or a materialized view of its own, beside its region, and exists whether or not the platform declares regions. While it is set the object is out of service: neither readable nor writable on any surface, offered in no data surface's schema or catalog, and a statement that names it is refused naming it as draft; no copy of it is built in any region and every copy that exists is removed. It stays fully editable in the admin, and the object returns to service when its domain's owners clear the setting. Setting and clearing it is part of owning the object through its domain and needs no other right. A move between regions can therefore be made with nothing held or read anywhere in between: the owner sets draft, the holder of data_residency for the first region removes its region, the holder for the second sets theirs, and the owner clears draft. (Amended 2026-10-04, A NEW TABLE OR VIEW STARTS AS DRAFT:) As a glossary term starts proposed (REQ-1835), a table or materialized view registered or created through the admin starts as draft -- including each table a bulk or discovery registration creates -- and serves nothing until its domain's owners release it by clearing the setting. A configuration file is explicit: a table or view it declares is draft only when the file says so. The admin lists show each object's status beside its region and can filter by it. (Amended 2026-10-04, AUTHORED IN DEVELOPMENT, RELEASED WHOLE:) Regions, draft and data_residency are authoring concerns. The model is built, reviewed and tested in a development environment and released to production by promotion, where it is not edited; there only who holds which rights changes, through the organisation's identity system. A promotion applies a released change in one step, so a move between regions authored through draft arrives in production with no state in between. A draft object may be promoted and stays out of service there until a later release clears it. (Amended 2026-10-04, NO REGION IS A REGION A GRANT NAMES; DRAFT RELEASES AN OBJECT TO BE CLAIMED:) A grant of data_residency names the values it covers, and no region is one of them, alongside the organisation's regions. Making an object global is a decision of its own, which an organisation can keep to a few. Changing an object's region from one value to another requires a grant covering both. While an object is draft it is released -- out of service, with no copy anywhere -- and its region may be changed by a holder whose grant covers the new value alone. So a move between regions is made by the first region's side setting draft and the second region's holder claiming the object by setting their region, and the object returns to service when draft is cleared. A save outside these rules is refused, naming the value the grant does not cover. (Amended 2026-10-05, A ROW-LEVEL TABLE IS READ ONLY IN THE REGION THAT KEEPS ITS ROWS:) A table replicated by row (REQ-1865) that names a region has its rows fetched and kept only by that region, and only for that region's own reads; no other region fetches a row of it into its storage. Where the home region's engine cannot read the table's source in place, the home keeps only the rows its own reads asked for by key, so the table is not readable from another region. A request through another region that reads it is refused, naming the table and its home region, before any row is fetched. Where the home region's engine reads the source in place, the table is not row-replicated there either, and another region reads it in place under the reader's rules exactly as any table its home reads in place, or is refused naming the region when its own engine cannot. None of this applies when the platform declares no regions. Amended 2026-10-08, A DRAFT'S OWNERS MAY LOOK AT IT: a caller holding the right to register tables in a draft's domain can preview and profile that draft in the admin before releasing it, with that caller's masks, row rules and limits applied as for a served table, and the read is audited as a draft preview. A draft stays out of service on every data surface, where naming it by any of its names, the domain-qualified one included, is refused as a draft and not as an unknown table. Where preview is offered the table is marked as a draft, and a caller without the right sees the control disabled with that reason.

Regions: separate clusters on one shared model. A deployment may run more than one Provisa cluster off a single model store (REQ-1919). The model -- every source, table, relationship, role, rule, view, freshness setting and limit -- is declared once and is the same for every cluster, so definitions cannot diverge between regions. Everything else belongs to a cluster. Each cluster is in one region and has its own nodes (REQ-1916), its own engine, its own storage for replicas and materialized views, its own cache, its own state store (REQ-1920), its own record, and its own address. A node is started for one cluster and region. Clients connect to a region by its address. What a reader may see is decided by the model's rules on the reader's attributes, the same in every region; where the work is done and where anything is kept is decided by the cluster the reader connected to. A reader in a country who connects to that country's address is served by nodes, an engine, storage and a cache that are all in the country; a reader elsewhere is served by another cluster and receives what the rules allow. Reach is not what separates regions. Every source of every region, and every region's stores, are declared in the one model, so any node can reach any of them; the rules say what it may do with them. The row and column rules decide what a reader gets, and a table's region decides where whole-table copies of it are built (REQ-1921). So a table that names a region is served to readers in other regions from that region's replica, read in place under the reader's rules. What is per cluster is the work and what it leaves: each cluster builds and refreshes only its own replicas and views, writes only its own cache, state store and record, which stay in its region, and applies the limits on background work (REQ-1915) to itself. A change to the model reaches every cluster by the same stamp (REQ-1914); each cluster then converges on its own. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1922 amendment, 2026-10-03 -- the platform declares the physical regions; each org's model selects the regions it uses and declares its own stores in each. Branded source types implemented over the generic API sources. A branded source is a named source type (Stripe, HubSpot, GitHub and so on) that adds only what is specific to that system on top of a generic source Provisa already has, and never a connector of its own. Two generic sources carry them. One, the remote GraphQL source, for a system whose API is GraphQL. GitHub is the first, reached by the generic connector with its schema loaded from a baked artifact (REQ-1875). Two, the OpenAPI source (REQ-314..321), for a system whose vendor publishes a usable OpenAPI spec. The preset is a pinned spec, an auth template, the pagination of each list operation, and, where the API offers one, the parameter a refresh uses to pull only what changed. A preset chooses no subset of the API. Adding a branded source makes every table the system offers available and registers none of them; the steward registers the tables wanted, as for any source, and that registration is the curation. A spec is usable only when it is well typed: every list operation chosen as a table declares a response schema with named, typed properties, since the table's columns are read from it (REQ-316). A spec whose responses are untyped objects, or absent, does not qualify, and a preset never patches the gap with a hand-written schema of its own. The steward picks the brand name and supplies credentials; nothing else is asked. A branded source is always a replica, like every OpenAPI and remote GraphQL source. Each system in that catalog is investigated on its own and given one verdict: GraphQL preset, OpenAPI preset, wrapper, direct loader, already covered, or dropped. The mechanism is never shown to the user; they see the brand name as an ordinary source type. (Amended 2026-10-02, GITHUB AS BUILT) GitHub is the first brand. It is picked as GitHub in the source list, asks for an access token and an optional table name prefix, and is shown as GitHub afterwards; the source row is a remote GraphQL source that records its brand. The token goes to the org's secrets vault and the row carries the reference, so a restarted process reads the source again without the token being re-entered. The tables on offer are listed by the Register Table picker from the schema that ships with Provisa (REQ-1875), and a table is registered through the same mutation every source uses. Three things are particular to a brand and declared by it, never inferred. One, the error type its remote returns, before running a query, for a field outside the credential's grant. When a table is registered its query is offered to the remote once, each field so refused is left out of the table, and the registration names what was left out; a table the credential may not read at all is refused with the remote's reason. Two, the error types its remote returns beside the data for one field of one row. That field is null in that row, as the remote returned it, the read stands, and the error is logged; an error naming the table itself fails the read. Three, the error types that mean a page asked for more than the remote computes in one query. The page is asked for again at half the size. Such a system cannot serve a wide table whole, so its tables are registered with the columns wanted. Description: Per-source cap on concurrent live reads. A source carries `max_live_concurrency` (an integer of 1 or more; unset means no cap, the behavior before this requirement). It bounds how many queries read that source live at the same time, on every route that reaches the source live: the DIRECT route, and the ENGINE route when the bound engine reads the source in place through its declared attach connector (DuckDB scans, the Postgres engine's foreign tables, Trino connectors). A source read through its replica (`replicate`, REQ-826; `load_protected`, REQ-1141; or an engine without an attach connector for it) is not a live read and takes no permit. The cap is an operator setting and part of the operator floor (REQ-030): no per-request input raises or bypasses it. It is the middle ground between never live (always replicated or load-protected) and unbounded live reads, for an upstream with load concerns that cannot manage its own backpressure. Permits are held from the start of execution until the result is fully delivered, failed, or cancelled, including for streamed results. A query that reads several capped sources live acquires one permit per source in sorted source-id order before execution, so two queries can never deadlock holding permits the other needs. A query that cannot get a permit waits, bounded by its remaining request deadline, and then fails with an error naming the source and its cap; it never falls back to another route or to a replica. With a real Redis the cap is cluster-wide: every Provisa instance sharing that Redis draws from one permit set per (org, source), a Redis sorted set of leases. Each permit is a lease that its holder renews while the query runs, so a permit held by a crashed instance expires on its own. With embedded fakeredis (no Redis URL) the cap applies per process. The setting is edited in the source form's "Load Management and Timeliness" panel and through the existing source create/update admin mutation, alongside the panel's other source settings (cache_ttl, change_signal, sentinel_path, freshness_gate, replicate, load_protected, off_peak_window, off_peak_tz), all validated with the same rules the config loader applies. (Amended 2026-10-05, DuckDB connection pools:) On the DuckDB engine a PostgreSQL source with `max_live_concurrency` set is attached with its own connection-pool size of `max_live_concurrency // workers` (the launch's worker count; 1 outside a launch) and an acquire mode of `wait`. A scan that finds every pooled connection taken waits for one (bounded by the extension's wait timeout) instead of opening another. Without this the postgres extension keeps up to 18 connections per attached database and connects past that limit, so the permits capped queries but not the connections a worker held to the source. A source with no cap keeps the extension's default pool. A cap below the worker count cannot be divided (a worker's pool holds at least one connection) and is refused by name, at save (`schema.max_live_concurrency_below_workers`, when the acting org runs on DuckDB) and at attach. Sources the engine reaches through its local pgwire child (Calcite-backed connectors) are not affected; that server is Provisa's own, not the source's connection budget.

Description: One write admission. Every data write on every surface (SQL over HTTP, pgwire, Flight SQL, MCP, Cypher over HTTP, Bolt, GraphQL) is admitted in one place in the semantic layer, and no surface carries a check of its own. A write is admitted by three things. The role holds the `write` right (REQ-868). Each column written lists the role in its `writable_by` (REQ-663): a column that declares none is writable by nobody, a DELETE and a MERGE need every column of the table, and visibility and masking neither grant nor deny a write. The role's row filter applies to the rows the statement touches (UPDATE, DELETE) and to the rows it writes: an INSERT or UPDATE that would leave a row outside the role's filter is refused, and an UPDATE by a filtered role that sets a filter column from row-dependent values is refused. Where the check is evaluated in process it never admits on doubt. One after-write step (`after_table_written`) runs on every surface: cached responses for the table are dropped, materialized views that read it are marked stale, change events and sinks fire, hot tables reload, and a replica rebuild is requested for a table that has a whole copy. A WRITE IS ALSO BOUNDED BY WHAT THE TABLE CAN TAKE. Each table has a write capability per operation (insert, update, delete), derived from its source and its registered write operations: a GraphQL source whose mutations do not follow the expected pattern, or a table read from Neo4j by a query, cannot take every write. A write the table cannot take is refused before the rights checks, with an error naming the table, the operation and that the source does not support it. Mutations and write routes are offered on every surface only for the operations the table supports, and the admin page shows which.

Nothing is defined through a query protocol. An object is defined in the model, or in the source and then admitted into the model; changing the contents of an object is a write (REQ-1925), creating, altering or deleting one is not. CREATE, DROP and ALTER are refused on every surface by one refusal in the semantic layer, Cypher included, where the refusal is made before the statement is lowered to SQL. The one exception is a session's own temporary tables. pgwire answers the refusal with SQLSTATE 0A000. There is no `ddl` capability, no `ddl_catalog` and no `ddl_schema`; a configuration that carries either field fails validation. No client statement registers a table into a role's context, client CREATE TABLE AS is refused, and the Airport create_schema, drop_schema and create_table calls are refused. (Amended 2026-10-19, TRUNCATE IS A DATA WRITE:) TRUNCATE is not refused here; REQ-1942 supersedes this requirement's TRUNCATE clause, and a TRUNCATE is a write admitted by the one write admission.

Every admin handler is gated. Each handler under /admin, in the mounted application with its sub-applications and in the admin GraphQL schema, reaches an authorization gate, or is named on an exemption list together with the reason it needs none. A test walks every handler's call graph, including its dependency callables, and fails the build for a handler that reaches no gate and for an exemption that no longer matches an ungated handler.

GraphQL is the canonical API, and gRPC, JSON:API and OpenAPI are derived from it. Everything a surface offers a role -- tables, columns, relationships, aggregates, filter arguments and commands -- comes from that role's compiled GraphQL schema: each role's gRPC .proto, its OpenAPI spec with the REST routes it describes, and its JSON:API resources are generated from that schema, as REST already is (REQ-256). The decision of what a role is offered (assignment, domain, kind, name, column visibility) is made once, in the role's GraphQL schema. No surface keeps visibility or naming logic of its own: whatever GraphQL offers a role, every other surface offers under its own wire conventions, and nothing more. COMMANDS: the other surfaces derive their command operations from the role's GraphQL command fields, never from the raw command list (REQ-1156). A field on Query, a query-kind command, is a read: REST `GET` with the same where, order_by, limit and offset parameters tables take; a gRPC RPC returning rows; a JSON:API read under its conventions for non-resource operations. A field on Mutation is a write: REST `POST`, a gRPC RPC, and a JSON:API write. Arguments and return types follow the GraphQL field. A command a role's GraphQL schema does not offer is not offered on any other surface. Every call is still checked by the one command admission in the executor, as defence in depth. NAMES follow each API's own conventions. GraphQL enforces cross-domain access control by not exposing cross-domain tables as root types; they are only reachable as nested fields via registered relationships.
