The federation engine is selectable from a registry. The registry lists every selectable engine with a label, a description and a config schema; each config field names the platform-config key it persists to and declares a type of string, number, boolean or select. Embedded (Provisa-managed) and bring-your-own variants of an engine are separate entries: the embedded Trino entry carries node role and execution tuning, the bring-your-own entry carries only the connection. An administrator with platform-settings rights reads the persisted selection, the running engine, any environment pin and the registry from GET /admin/federation-engine, and persists a selection with PUT /admin/federation-engine, which rejects a key not in the registry and stores only the fields the chosen engine declares, resetting keys declared only by other engines. The change takes effect at the next service restart, because the engine is bound once at boot. The admin UI renders the selector and the selected engine's fields generically from the registry.

Encryption is configured from the admin UI. The registry of encryption providers is shown with each provider's label, description, availability and config fields; a provider whose runtime is not installed is shown but cannot be saved, so selection fails closed. An administrator with platform-settings rights reads the selected provider, the key id and whether a local master key is present, and saves a provider with its own config fields; the provider binds at startup, so a provider change takes effect on restart. A fresh AES-256 master key can be provisioned into the OS keychain, or the host file keystore, under a key id; provisioning takes effect immediately, without a restart, by rebuilding the live encryption service on the same provider. The key is never returned: when no keystore can hold it, provisioning refuses and the operator supplies the key out of band through PROVISA_ENCRYPTION_KEY. (Amended 2026-10-07, maintainer: provision only.) A key is provisioned only while none exists: once a key is present for the key id, or the deployment has recorded the key its secrets are written under, provisioning is refused and the key is shown by its fingerprint. No surface offers to replace a master key, because replacing it loses every secret written under it.

The authentication provider is configured from the admin UI. The registry lists the providers none, firebase, keycloak, oauth/OIDC and simple, each with its config fields, secret fields marked. An administrator with platform-settings rights reads the selected provider, the per-provider config and the common role settings (default role, assignments source, trust upstream, allow simple auth) from GET /admin/auth, and saves them with PUT /admin/auth. An unknown provider is rejected with a 400, and only the config keys the chosen provider declares are persisted. The provider binds at startup, so a change takes effect after a service restart. Secret fields, the simple provider's JWT signing secret and client secrets, are write-only: the GET returns a bit saying whether a value is set, never the value.

An organization may hold its own API key for each LLM vendor whose provider takes a plain api key; the set is anthropic, openai, cohere, groq, mistral, xai, deepseek, together, fireworks, nebius, sambanova and inception, plus a separate Jev key. The keys are org secrets, encrypted at rest, and an administrator sets, replaces or clears them on Admin / AI Models; a blank value clears a vendor's key. The keys are write-only: the surface reports only which vendors have a key set, never a value. When the org's LLM calls, model listing and natural-language queries build a client, they use the org's key for the role's vendor; a vendor with no org key falls through to the deployment's environment credential. Vendors whose auth needs more than a key, and keyless local endpoints, are not offered. A stored value may be a ${secret:NAME} reference to the org vault, resolved when the client is built (REQ-1580).

Description: Query results are cached in a Redis-backed application-layer cache behind a CacheStore interface: get, set with TTL, invalidate by key pattern, invalidate by table id. Cache check runs before execution and store after, transparently; a miss executes normally. Redis is optional at startup: with no Redis URL a no-op store is used and caching is disabled. (Cache control per source/table is Phase Z; per-request opt-in is amended into REQ-544.)
Provisa mutations (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) invalidate cache entries that reference the mutated table.

Materialized views are invisible in the GraphQL SDL by default: users query the same schema and the optimization is transparent. An MV registry stores definitions, last refresh time, target table, row count and status (fresh, stale, refreshing, disabled), and the steward controls MV lifecycle (create, refresh schedule, enable/disable, drop).
Mutations on source tables mark affected materialized views as stale; a stale view is not used for rewrite and the original SQL executes.

The MV rewrite runs after row-level security is applied: the rewritten query keeps the WHERE clauses and parameters injected for row-level security, carried onto the view's columns; a predicate the view cannot carry leaves the query to its tables.

A steward may set expose_in_sdl: true on an MV definition. The MV target table is then registered as a table with its own columns, domain and visibility rules and appears as a queryable type in the schema, under the same governance (RLS, column visibility) as any registered table.

Kafka topic registration as data source: register a Kafka cluster (bootstrap servers, auth); each topic + schema becomes a registered table, schema from Schema Registry, manual JSON schema, or sample message inference; the engine Kafka connector handles reads; primitives become native columns, complex nested values become JSONB; complex objects are not filterable and carry no relationships.

The Relationship model accepts an optional alias field, a relationship type name (for example WORKS_FOR) that defaults to None. The alias is persisted with the relationship row and exposed to the Cypher label map.
A relationship alias is unique per source table. Saving a second relationship with the same alias on the same source table fails with a ValueError naming the alias and the source table.

CypherLabelMap indexes relationships by alias so a Cypher relationship type written as the alias resolves to the mapped source and target tables. RelationshipMapping carries the alias, defaulting to None, and a wrong arrow direction or unknown type yields an empty result.
When several source/target pairs share one relationship alias, the aliases index stores every mapping under that alias and the Cypher translator emits a UNION ALL across them.

Registered commands (tracked functions and webhooks) appear as POST paths /{domain}/commands/{name} in the REST OpenAPI spec, filtered by domain and by the role's visible_to, with argument types mapped to OpenAPI schemas and one path per command despite prefixed aliases. Natural-language jobs and /nl-to-sql take a strict flag. Strict mode runs one NL to GraphQL to SQL to Cypher chain, schema-validated, shared by the graphql, sql and cypher branches, so join reachability and aggregate shape come from the schema's relationships. Non-strict generates SQL and GraphQL directly and independently from the LLM and derives Cypher from the SQL result. grpc, jsonapi and openapi are unaffected. Defaults: /nl-to-sql True, NL job and nl_router False.

A sandbox visitor's account is deleted when the visitor leaves the sandbox. Signing out of the sandbox org asks the visitor to confirm, and on confirmation the visitor's sign-in identity at the identity provider, their sandbox membership and role assignments, and their profile are removed. The deletion is refused unless the sandbox is the caller's only org membership, so an account that also belongs to another org is never deleted this way. The identity provider's record is deleted first, so a failure there leaves the rest in place.

The platform state store. The control plane has three stores. The model store (REQ-1919) holds the model, per org, shared by all the org's regions, and projected to git. The state store (REQ-1920) holds operating state and the request record, per org and region. The platform state store holds platform-level operating state: there is one per deployment, in the platform database. What it holds is never part of a model, never projected to git, and never copied, exported or deployed with an environment. Its first members are the node heartbeat and cluster node list (REQ-1916) and the consistent-masking surrogate mapping (REQ-1494); the mapping is durable and cannot be rebuilt, so a member of this store is not assumed to be discardable the way state in the state store is. platform_admin has no data access here either (REQ-1327): the store's contents are readable through an admin API only as far as each member's own requirement says.

A registered table's SQL address is unique within its domain. The address is the domain's SQL name and the table's name in it: its alias, else its registered name under the naming rules, as the compiler spells it. Registration refuses a table whose address another registered table in that domain already holds, and the refusal names the table that holds it; the operator gives the new table a different name or alias, or registers it in another domain. The refusal is at the one write path the admin and config load share, so a config file that declares two tables at one address fails its load the same way. A table the same config load removes, because its file no longer declares it, holds no address against the tables that file declares. A name is never qualified with its schema or source to make it unique, and no rule chooses between two tables at one address: which table kept the bare name was only the order the tables were listed in, and two tables of one exact name both kept it, so a statement read whichever the compiler met first. A model that holds two tables at one address is an error when the schema is built.

Description: A DATA PROFILER is a source type, registered and used the way the data-quality checker sources are (REQ-1443, REQ-1663). A profile is an observation about a governed table, so it is DATA: it lands through the ordinary source path and inherits cadence, freshness, events, lineage, governance, row and column rules, the grid and export instead of building them. Lineage runs from the profiled table to its profile, derived from the table's membership of the profiler and never hand-declared. Each profiled table has its own result tables, never tables shared across the estate; an estate-wide view is a materialized view over them.  A profiler source and its members. A Data Profiler source holds a name, a schedule and its run defaults and nothing else. The schedule is a recurrence of the kind scheduled triggers use, for example daily at 02:00. The run defaults are the whole table or a sample above a stated size, the low-cardinality limit, the bounds on dependence work, the drift window and its season, and the drift thresholds, each with a field on the profiler's form. The source is never introspected and shows no schema or table picker. A table joins a profiler from the table editor: Add to Profiler lists the profiler sources with their schedules and the operator picks one; a table belongs to at most one, and moving it is removing and adding. A member table's editor offers Remove from Profiler, Run Profile Now and View Profile Runs. A profiler source can also be run at once for all its member tables.  THE PROFILER IS BUILT IN: unlike a checker it is not an external prerequisite. A run reads the table through the one governed pipeline as the organisation's administrator, in the region of the node that runs it, with that region as its region attribute (REQ-1921), so it describes exactly the rows and values that administrator may read there. That administrator's row rules and masks, a region rule among them, apply to the read, no reader's rules do, and nothing else alters the result. Each region profiles for itself, and no region's profile is copied to another. The core measures come from one statement of aggregates pushed down to the engine, over the whole table or a sample whose size the run defaults state and the results record; a sampled run counts the table's rows first, so every run, the first included, samples at the stated size. Fits are computed from that statement's aggregates, never a second scan; dependence between columns takes a few further aggregate statements over the same sample. Each run is written once, in one form.  What a run records, per column: data type, row count, null count, approximate distinct count, minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, quantiles, a histogram and the most frequent values, which are kept for every column; for text, the length range and distribution and the most common value shapes -- each value with its characters reduced to classes (an upper-case letter A, a lower-case letter a, a digit 9, other characters kept) -- with their frequencies. For each numeric and temporal column it also records what describes its distribution: a 101-point quantile sketch, its moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, and the mean and variance of the logarithm where every value is positive), whether every value is an integer, the share of zeros, the ratio of distinct values to rows, the full value frequencies when the column has no more distinct values than the low-cardinality limit, and closed-form fits of the normal, log-normal, exponential, uniform and gamma families (Poisson and negative binomial for integers), each with its goodness of fit against the sketch and a rank.  Plausible type. Each run records, per column, its plausible type -- what the column holds, inferred from its profile, name and tags -- one of email, person name (first, last or full), phone, address part (street, city, region, postal code or country), url, identifier or code, category, free text, numeric distribution, temporal, boolean or unknown, with a confidence and a short statement of the evidence. It is a label, not a value.  Fan-out and duplicates. For each declared relationship where the profiled table is the parent, a run records the distribution of children per parent: its quantile sketch, mean, maximum, the share of parents without children and the number of parents. Each run records the table's duplicate rows -- the rows that repeat another row in every profiled column, as a count and a share of the rows read, with the most repeated rows' repeat counts -- and, where the table declares a primary or unique key, the key values held by more than one row, as a count.  Dependence between columns. A run records a rank-correlation matrix over the numeric columns and the categories, each category entering as the slice of 0 to 1 its share occupies, never as an arbitrary number; for each category and number pair, the share of the number's spread the category explains; and a dependency network, each column with the set of up to two columns, its own table's or its parent table's through a relationship, that tell most about it, with that set's mutual information and the joint counts of categories and bucketed numbers it rests on. A readable ranking lists, for each column, the columns and sets it depends on most strongly. The run defaults bound the work: the most numeric columns entered in the matrix, and the most distinct values a category may have to enter a joint count.  Freshness. Each run records the table's freshness: the time from its newest row, by the column the table names as its watermark, to the run. A table naming no watermark records no freshness.  Comparison with the previous run. Each run compares itself with the table's previous successful run, as a measure of the current run recorded with it: the change in row count and in duplicate rows; columns added, removed or changed in type; for each column the change in null share, distinct ratio, minimum, maximum and mean, and the shift between the two runs' quantile sketches (the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and the population stability index); categories that appeared or vanished and the largest changes in category shares; the shift in each relationship's fan-out; and correlations and dependencies that strengthened or weakened. A table's first run records that it has no previous run.  Drift across runs. Each run also measures how it stands against the trend of the table's recent runs, over a window of previous successful runs set in the run defaults. The window may follow a season -- none, daily, weekly or monthly -- so a run is measured against the previous runs at the same point in the season, the last Mondays for a Monday run; the window then holds that many runs at that point. For each measure, freshness and row count included, a run records the window's baseline (its median) and spread (the median absolute deviation, so one past outlier does not widen the band), how far the run lies from the baseline in units of the spread, the slope of the measure over the window's run times, so a gradual drift no single step reveals is caught, and, for each column's distribution and each category's shares, the shift from the window's pooled distribution (the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and the population stability index). A measure is marked drifting where its distance, slope or distribution shift passes the profiler's thresholds. Until the table has as many previous successful runs as the window holds, a run's drift measures -- baseline, spread, distance, slope, distribution shift and the drifting flag -- are null and the run records how many previous runs it had; the comparison with the previous run is still recorded from a table's second run.  Constraints. A profile proposes constraints its evidence supports -- a column never null, a column unique, a column holding only its recorded values, a number within its observed range, one date never before another -- each with the evidence for it, the share of rows it held for, and the sample it rests on. Nothing is applied by proposing it. The operator accepts, edits or dismisses each one in the table editor; an accepted constraint becomes a check on the table's data quality, flagged when a later run or load breaks it, and binds synthetic generation (REQ-1939). Every run checks the table's accepted constraints and records, for each, the share of rows that met it and the number that broke it, as measures of the run, compared and marked for drift as the other measures are. The operator may export an accepted constraint as a check of a data-quality checker source whose contract scans the table, so it runs on that source's own schedule; export is refused by name where no such source exists.  Exceptions come from checkers. The profiler records drift and does not raise exceptions. Its drift results are a result table a data-quality checker source can scan -- one row per measure per run, with the measure, its baseline, spread, distance, slope, distribution shift and drifting flag -- and an exception is raised by registering that table and pointing a Soda or Great Expectations checker source at it, with checks such as no drifting measure in the latest run or a column's population stability index under a bound; the checker source's own schedule, history and notifications then apply, each check setting its own thresholds. View Profile Runs offers Create drift check, which adds the check that the latest run has no drifting measure to a checker source already scanning the registered drift table, and is refused by name where none does. A run's measures may also be checked against expectations produced outside Provisa -- by a person, a spreadsheet or a forecasting model -- held in any registered table of the published expectations shape (measure, column, period start, period end, low, expected, high, source), where measure names any measure of a run, a constraint's pass share among them. View Profile Runs offers Create expectation check, which, for a chosen registered table of that shape, adds to a checker source already scanning the registered profile results a check that the latest run's measures lie within the low and high of the expectation whose period holds the run; it is refused by name where no such checker source exists or the table is not of the shape. The expectations table is governed as any table is.  THE RESULTS SCHEMA IS FIXED AND SHIPPED. The results are a historical record -- every run is kept, keyed by its run identifier with its run time as the watermark, and nothing is overwritten -- laid out as related tables rather than one table packed with structured values, each readable at its latest run as well. A profiler's result tables for a member table are named <table>_<id>_profile_<kind>, so two profiled tables of the same name each have their own. The kinds are runs (one row per run with its time, region, row count, sampling and outcome), columns (one row per column per run with its shape and scalar measures, naming each column's physical column too), quantiles (with a measure of value or length), histogram, top_values (the most frequent values, and the full value frequencies of a column under the low-cardinality limit), fits, fit_quality, fanout, fanout_runs, shapes, plausible_type, correlations, dependencies, joint_counts and drift.  Exposure by registration. A profiler's results are exposed only by registration: its catalog lists the result tables it produces for each member table, and registering one is the ordinary curation step, after which grants decide who reads it. With no registration no reader sees any profile, and viewing a table never shows its profile to a reader not granted it. A registered result table is an ordinary governed table: its own grants, masks and row rules decide who reads which of its rows and columns, as for any table, and the profile carries no further per-reader treatment. The registration form starts from the profiled table's rules. The roles that may read the profiled table may read the result table, and each described column's rows are visible, and its values masked, to the same roles as that column. The operator may change any of it before saving; once saved, the result table's rules are its own and do not follow later changes to the profiled table.  View Profile Runs. Opened from the table registry and shown only to those who may edit the table, it shows the table's run history and results, each run safe for the person viewing it, worked out when it is shown from that viewer's roles and the profiled table's current rules: a column the viewer may not see is left out; a column masked to the viewer or tagged pii shows its shares, data type, length range and plausible type, with its values -- minimum, maximum, quantiles, histogram, most frequent values, shapes and fitted parameters -- left out; every other column shows in full. It shows each run's comparison with the previous run beside the run, and a measure's history across the drift window with its drift marked, safe for its viewer as the run is. The table view's Quick Profile -- a sample computed in the browser and stored nowhere -- stays as it is. The result kinds also include duplicates and repeats (the duplicate rows and duplicate keys of a run), constraints (the proposals and their decisions) and constraint_checks (each accepted constraint's pass share and violations per run). A profiler's run defaults also bound the number of category columns entered in the correlation matrix and the joint counts, the most frequent categories being kept.

Under multitenancy a request acts in the org it names, and there is no implied org. A principal holding the cross_org right who names no org is refused by name on every surface, as any principal is: HTTP answers 401 naming the subdomain and the X-Org-Provisa header, with the code auth.org_selection_required, which the UI answers with a prompt to select one of the caller's orgs (or, when the caller belongs to none, to ask an organization administrator for an invitation); pgwire, Bolt, Flight, gRPC and MCP refuse the session naming how that surface names an org. The break-glass account likewise names its org by its subdomain and is refused when it names none. The platform-plane routes (/auth/, /setup, /admin/orgs, /billing) still serve a request that names no org, with no org bound. A cross_org principal naming an org acts in it. A single-tenant deployment is unchanged: its one org is the answer.

A browser session's stored bearer is cleared only when the identity provider says the credential is dead (signed out, revoked, or a refresh rejected for the credential itself). A failure to reach the provider -- a network error, a timeout, rate limiting, or the provider's internal error (Firebase auth/network-request-failed, auth/timeout, auth/too-many-requests, auth/internal-error) -- is not a signed-out state: the stored bearer is kept, the request that needed a fresh one uses it, and the next request asks the provider again (REQ-1434). Treating a transient failure as sign-out deleted a still-valid bearer on a network blip and forced a sign-in the user did not ask for.

Every results grid -- the SQL explorer's results, the admin reports and the governed table viewer, which share one grid -- filters each column Excel-style, typed by the column's type, beyond today's case-insensitive contains. Each column's filter offers operators for its type: text (contains, equals, starts with, ends with, does not contain, is empty); numbers (=, not =, <, <=, >, >=, between); dates and times (before, after, between, and relative periods such as the last N days or this month); booleans and enumerations a checklist; every type is-empty and is-not-empty. A value checklist lists the column's distinct values in the rows the grid holds, with their counts and a search box, and filters to the values ticked. The column's filter box also takes a quick syntax -- >100, 10..20, !text, a, b, c, =exact -- and plain text keeps meaning contains, so nothing a reader types today changes meaning. A column's type comes from the result's column types, or is inferred from its values when the result carries none. Active filters show as removable chips above the grid, next to the clear-filters control (REQ-1442). Filters on several columns combine with AND. When the grid holds only part of the result -- cut at the row limit or with more pages to fetch -- it says the filter applies to the rows loaded, naming their count, so a filtered page is never read as the whole answer; the server-paged governed viewer sends the same typed filters into its query. A table-level builder with OR and nested groups is not part of this requirement. Every new label is translated in every locale.

The add-source form chooses its source type from a picker as well as its select. Browse opens a wide dialog listing the same grouped types the select lists, with the same reach labels and the same types disabled. A search box filters by name and common aliases (mssql finds SQL Server, pg finds PostgreSQL); a row of category chips, wrapping as needed, shows one category or all; a recently-used row, remembered per browser, leads when nothing is filtered. The categories are laid out as sections that pack into as many columns as the dialog's width fits, each type a compact row of its logo and name, so the whole list fits on one screen on a wide display and collapses to fewer columns on a narrow one. Logos are the source's published mark from simple-icons (CC0 icon data; each mark remains its owner's trademark and names the source only); a type with no published mark is a lettered tile in its category's colour. Up and Down move between rows, Enter picks, Escape closes. Picking a type sets the form's type exactly as choosing it in the select does. Every label is translated in every locale.

A synthetic dataset is a model object that fills an environment with generated data shaped like the estate it is drawn from, at a chosen scale, so tests run over larger volumes, or smaller ones, with similar processing characteristics. It is built from data profiles (REQ-1934), the model's relationships, and the fake attributes declared on columns (REQ-1494).  Definition. A synthetic dataset names its tables as pairs of a table and one of its profile runs, so it reproduces exactly and its tables describe the same moment, together with a scale factor, a seed and the environment it fills. The scale may be a fraction as well as a multiple (x0.5, x2, x10), and a table may carry its own scale to override it. A dataset that names a table without naming the parent of one of its relationships is refused, naming the missing parent. A dataset may name profile runs held by another environment of the same organisation. Its settings also include its conditional fan-out, its assertions, and its closeness threshold and number of draws, each with a field on its form.  Belongs to an environment. A synthetic dataset belongs to the environment it fills: it is defined, generated, regenerated and dropped from that environment in the admin, beside the environment's other settings, because an environment is where tests are built around a dataset; the production environment cannot hold one. It is generated into the environment's warehouse store (REQ-1493), in a schema of the dataset's own, whatever its size, and in that environment only its tables take the place of the real tables: each named table's binding there reads the synthetic copy, so queries and tests in the environment run against it while every other environment is unchanged. In a read-write environment its tables take writes through change logs in the environment's relational store (REQ-1493). Dropping the dataset restores the environment's bindings and removes its schema. Creating an environment may seed it with a synthetic dataset as an option: the operator names the tables, the environment whose profile runs describe them (typically production) and a scale, and the new environment is built on synthetic data shaped like that estate, so development starts on plausible data without any production row reaching it.  What generation keeps. Row counts follow the scale with the ratios between tables kept. Key uniqueness and density are kept. The number of children per parent for every relationship is drawn from its profiled distribution, kept at any scale, so join fan-out and its skew survive a reduction as well as a growth. A column whose distinct count follows its rows, by its profiled distinct ratio, scales with them; one that does not keeps its distinct count, its rarest values able to drop out at a small fraction. Frequencies keep the generated values' skew -- as many distinct values with the same shares -- so hot keys survive. Null and zero shares and integer-only columns are kept.  A column's fake settings decide its values. Every column is generated through the fake attributes declared on it (REQ-1494) -- its kind of fake, its arguments and whether it is stable -- the same declaration that masks it, so a column fakes alike whether it is masked or synthesised. A column with a declared fake kind has every value generated by that fake; a numeric or temporal column whose kind names a profile is drawn through that profile. A real value reaches a synthetic cell only through a column's declared categories fake. A column with no fake kind has every value generated from its profiled value shapes and lengths, so codes and references keep their format and proportions, or, for a number or date, drawn from its distribution through its quantile sketch, whatever the table's size and never from its recorded most frequent values. A boolean column with no fake kind is generated as if it declared bool(), true at its measured share and evenly on an empty table. A column tagged pii with no fake kind refuses the generation by name, listing every such column, until a fake kind is declared for it. The generation report names every column generated with no declared fake kind, so the operator sees what is undeclared.  Dependence kept. A synthetic dataset keeps the dependence its profile measured. Numbers and categories are drawn jointly through the profile's rank-correlation matrix, each mapped back through its own measured distribution or category shares; a column the dependency network ties to others is drawn after them, from the joint counts given their generated values, a parent table's columns included. A column with a declared fake keeps its fake, the dependence deciding only which of its values or which share is drawn.  Accepted constraints bind generation. A synthetic dataset honours the profiled table's accepted constraints (REQ-1934). A column constrained unique has unique generated values, a key or not; a column constrained never null has none; an accepted ordering between two date or time columns is generated as after or before, and one that one number never exceeds another as greater_than or less_than (REQ-1494), where the column declares no fake of its own.  Conditional fan-out. A synthetic dataset may give a relationship conditional child counts, each a condition on the parent row, in the sql subset of REQ-1494, and the number of children a parent meeting it is generated with -- a fixed count, a range drawn evenly, or the fan-out the profile measured for parents meeting the condition -- for example no shipments for an order whose status is cancelled, at least one reward for a gold member. The first condition a parent meets decides its count; a parent meeting none takes the relationship's measured fan-out.  Generation in passes. Generation runs in the engine, in parallel partitions written through the bulk load paths, so a dataset of billions of rows never passes through a client. It proceeds in passes, each a statement in the engine over the generated tables. First every row of every table is generated: parents before children, child counts decided by the conditional fan-out as the parent's children are generated, each row's independent fakes and then its relative fakes in the order their references require. Then every sql_group and sequence fake (REQ-1494) is computed, in the order its references require, since each reads rows the first pass produced: a window over a partition, a sum over a parent's children. Then every column whose fake names a sql_group column is computed again from the group value, in the order its references require. A cycle anywhere among a dataset's fakes is refused by name when the fakes are saved. The same seed and scale give the same data, so runs can be compared.  Not too close to a real row. When it generates, a synthetic dataset reads a sample of each table's real rows as the organisation's administrator through the governed pipeline, as a profile does, and measures each generated row's distance to its nearest real row over the columns with no declared fake, numbers scaled by their spread and categories counted as matching or not. A generated row nearer than the dataset's threshold, a share of the real rows' own typical distance to one another, is drawn again, and a row still too near after the dataset's stated number of draws is dropped and counted.  Assertions. A synthetic dataset may carry assertions, each a statement over its generated tables returning true or false, for example that every customer's amounts sum to zero. After generation each assertion runs and its result is reported with the statement; an assertion never rejects, regenerates or alters the generated data.  Differential privacy. A synthetic dataset may be declared private with a privacy budget ε, a setting with a field on its form. Before generation, calibrated noise -- the Laplace or Gaussian mechanism, accounted against ε -- is added to every statistic the generator draws from the profile: value frequencies and category shares, joint counts, the correlation matrix, quantile sketches, fan-out sketches and hot-key counts. Categories and joint-count cells below the threshold the noise implies are dropped, and hot keys keep only their noised counts, never exact ones. Faked reads are unaffected. A dataset not declared private carries no privacy guarantee, and its report says so.  Marking and the report. The generated tables are marked as generated (REQ-1495), and an environment filled this way holds no personal data (REQ-1493). After generation the synthetic tables are profiled and a comparison report compares them with the source profiles -- row ratios, fan-out, skew, null shares and distributions, the difference between the measured and generated correlations and dependencies, each conditional fan-out's parents and children, the distribution of generated rows' distances to the nearest real row beside the real rows' own and the rows redrawn and dropped, each assertion's result, and, for a private dataset, its ε, its mechanism and what the noise dropped -- so the reader can see how close they are. The report also gives named privacy measures: each generated row's distance to its closest real row and the nearest-neighbour distance ratio, each beside the real rows' own, and the result of a membership-inference test. A dataset not declared private is reported as carrying no privacy guarantee. A column's synthetic rule, where declared, decides its generated values; else its fake; else its profile (REQ-1494). A column tagged pii with neither a fake nor a synthetic rule refuses the generation by name. A private dataset reads nothing from a profile run's recorded values, which were measured without noise: every statistic it generates from is measured at generation, from the tables, as the organisation's administrator, by a mechanism of bounded sensitivity charged to the dataset's privacy budget, the profile supplying only the structure: columns, their families and relationships. Numeric and date ranges come from bounds the operator declares, or from noisy quantile estimates charged to the budget, and values are clipped to them. Because no observed value may be released, a private dataset refuses by name a categories() fake, asking for its values to be declared, a pattern() fake, and a text column that declares neither a fake nor a synthetic rule, asking for one, every refused column named in one refusal. The charges across every statistic sum to the dataset's budget, and the report shows the sum.

Every admin page that lists items (sources, tables, security roles and rules, relationships, views, commands, metrics, data products, team, requests and the like) presents its list in one style, the style of the Register Tables page: the same list component, header row, row height, spacing, typography, action placement, selection and expand behaviour, empty state and loading state. A page differs from another only in its columns and actions, never in how a list looks or behaves; a new list page uses the shared style rather than its own.

Every environment other than production has one data mode, chosen when it is created and changeable afterwards: Inherit, Unbound, Test (fake) or Test (synthetic). Inherit: each source's connection details are copied from the parent environment when it is created, exactly as written. A value that is a reference to a secret or an environment variable is copied as that reference, so rotating the secret or changing the variable reaches the copy with nothing to do, and a literal value does not follow later changes to the parent, which is the operator's choice to make by using references; the tables show the parent's data. Unbound: the whole model with no connections; each source reads nothing until the operator binds it to a database of their own. Test (fake): the parent's real rows, with every column that declares a fake read through its fake. Test (synthetic): rows generated from the parent's profile runs into the environment's own store. Mutation handling is chosen alongside the mode and applies to any of them: Refused, where every mutation is refused, naming the environment; Reversible, where mutations work, but the data underneath is never changed: they are kept in the environment's own change log, reads show the data with the log applied (the latest version of each key, deleted rows dropped), and Reset mutations returns the environment to its baseline, whether that is the parent's real rows, the generated rows or a database of its own; Direct, where mutations change the data, offered only where the environment owns it (the synthetic store, or a source bound to a database of its own) and never over an inherited source. A mutation is any semantic SQL statement in the one query pipeline that inserts, updates, deletes or merges rows -- TRUNCATE among them, identified as a mutation and run as itself, never rewritten; because a TRUNCATE cannot apply a row filter, it runs only when the role holds write and has no row filter on the table, and is otherwise refused, naming the filter and pointing to DELETE; under Reversible it is kept as one entry deleting every row -- or any command declared kind mutation, whichever surface it arrived on; every surface reduces to semantic SQL, so mutation handling is decided once, in the pipeline, and a surface never adds a rule of its own. DDL -- any statement that creates, alters or drops an object, a table-creating SELECT among them -- is never accepted in SQL on any surface; objects are declared in the configuration or the UI. The one exception is a session's own temporary tables (REQ-615): a session may create, write and drop them, they are not model objects, and writes into them are not mutations, since they never reach a source or the environment's data and end with the session. Provisa's own writes -- replica refresh, profiler results, synthetic generation, copy and move -- are not mutations and are not subject to mutation handling. A new environment's mutation handling is Refused. Reversible needs a primary key on every table it writes; an API mutation cannot be reversed, so under Reversible it is refused, and under Direct it is allowed only to an API bound to an address the environment owns. The parent an environment was created from is always recorded, whatever its mode. Once created, an environment's sources are its own: every field of a source is editable on the Sources page in that environment, a source with no connection is one nobody has filled in yet, and Re-copy from parent copies a source's connection from the parent again on demand, so any environment can be switched back to Inherit at any time. No connection is resolved through the parent at build time; an environment never depends on its parent existing. Test (synthetic) generates the whole model: every table except an API table that needs a required parameter, each from a profile run the operator picks in one modal that lists every table with its profile status, preselected to its latest successful run in the parent, or from a declared profile: the same facts a profile run measures, written by hand -- the table's row count; each column's null share, distinct count, range or distribution and, for a category, its values and weights; each relationship's fan-out; optionally the dependence between columns -- so a table with no data to profile can be generated, and a profile run can be copied into a declared profile and changed to generate a what-if (ten times the orders, a new region's mix) without touching its source. A column a declared profile leaves out takes its fake or its synthetic rule. Generation reads a measured and a declared profile alike. Generate is enabled once every such table has one or the other, and a table with neither, or a column with no profile fact, fake or rule, is named as the reason it is not. Generating binds each generated source to the environment's synthetic store as a connection of its own, so the environment's sources point at the generated data and an environment created from it inherits that data through its connections like any other; dropping the dataset or leaving Test (synthetic) restores each source's previous binding. Generating changes each generated source's type as well as its connection, to the synthetic store's, so nothing in a Test (synthetic) environment calls a source API: an API table that can be read in full is generated like any table; an API table that needs a required parameter has no full set of rows to measure, so it is generated from a declared profile -- after which it is an ordinary table in the synthetic store, its required parameter a filter on it, readable in the environment and ready for a developer's own copy of the API to serve -- and without one it is not available in a Test (synthetic) environment, a read of it refused naming why and that declaring a profile generates it; and the commands backed by a generated API source are not defined there, a call to one refused naming why. Pressing Generate first shows a Limitations of Synthetic Data warning and generates nothing until the operator confirms it. The warning explains, in general, that a synthetic environment calls no source API, that tables needing a required parameter and the commands of a generated API are unavailable, and how a developer can restore them by hand, for example by standing up their own instance of the API that reads the synthetic tables and editing the source to point at it; and, for this generation: each table to be generated with its profile, measured or declared, the scale and an estimate of rows and time; each source whose type and connection will change to the synthetic store; each table that will not be available, and why; each command that will not be defined, grouped by its source, stated as a warning to the developer; and any kept mutations that generating will discard. Generation runs in the background: the environment shows Generating, then Ready or Failed with the reason, and the report when it finishes; until it finishes the tables read what they read before. The environment list opens a detail panel for each environment, as every list does, showing its parent, data mode, mutation handling, each source's binding and where its mutations land, its test data (faked column count and sensitive columns without a fake, or the synthetic dataset's status, settings and report) and its kept mutations with Reset mutations, with an Edit that changes the data mode, the sources' bindings, the mutation handling, the synthetic settings and the expiry; the name is not editable. A change of data mode that changes row keys -- to or from Test (synthetic), or regenerating it -- discards the kept mutations, which the edit form states and asks to confirm; a change between Inherit and Test (fake) keeps them. Changing an environment's data choices, including creating it as Inherit, needs the environment_data right; creating or switching an environment to Inherit also needs the right to read the parent's data, and is audited with the real data it makes visible and to how many members. environment_data is held by org_admin by default and by no developer. Test (fake) never shows a sensitive column (REQ-1943: one carrying a tag with the Sensitive data option, pii among them) unless that column declares a fake: creating or switching to Test (fake), and every request into a Test (fake) environment, is refused while any sensitive column has no fake, naming the columns and that a holder of the sensitive_data right can fix them. Prod has the detail panel but no data mode; it is always real. Generation does not try to keep any API working; once it has run, a developer may fix up the environment by hand -- for example by editing a source back to an API of their own on the Sources page -- and that is theirs to do. (Amended 2026-10-07, maintainer: how a source is bound to the synthetic store.) A source generated for Test (synthetic) carries a fourth binding, synthetic: its type becomes the synthetic store's type, its connection fields are cleared and its schema in the store is recorded on it; the platform resolves the store, so no store credential is written into a source. The type of a source bound synthetic is never carried by a merge or a deploy. Generating records each source's previous type, binding and connection in the control plane; leaving Test (synthetic) or dropping the dataset restores exactly that and removes the record. Generation is asked for in two calls: the first returns the Limitations of Synthetic Data warning and a digest of what was shown and generates nothing; the second repeats the request with the digest and starts generation, and is refused with the fresh warning when the model or its profiles changed in between. A measured profile copied into a declared profile keeps the real values of a category column that is not sensitive; the documentation says so.

A tag definition carries a Sensitive data option, and a column carrying any tag with that option set is a sensitive column. The built-in pii tag ships with Sensitive data set and locked; an organisation may set it on tags of its own, such as mnpi. The sensitive_data right governs every way a sensitive column's values are revealed or hidden, in every environment, production included: adding or removing a sensitive tag on a column; setting or clearing the Sensitive data option on a tag definition; and changing any hiding definition on a sensitive column -- its role masks, its fake and its synthetic rule -- or its column grants. masking_config governs role masks on columns that are not sensitive; fakes and synthetic rules on columns that are not sensitive are open to anyone who may edit the table, developers included. In a Test (synthetic) environment a sensitive column may not take a synthetic rule that copies real values (a categories() drawn from the profile, keys drawn from real values), and Test (fake) never shows a sensitive column without its declared fake (REQ-1942). The sensitive_data right is held by org_admin by default and is meant to be granted to a data steward role; no developer holds it by default. A column derived from a sensitive column -- a view's column, a calculated column -- is sensitive only if it carries a sensitive tag; sensitivity is never propagated, and tagging a derived column is the operator's concern.

A standard data_steward role is seeded in every organisation: the owner of a domain's governance. It governs the role-based access to its domain's tables -- which roles see each table and column, and how values are hidden from them: masks, fakes and synthetic rules -- and their row rules. It holds access_config and column_grant (visibility), masking_config (masks and row rules, REQ-1531), masking_config, sensitive_data (REQ-1943), glossary_read and glossary_rw, data_product_read and data_product_rw, usage, query_development, full_results and view_governance, and nothing operational: not write, source_registration, table_registration, user_management, org_settings or environment_data. A steward's rights apply only within the domains its role reaches: every edit those rights allow -- a visibility setting, a row rule, a column grant, a mask, a fake or synthetic rule, a mutation command's reclassification as read-safe (REQ-870), a sensitive tag, a fake or synthetic rule on a sensitive column, a glossary term, a data product -- is checked against the domain of what it changes, and an edit to anything outside the steward's domains is refused naming the domain. The seeded data_steward role reaches every domain, because a deployment may be a small team with one steward or an enterprise with many; best practice in production is several domains, each with a steward aligned to it, made by copying the role per domain (a sales steward reaching only sales). org_admin holds every one of these rights across all domains, and org_glossary_rw stays org_admin's alone (REQ-1592). Defining roles and assigning them to people are not the steward's: roles are organisation-wide and stay with org_admin. The data_steward role is a seeded collection of rights over a set of domains and nothing more: no check anywhere tests a role's name; every check asks whether the caller holds the right in the domain of what changes, so a copy with another name, or a role an organisation composes with the same rights, behaves identically.

The product tour is a short core tour followed by a menu of topics. The core tour -- welcome, Polly, registering a source and a table, querying it -- starts on its own for a new user and ends on the topic menu. Every step of the core tour carries a Deep Dives button that leaves it for the topic menu at once. The menu, called Deep Dives, shows one card per topic, each with its title, one sentence on what it covers, its number of steps and a mark once the viewer has completed it; the tour button opens the menu once the core tour has been seen. Each topic is a tour of its own, and Done, or leaving it, returns to the menu rather than continuing into another topic. The topics are: Connect your data (source types, registering tables, replicas and live reads); Relationships (a headline choice of its own: the relationships the model declares between tables, whether or not a source declares them, within a source and across sources, which every surface (joins, GraphQL fields, the graph) follows); Model it (the derivations and extensions Provisa adds beyond what the sources provide: views, calculated columns, metrics and commands, ending with lineage: the dependencies those derivations generate, what each is built from and what depends on it, as the lineage page shows); Govern it (roles and domains, row rules, masks, sensitive data, the data steward); Query it everywhere (SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, REST and MCP through one governed pipeline); Test data and environments (the profiler and the checks it exports to Soda and Great Expectations, fakes, synthetic data, environments, data modes, mutation handling); Publish it (data products, with the glossary terms that define them and the data-quality results they publish; data catalogs and lineage, published to the external tools an organisation uses, each target receiving what it supports (catalog entries, data products, lineage), since a catalog need not hold data products (Apache Atlas) and a data product registry need not be a full catalog (BigQuery Dataplex); lineage also goes over OpenLineage); and Operate it (caching, observability, settings, releases, and exporting the model's configuration). Which topics a viewer has completed is remembered for that viewer. Each topic is written to the product as it stands, so a feature that changes rewrites one topic. A step that refers to Polly opens Polly as the step is shown, through the control a user opens it with, so the step points at Polly itself and never at a closed launcher. (Amended 2026-10-07, maintainer: the tour opens Polly when referencing it.) The core tour explains querying in one step, in general terms: the same governed model answers in whichever language or tool the user asks. What each query surface offers is in the Query it everywhere topic, not the core tour. (Amended 2026-10-07, maintainer: two query panels in the core tour were awkward; one card, the rest in the deep dive.) Every card of the tour, a topic's steps as well as the core tour's, carries the Deep Dives button, and the Deep Dives side offers a way back to the first step of the core tour. (Amended 2026-10-07, maintainer: start from a deep dive card goes back to the core start; a deep dive button on every card goes to the catalog.) A Deep Dive topic has at least four cards, each on a feature the product has and anchored on it. (Amended 2026-10-07, maintainer: deep dives have room for more detail; target 4+ cards per deep dive, otherwise it is not deep.) (Amended 2026-10-08, maintainer: data quality is its own Deep Dive; this supersedes the topic list above where it puts quality checks under test data:) The Deep Dives are Connect your data, Relationships, Model it, Govern it, Data quality, Query it everywhere, Test data and environments, Publish it and Operate it. Data quality answers whether the real data is good: a quality checker registered as a source, its contract, profiling a table, drift and exported checks. Test data and environments answers how to get safe, realistic data to build against, and opens with a card saying how its parts fit: an environment is a branch of the model, its data mode decides what its sources read, the profiler measures real tables, fakes replace identifying values, synthetic generation builds tables from profiles, and mutation handling decides what a write does. The profiler appears in both topics, for what it does in each.

Salesforce is a source type. A Salesforce source names the org's My Domain login URL and one complete credential set -- a connected app's consumer key and secret (client credentials), a username and password with the consumer key and secret and an optional security token, or a pre-issued access token with its instance URL -- and optionally an API version; every sObject the credential can query is a table the steward may register, and nothing is registered automatically. On Trino the source is read through the trino-salesforce connector, which reads only. On every other engine it is reached through the bundled pgwire-salesforce server, the way a SharePoint source is reached through pgwire-sharepoint, and through that server it is read and written: insert, update and delete on a registered sObject are mutations, governed, audited and handled per environment as any other mutation is. A SharePoint source is written through pgwire-sharepoint the same way. The write goes to the source's own pgwire server whatever engine serves the reads: on Trino that server runs beside the read-only connector and carries only the writes, so these sources are written on every engine. (Amended 2026-10-07, maintainer: write on every engine; replaces a refusal on Trino.) Salesforce appears in the source pick list under Enterprise, in the source documentation, and in every count of source types the product states, the tour's among them. Both adapters are fetched from the pinned engine release, as the SharePoint ones are.

Cloud inventory is a source type. A cloud inventory source names the credentials and scope of one or more of Azure (tenant, client id and secret, subscriptions), AWS (access key and secret, region, accounts, optionally a role to assume) and GCP (a service-account credential, projects), and offers the same tables whichever clouds it names: compute resources, storage resources, Kubernetes clusters, database resources, network resources, IAM resources and container registries, each with one set of columns across the three clouds and a column naming the cloud a row came from. It reads only. On Trino it is read through the trino-cloudops connector; on every other engine through the bundled pgwire-cloudops server, as a SharePoint source is read. Its tables are registered by a steward like any other, and its credentials are secrets. It appears in the source pick list under Enterprise, in the source documentation, and in every count of source types the product states.

A relationship request is decided by the domains it touches. The domains involved in a request are the domain of its source table and the domain of its target table. An approval of the request counts only from a user whose right to create relationships reaches at least one of those domains, as a governance right reaches only the domains of the roles carrying it (REQ-1944); an approval from anyone else is refused, naming the reason. The request is executable when it has two approvals from two different users, neither of them the requester, and every domain involved is reached by at least one of the approvers: a relationship across two domains needs a yes from each side, and a relationship inside one domain needs two approvers of that domain. A rejection may come from any user who could approve. The requests list shows a user only the requests they can decide and the ones they made, and shows for each request which domains it still waits on. No check tests a role name.

A read that a role's row limit cut short says so. When a role without the right to full results reads more rows than its limit allows, the answer carries a warning naming the limit and saying the answer was cut there; an answer that fits within the limit carries none, so the warning is given only when rows were in fact left out. The warning is a statement warning, delivered on every surface in that surface's own channel as the other statement warnings are -- SQL over HTTP, GraphQL, Cypher, pgwire, Bolt, Arrow Flight, gRPC, MCP and the UI's result panel -- and an exported or redirected result carries it too. A temporary table filled from a cut read carries the same warning. The warning never changes what is returned and is never an error.

A creation request of any type -- relationship, view, table, source or webhook -- is carried out only through its approvals, and carrying it out creates what it asks for. An approval counts from a user who holds the right the request names (for a relationship, whose right reaches a domain the request touches, REQ-1948), who is not the requester, and who has not approved it already; the requester is recorded as a user on every path that queues a request. The approval that completes the request's required count (one; two for a relationship) performs the creation through the same code the direct mutation uses, and only then is the request marked executed. Executing is refused until the count is met and afterwards serves to retry a creation that failed; a failed creation leaves the request pending and answers with the failure's own code. A request may be rejected by any user who could approve it, and the author of a request other than a relationship's may withdraw it. The rule, its refusals and its admin-trail entries -- every approval, rejection, withdrawal, creation and refused attempt -- are the same over REST and GraphQL. A webhook declared in configuration is approved at load and is outside this rule (REQ-209).

A Debezium topic encoded in Avro with a schema registry is read as its rows. A Debezium source may name a schema registry -- its URL and how it is authenticated: not at all, by basic credentials, by a bearer token, or by mutual TLS with a client certificate, each secret held through the secrets contract -- and a message in the registry wire format is decoded with the writer schema its id names, fetched from the registry and kept by id, so a change of schema on the topic is followed message by message. Inserts, updates and deletes arrive as they do from a JSON-encoded topic. A topic whose messages are Avro when the source names no registry, a registry that cannot be reached within its bound, and a schema id the registry does not know are each refused by name; an Avro topic is never read as JSON. The fields a method needs are checked when the source is saved, and a missing one is refused by name. The Avro codec is a declared dependency; the Kafka client stays the one the product ships.

A role is the one the request runs as, on every data route, and a catalog is listed for the caller it is listed to. A data route takes its role from the authenticated request -- the role header checked against the caller's assignments, one held role or a set of held roles acting as their meta-role -- and never from the request body or an unchecked header; a body that names a different role is refused, naming both. A route that names a role in its path accepts the same thing the header does, through one resolver. With authentication on, Arrow Flight's catalog calls -- listing flights, flight info, schema, and the catalog ticket -- require a credential as every other surface does, and list only the tables, columns and commands the caller's role or roles may see; with authentication off they answer as they did. The gRPC explorer and the other explore pages act as the role or roles the session acts as, and show the server's own refusal.

ServiceNow is a source type. An instance is registered with its address and a credential; [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1954, 2026-10-12 -- the instance's whole table list is offered, grouped by theme; see the amendment below. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] its tables (incidents, changes, requests, the configuration database, users and groups) are offered for registration and nothing is registered until a steward registers it. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] A registered ServiceNow table is read in place through the instance's own API, with filters, column selection and paging sent to the instance where it supports them, and is governed, related and served on every surface as any other table. ServiceNow is listed with the enterprise sources in the source picker, the documentation and every stated count of source types. (Amended 2026-10-12, WHOLE TABLE LIST, METADATA ON SELECTION:) Maintainer, verbatim: "servicenow can have thousands of tables grouped into themes. we need to have a way to identify these tables. Its fine if the list of tables is very large. But servicenow should not resolve the table metadata until they are selected in the table registration process." Every table of the instance is offered for registration, grouped by theme, each named so a steward can identify it (its name and its label); nothing is registered until a steward registers it. A table's columns are read from the instance only when the steward selects it for registration; listing the tables reads no table's columns. (Amended 2026-10-12, TABLE WRITES:) Maintainer approved writes: a registered ServiceNow table takes inserts, updates and deletes through the source's own server, as a SharePoint or Salesforce table does, and a write returns the record the instance holds after it. GraphQL mutations, gRPC inserts and SQL writes reach it through the same write admission and rights as any other table. (Amended 2026-10-12, COMMANDS:) ServiceNow is complete only with its commands: the instance's non-table APIs (for example Import Set, a Service Catalog order, a scripted REST API) are registered as Provisa commands from the API specification the instance itself publishes, never from a hand-written list. Phase order: reads, then table writes, then commands. (Amended 2026-10-12, IMPORT SETS:) When a steward registers a ServiceNow table, they may bind it to one of the instance's import sets, chosen from the instance's active transform maps into that table; the choice is offered only when the table has one, and a table with several makes the steward pick which. A bound table's inserts go through the instance's Import Set API and that map; an unbound table's inserts, and every update and delete, are written to the table directly. Each inserted row's transform result is the write's outcome: a row the transform rejects is refused by name, and rows already written stay written. (Amended 2026-10-12, COMMANDS FROM THE INSTANCE'S OWN DOCUMENTS) The instance's APIs are read from what it publishes -- its list of APIs (GET /api/now/doc) and each API's OpenAPI 3 document, the one its REST API Explorer exports (GET /api/now/doc/oas_3, by namespace and API name) -- with the source's own credential. They are offered through an OpenAPI source kept beside the ServiceNow source and named after it (<id>-api), written whenever the ServiceNow source is saved and removed with it; its specification is assembled from the APIs a steward adds on the ServiceNow source's page, read from the instance when the source is loaded. Everything after that is the ordinary OpenAPI path: an operation with a body is a command (an untyped body, as the instance publishes them, is one JSON argument, REQ-1924's body rule for every OpenAPI source), and a GET is a command that reads and a table whose columns the steward declares (REQ-1924, DECLARED COLUMNS). An import set added on the page, the import set of one of the instance's active transform maps into a table, is offered as a typed insert whose fields are its staging table's columns, read from the instance, without the system ones.

A source built from a published API specification carries exclusions: operations and request arguments of the specification that the source does not offer. An excluded operation is not listed for registration as a table or a command; an excluded argument is not part of an operation's arguments, is not shown, and is never sent. An exclusion names an operation by its path and method, or an argument by its name on one operation or on every operation that has it. A branded source ships the exclusions that are part of its curation -- the Stripe brand excludes the deprecated token and inline-source payment inputs and the operations that exist only for them, and offers the Payment Intents, Payment Methods and Setup Intents operations -- and an operator adds exclusions of their own on any specification-built source, in its configuration and in the source form. Something already registered that an exclusion later covers is reported by name, not silently dropped.

Feature: Row-level security, column visibility and masking
Description: The admin API answers a caller with the catalog that caller may see, as every data surface does. Its listings of tables, columns and relationships answer the whole catalog only to a caller holding a catalog-administration right -- table registration, or a right to hide tables or columns -- and only within the domains that caller's roles reach; every other caller is answered the tables, columns and relationships its acting role is served, from the one role-narrowing the Flight catalog and the MCP catalog tools use. A column's grant lists and mask settings (who it is visible to, writable by and unmasked for, and how it is masked) are returned only to a caller holding the right to view governance (REQ-1134). Domains are listed to a caller for the domains its roles reach; a source is named to a caller that is served a table from it; a metric is listed to a caller its visibility admits; a caller holding the administration right for that kind of object is answered all of them. Narrowing is by rights and domain reach, never by a role's name (REQ-1337), and a platform administrator is answered no data catalog by this rule (REQ-1327). What is public is available to all domains: a public table, relationship, metric or other item is answered to every caller, whatever domains its roles reach, as it is on the data surfaces. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1958, 2026-10-17 -- a deployment with no auth provider is answered the catalog of the roles the request names. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] A deployment with no auth provider is unchanged. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] The application's own pages are built from these answers, so a picker never offers a table the caller's query would be refused. A registrar who is not shown the grant lists and masks of a table may still edit the table: the editor opens without those columns and its save names none of them, so the store keeps them. (Amended 2026-10-17, NO AUTH PROVIDER:) A deployment with no auth provider enforces no right, but its admin catalog is still the one the roles a request names carry and reach: the role picker's selection (X-Provisa-Role), as a signed-in caller acting as those roles is answered. Only a request no middleware resolved at all is answered the whole catalog.

What is public is available to all domains. An item marked public is served to every role of the organisation whatever domains that role's domain access reaches: a public column is served, with the table it belongs to, to a role with no reach into that table's domain, and only that table's public columns are served to such a role; a relationship both of whose ends are served is served; a metric marked public is listed. Public is decided in the one place a role's served set is decided, so every surface -- SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, pgwire, Bolt, Flight and its catalog, gRPC, MCP, JSON:API, the JDBC driver's metadata and the admin API's listings (REQ-1958) -- agrees, and none has a rule of its own. Public widens who is served and nothing else: masks, row rules, the relationship guard and row limits apply to a public item as to any other, and a column's own visibility list still applies within its scope. An item is public only because someone with the right to set it said so; nothing is public by default. A restricted item is served only as its own visibility list says.

A files source may declare an HTML crawl, and Wikipedia is a source type carried by it. (1) THE CRAWL. A files source whose mapping carries a crawl reads web pages before it looks for files: the file adapter follows links from the start pages, and each HTML table and each linked data file (CSV, TSV, Excel, JSON, Parquet) lands in the source's directory as an ordinary file, which is then a table of the source like any other. Adding the source registers nothing; a steward registers the tables wanted (REQ-316). The crawl's settings are the adapter's own and every one can be stated: start pages, link depth, page limit, delay between requests, how long a crawl is kept, the name the crawl gives itself, the part of a page that is read, parts left out of it, which links are followed, link patterns left out, which tables are read with the fewest and most rows, data file types and size limits. A setting the adapter does not read is refused by name. Every engine's files connector is given the same crawl (REQ-1730). (2) LINKS ARE CHOSEN BY WHAT THE PAGE SAYS THEY ARE. A link is followed for what the link element itself carries -- its classes and attributes, which the site's markup states -- and for where it sits in the page, never for a name in its address: such a name differs in every language edition and also occurs in ordinary titles (maintainer ruling 2026-10-08). A pattern over addresses remains a setting for other sites and is empty by default. (3) WIKIPEDIA. Wikipedia is in the source pick list. Its setup names the pages to start from (titles or addresses of the chosen language edition), the language edition, link depth (default 1), page limit (default 25) and a contact sent with each request. Only links in the article's own text, lists and data tables are followed: navigation, information and navigation boxes, notes, citations, categories, file pages, other wikis, external sites and pages not yet written are not. Only tables marked as data tables become tables. (4) SEE ALSO IS A CHOICE. Links in an article's See also section are looser than links in its text, so following them is an option of the setup, off by default (maintainer ruling 2026-10-08). The section is identified by its heading, which is the one name the brand uses: an edition has no other mark for it. Provisa knows the heading of the common editions and asks nothing about them; only for another edition does the setup ask what that edition calls the section, in the operator's terms -- its title as a page shows it -- or the operator follows those links. The setup asks for no credential (REQ-1923), and the crawl's own settings, which all have defaults, are folded away until wanted (maintainer ruling 2026-10-08: the setup must be clear to someone who does not know how a page is built). (5) THE SOURCE SAYS WHAT IT CRAWLS. The crawl is written into the source in full when it is created or edited, and its files land in a directory of the source's own under the data directory unless the operator names one.

The model records the precision and scale of a numeric column. Registration takes them from the source the same way whichever engine introspects it -- from the precision and scale each engine reports for the column, not from how that engine happens to print the type name -- and stores them with the column; the column editor shows them and lets the registrar set or clear them. A numeric column with a recorded precision and scale is an exact decimal of that precision and scale on every read path, on every engine and surface, and in every catalog listing. A numeric column with none recorded is floating point on every read path and in every listing, the same for an empty result as for a full one, and is documented as approximate. A column's type is never sized from the rows a read happens to return. The type a catalog lists for a column is the type a read of that column returns. (Amended 2026-10-13, WHAT IS DELIVERED:) Delivered: a numeric column's precision and scale have one stored spelling, numeric(p,s), written and read in one place, taken at registration from the precision and scale the engine reports, and a size no numeric can have (precision 1 to 76, scale 0 to the precision) is refused with a code naming the column; the column editor sets or clears them beside the type; a read types each registered column as its registered type on pgwire's row stream, Flight's buffered answers, an Airport scan and an engine's Arrow stream, a value that is not that type is a read refusal with a code, and only a result column that is a registered column is typed by the model; a numeric with no recorded size is cast to double precision by its source inside the governed statement, so its type depends on no row; the type a catalog lists is the type a read returns. Verified on a running server over Flight and pgwire (the catalog, rows, no rows and a computed column). Not yet verified surface by surface: GraphQL, gRPC, REST, JSON:API and Bolt.
