Description: A read that needs a table whose replica could not be built is refused, naming the table and the error the build recorded: HTTP 503 with code query.replica_build_failed and the table and reason as parameters, gRPC UNAVAILABLE, and the same message on the transports that carry only a message. It is one of the refusals for a read the deployment cannot answer now, with a read whose home region is unavailable (REQ-1922), and every surface answers that family in one place; no surface names a member of it.

A multi-tenant deployment reads role assignments from Provisa, never from sign-in claims: a configuration that sets multitenancy with auth.assignments_source claims, stated or by default, does not load, the deployment does not start on it, and a settings change that would produce it is refused, each naming both settings and the value to use. A single-tenant deployment may use either.

Semantic SQL has no array, struct or map type; nested data is a JSON column, and JSON is the type every catalog and every wire lists for it, on every federation engine and every source read directly, so a registration answers the same on every engine. A datasource hands a native array, struct or map over as JSON, by a cast the source or engine executes; such a column is registered as JSON -- JSON is the type registration suggests for it, never text -- and registering one is never an error, though reading one from a backend with no verified way to produce JSON is refused by name. A column carries three hidden attributes, recorded from the source at registration, stored with the column, not offered in the registration form and available to every translator: its array depth as an integer -- 0 for a column that is not an array of a primitive, 1 for an array of a primitive, 2 for an array of arrays of a primitive, and so on for each level of nesting -- the semantic SQL type of its innermost element with precision and scale where it has them, and the native type of the source in its own spelling. A backend does not need a JSON type to carry such a column, only JSON functions: where a backend has no JSON type the value is held and passed as text, and what makes a backend supported is that it can produce JSON from a native value and operate on JSON text with its own functions. Only an array whose innermost element is one primitive type has a depth above 0; a struct, a map, an array of structs or an array whose elements are of mixed types is a plain JSON column of depth 0 with its native type recorded, and a column that is JSON at its source carries none of the three. Semantic SQL offers one portable set of JSON operations -- element and field access, length, contains, unnest, construct, and aggregate into a JSON array -- spelled as the SQL standard JSON functions, with the PostgreSQL operators accepted as the same operations, and translated to the dialect of the backend a statement is routed to from one rule table covering every operation on every backend class. For an array of a primitive, at any depth, the attributes are an input to that translation: an innermost element that is extracted or unnested is cast to the element type and a literal compared with one is cast to it, inside the generated statement, and where the statement runs on the source and its column is natively an array, element access, length, contains and unnest use the native operation, except that on the PostgreSQL family, whose array type does not record its dimensions, unnest always goes through JSON, so its answer never depends on the dimensions of the value. A typed extraction that goes fewer levels into an array than its depth is refused when the statement is compiled, naming the column and its depth. The native type is recorded for casting in: its being recorded is what tells a translator the column must be converted to JSON on the way out, a conversion that is the same whatever the type, and its content is what a value is cast into on the way in. That holds for a predicate as for a write. In a predicate that runs on the source, the JSON or literal a statement compares with such a column -- with the whole value or with an element -- is cast into the native type, so that the comparison is made on the native column by the source and can use its indexes, and the column is not converted to JSON to be compared. In a write, the JSON a statement gives for a column that is natively an array, struct or map is cast into the recorded native type by the source that stores it, inside the generated statement, through the one write path; a value the source cannot cast is refused with the error of the source, and a backend with no verified way to build its native value from JSON refuses the write by name. A decimal element with a declared precision is written into the JSON as a string and cast back, so it is exact on every engine; a timestamp element keeps its instant; an element that is not a number or is infinite is refused by name. Inside a struct, a map or an array of structs nothing is typed: the whole value and the untyped operations work, and a typed value from inside one needs a cast the user writes. Once a source or an engine has produced a value, Provisa does not parse, convert or re-encode it on any route; the translation is derived once with the governed statement, not per request. An operation a backend cannot perform correctly is refused by name; an operation that is correct but slow is allowed and runs. The user is responsible for what will not perform, and the product says so: the query plan notes, for each JSON operation that the backend it is routed to cannot serve from an index or that is not known to be pushed down, the column, the operation, the backend and the documented alternative, as advice that never blocks or changes the statement and is shown with the plan only; the documentation states the same per backend class from the same rule table. When the type of a source column no longer matches what was recorded, reads of that column are refused, naming the column and both types, until it is registered again. The hidden attributes are standard metadata that a surface able to state a list may read: GraphQL declares a column whose depth is above 0 as a list, nested to that depth, of the GraphQL type of its element, from the attributes alone and never from the spelling of a source type, and declares every other JSON column as the opaque JSON value; the value it serves is the JSON the source or engine produced. Bolt carries a JSON column as a JSON string. (Amended 2026-10-13, WHAT IS DELIVERED:) Delivered: a native array, struct or map registers as JSON with its three hidden attributes recorded from the source (depth, element type, native type, and whose spelling that is), and registering it as any other type is refused by name; a read of such a column is the backend's own to-JSON expression on DuckDB, PostgreSQL and Trino, resolved in the one transpile step every route takes; a replica lands it as JSON the source or engine produces (jsonb on PostgreSQL); GraphQL declares a column of depth above 0 as a list of its element type from the attributes alone, a decimal element with a declared precision as String, and every other such column as the opaque JSON value; gRPC carries it as a JSON string. A parameter is an argument, not a column: an array parameter (a query vector, REQ-1986) stays a list of its element type on GraphQL and gRPC. An embedding column (REQ-424) is exempt end to end: registered as the native array it is with no hidden attribute, landed as a vector where the engine indexes it and as text elsewhere, read without a JSON conversion, and a list of its components in GraphQL. Not yet delivered: the portable JSON operations and their rule table, typed extraction and its compile-time depth check, native element operations on the source, the plan notes, the cast into the native type in predicates and writes, refusing reads of a column whose source type drifted, and Bolt's JSON string.

Description: The model export offers a dbt sources file (sources.yml) written by Provisa directly, for dbt projects that do not use the semantic layer and so cannot load the semantic manifest of REQ-1966. It lists each registered table the requesting role can see as a dbt source table under its source and schema, with the table's description, each column's description, and the standard dbt tests the model can state: unique and not_null for a primary key, unique for a unique constraint, not_null for a column registered as not nullable, and relationships for a registered relationship. It carries no metrics (a sources file has none) and nothing of row security, masking, roles or lineage, and the export surface says so. It is derived from the governed model on every read, as the Ossie document is.

Every form in the UI is laid out by one shared form layout, and a field is as wide as what it holds, not as wide as the form. A field declares a size class (short for numbers, ports, durations, switches and short choices; medium for names and hosts; long for addresses, paths and one-line descriptions; full for multi-line text and editors only), and each class has a minimum and a maximum width, so a field neither stretches across the form nor collapses. Fields flow into as many columns as the screen allows and wrap on a narrower one, with no form carrying its own breakpoints; fields that belong together (host and port, precision and scale) are declared as a group and wrap as one. A single-line field is never full width; full width is for multi-line text, editors and tables. Identifier fields, where a form has them, are not in the flow: they sit at the top of the form in a section of their own. A form's action buttons are at the bottom, aligned to the start of the line (left in a left-to-right language, right in a right-to-left one), primary action first. Reading order and keyboard order are the same after any reflow. Minimum widths hold each field's label in every shipped locale. Creating an object follows one pattern on every page: a button at the top of the page named for the object ("+ Table", "+ Source") opens the form, and the form ends in Save and Cancel. Save creates the object, Cancel closes the form with nothing created; the form's own button never repeats the opening button's label, and an edit form ends in the same two actions in the same order. A button is as wide as its label, with one shared minimum width, and never grows to fill its container: it is not a direct child of a stretching stack or grid cell but sits in an action row at its natural width. A full-width button is allowed only where it is named as an exception: the single call to action of a narrow card (sign-in, an onboarding step), a row of a menu or list that is itself the action, and a phone-width screen. The rule is held by a guard test: a form that lays its fields out outside the shared layout, a single-line field stretched to full width, action buttons aligned elsewhere, a button stretched by its container, and a full-width button outside the named exceptions each fail it. Nothing is rendered between a field label and its control: a brief explanation (one short sentence) sits below the field, and a longer explanation is reached from a help icon immediately to the right of the label. Controls in one row share a baseline. A form takes its natural height; it never scrolls inside a box that hides its first or last row.

On a list page a row's detail opens in a right-hand panel beside the list, not under the row. The panel is resizable and can be expanded; one row's detail is open at a time. Whether a page uses the right-hand panel or an inline detail is chosen per page. The right-hand panel is used on Tables, Views, Sources, Relationships, Metrics, Commands, and Security's Roles and RLS; Data Products keeps its inline detail. A page's list stretches to the width of the viewport.

The head of a detail panel is pinned: the item's name, then its actions. While the item is being edited, Save and Cancel take the place of the actions in the head; nothing is pinned at the foot of the panel. The actions in a detail panel's head share one style: no background and no border.

An item's detail is divided into sections shown as top-level tabs, not as one scrolling form with expanding sections. The read view and the edit view use the SAME tabs, and the read view summarises every detail of the item. For a table the tabs are Identity, Associations, Load and timeliness, Query, Quality, Columns.
The column editor is four tabs: Naming, Type and keys, Access, Testing. The column's name comes first on each tab, and a hover on the name shows the column's full definition.

Creating an object is short. The page's + button asks only for what the object needs in order to exist; the object is then created, selected in the list, and its detail opens in edit. The create form is a subset of the edit form. For a table, creating registers every column.

A working surface is not modal: an editor or a form an operator works in is part of the page. A dialog is used only for a short interruption. Every delete of saved state asks for confirmation. Leaving a panel form that has unsaved changes asks "Discard your changes?".

The explorers are outside the form and detail-panel rules: the pages at /query, /graph, /sql, /jsonapi, /openapi, /explore and /lineage are a different experience and keep their own layout. The Schema Explorer's fonts and colours follow the application's styles.
The application has one tooltip style: the style of the ERD icon button on the Tables page. A tooltip opens on hover and on keyboard focus and is announced to a screen reader.

Changing the domain of a registered table or view requires the caller to hold the registering right in the domain it is in AND in the domain it is going to. This applies to an update of the table or view and to a registration that lands on an existing address.

The `deprecated` system tag applies to every object of the model: metrics, commands, roles and row-level rules, as well as source, table/view, column and relationship. The rules are the same for all of them: a reason is required, and expires_on is the planned removal date. The tag is shown wherever the object is listed and is carried into every client schema and catalog export the object appears in. A deprecation changes nothing else about the object.

Amazon Athena is a source type. (Amended 2026-10-12, WRITES AND REACH) Maintainer ruling: an Athena source is written as well as read. Every table takes INSERT; an Iceberg table also takes UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE, and those are refused on a Hive table, naming the table and the operation, before anything is sent. A statement on Athena's tables alone runs whole in Athena, its filters, columns and limits with it. A statement that joins an Athena table with another source's reads it from a replica landed from Athena, each landing a full read that Athena bills; the documentation says so, and no further rule applies to it. The source is reached with its region and database, an optional workgroup, data catalog and query-result location, and either an access key pair or none, for the AWS credential chain, with an optional role to assume. Its catalog is read through Athena's metadata API, which runs no query, and a table's columns are read when it is selected.

Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL is a source type (cosmosdb): an account endpoint, a database, and either the account key (a secret reference) or a Microsoft Entra service principal (tenant, client id, client secret as a secret reference), each set on the Sources form. A table of the source is either a container, whose documents are projected onto the declared columns (a column's path reads a nested field), or a Cosmos SQL query held in the table's query_template, each @name in it a parameter of the table (REQ-1986, reaching the source as query_arg) whose value the SDK sends as a query parameter, never inside the query text. A container table may expose its partition key as an optional parameter, which a steward can make required; a read that gives it reads one partition. A hierarchical partition key has one parameter per level, in the table's column order; a read that gives the top levels reads that prefix of the key, and a level given without the level above it is refused. Provisa reads the source itself on every federation engine, which none reaches; a table keyed on id and its partition key is fetched by point reads. Register Table previews a container or a query with sample values and suggests typed columns from the documents, leaving out the system fields but _ts. Rows are checked against their columns on the way out; a date or timestamp column reads an ISO 8601 string. A table on the native change signal follows the container's change feed (latest-version mode), so changed documents are seen as they are written and a deleted one at the next full refresh. Vector and full-text search run as query tables, and a query command of kind source_query runs a Cosmos query whose output has no stable shape (REQ-1988).

Qdrant is a source type. (Amended 2026-10-12, DESIGN AS RULED) Rulings, through the lead: "(a) a native connector over qdrant-client, Cosmos-style (my call); (b) search tables (the maintainer's choice), with cosine_similarity not wired to Qdrant; (c) reads only (the maintainer's choice); writes later as their own item." A Qdrant source is reached at its URL with its API key (a secret reference, resolved at use; none for an instance without one), over REST or, by choice, gRPC, through Qdrant's own client on every engine; no federation engine reaches it. It has one schema. A collection is a table: its point id (its key), its payload's fields (an indexed field typed by its index, any other as its points suggest, nested fields flattened with their path), and its vectors, offered unselected; [SUPERSEDED by REQ-2000, 2026-10-12 -- Qdrant is a live-only source type: no replica, no keyed fetch. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] it is landed whole as a replica and refreshed on its TTL, and a keyed read by point id is one retrieve. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] Vector search is a search table, holding a Query API request: its collection, its query, and optionally the named vector it searches, a Qdrant filter, a limit, a score threshold and a registered embedding model. The query and any value written "@name" are arguments, parameters of the table (REQ-1986) converted strictly to their declared types and placed into the request as values, never into its text; the query's argument is a vector and required. A search is read per statement under its arguments: the filter is applied by Qdrant before its nearest points are chosen, an optional argument not given filters nothing, and a statement's other conditions narrow the points returned. Each row carries its score, the collection's own metric for the vector searched, which Register Table shows. With an embedding model named, a text query is embedded by that model (REQ-430) and a vector query must have its dimensions (REQ-429). [SUPERSEDED by REQ-2000, 2026-10-12 -- a single-source statement on a Qdrant source routes DIRECT: its writes upsert and delete points, and ORDER BY cosine_similarity(<named vector>, q) DESC LIMIT k becomes query_points. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] cosine_similarity (REQ-423) is not translated for Qdrant. Writes to Qdrant are not supported. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK]

Node is a source type. A source holds a Node bundle (TypeScript, or JavaScript with JSDoc types); each exported function tagged with the JSDoc tag @table is offered as a table and each tagged @command as a command; untagged exports are ignored. A table's rows are its function's return value; the function's parameters are the table's parameters (a non-optional parameter is required by the source, an optional one can be made required by a steward); its columns come from the function's TypeScript return type, or, when the element type is loose (any, unknown or a Record), from a preview; every other type that cannot be mapped is refused by name. The JSDoc text is the description. No Provisa package is imported by the bundle. An unknown tag, or a tagged function whose types cannot be mapped, is reported by name when the bundle is loaded. Each exported async generator function tagged @stream is offered as a live table: each row it yields is delivered as it arrives, on the surfaces that serve subscriptions, and its parameters and columns follow the same rules as @table. The types a tagged function refers to (its parameters, its return type and every type they reference) become types on every surface; a type that cannot be mapped is refused by name when the bundle is loaded. A function tagged @table returns a collection (an array or an iterable, synchronous or asynchronous) whose elements are the table's rows; one that returns a single object is reported by name when the bundle is loaded. The source names its runtime: Node, Bun or Deno; a bundle's tables, commands and streams are the same on each. A bundle is JavaScript plus TypeScript declarations carrying the tags; any language that compiles to them can be used, TypeScript being the one tested and documented. A source names its code in one of three ways: an npm package at an exact version, from a public or private registry; a Git repository at a commit or tag, with a subdirectory; or an archive uploaded to Provisa. The reference is pinned, and the content's hash is recorded with the source. The bundle carries a lockfile (or is a single pre-bundled file); its dependencies are installed with the runtime's frozen-lockfile mode when the bundle is loaded, not per call, and cached by content hash. Package registries are an organization setting with its own admin page: npm registries, each with a URL, an optional scope and a credential, one of which may be marked the mirror every install goes through; and Git hosts, each with a host and a credential. Every Node install uses them, for the source's own code and for its dependencies, through configuration written into that install's isolated directory and removed after it; credentials never reach the bundle or its cache. The public npm registry needs no setup, and a single pre-bundled file needs no install. Every field of a registry or Git host, its URL and credential included, holds what was entered and is resolved at use with the standard resolution, so any of them can be a secret reference. Installs run with install scripts disabled. The worker is sandboxed: it has no file access beyond its bundle, and its network reaches only the egress allow-list, through Deno's permissions on Deno and an OS-level sandbox on Node and Bun. Runtimes are fetched on demand, pinned and hashed, and cached as the pgwire bundles are. Each subscription to a @stream table starts its own generator with that subscriber's arguments; its rows go only to that subscriber, governed by the subscriber's role, and no key is required. The types become named types as REQ-1987 states. A Git host's credential is an HTTPS token. An uploaded archive is kept in the platform plane by its content hash. A TypeScript number is a double, and any or unknown is json. Each Provisa process runs one worker per bundle. A command is a mutation unless a steward sets it as a query.

A table on a MongoDB source can be registered from an aggregation pipeline instead of a collection. The table stores the pipeline with its input collection. Each pipeline argument is a parameter of the table (REQ-1986, how it reaches the source being query_arg, an argument of a source's native query): it has an IR type (an array type such as array(double) for a query vector), and it is optional unless a steward makes it required. A caller passes the arguments the way it passes any parameter column: as GraphQL field arguments, or as equality conditions on the parameter columns in SQL. Each value is checked against its declared type and bound into the pipeline as a BSON value; it is never spliced into the pipeline text. A query that omits a required argument is refused by the REQ-1986 rule. The output columns are fixed at registration, either declared or typed from one preview run with sample arguments, and every row the pipeline returns is checked against them on the way out. Provisa runs the pipeline itself (an aggregate call), on every federation engine, so Atlas Search ($search, $searchMeta) and Atlas Vector Search ($vectorSearch) stages run. The table can be joined with any other table and is governed on every surface like any registered table. A pipeline with no arguments behaves as a view.

A MongoDB source can be reached by a connection string, so a MongoDB Atlas cluster can be registered. The source's host holds either a host name (with the port in its own field, as today) or a mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// connection string carrying the hosts and the connection options, among them tls. The credentials stay in the source's username and password, where a secret reference is resolved at use, and are percent-encoded wherever they are written into a connection string. With a connection string the source has no port; a source that gives both is refused, naming the source. Every reach of the source uses the same connection: the native reader, the change-feed check, and the Trino and DuckDB attaches. The ClickHouse engine's MongoDB table engine takes one host and port only, so a source given by a connection string is refused there, naming the source and the engine. On the Sources form, a connection string in the host field hides the port.

A table declares its parameters: the values a caller passes to the source to read the table. Each parameter has a name, a type, and how it reaches the source: a path parameter or a query parameter of an OpenAPI operation, an argument of a remote GraphQL field, a field of a gRPC request, or an argument of a source's native query (a MongoDB pipeline, REQ-1980; a Cosmos DB query, REQ-1982). Each parameter is optional or required. It is required when the source requires it, or when a steward has made it required for this table. A parameter the source requires is required for good; a steward can make an optional parameter required, and can make it optional again. Registration records every parameter the source describes, the optional ones included, with whether the source requires it. One rule holds for every source kind and every surface: a read of the table that leaves a required parameter without a value is refused before anything is sent to the source, and the refusal names the table and the parameter. GraphQL marks a required parameter's argument non-null. The admin API reads and sets the steward's switch per parameter. The table page has a Parameters section listing each parameter with its type, how it reaches the source, and the switch, which is on and locked where the source requires the parameter.

A query command can run a MongoDB aggregation pipeline whose output has no stable shape (implementation kind source_query). The command holds the native query as its binding, in the same {"inputCollection", "pipeline"} form a pipeline table holds (REQ-1980). Its arguments are the command's typed arguments, each a "{{name}}" placeholder in the pipeline, and a call converts each one to its type and binds it into the pipeline as a BSON value, never into its text. A call returns the documents the pipeline gives, as JSON, so each may have its own shape. A command that declares output columns has its rows checked against them on the way out, as every command's output contract is. Registration refuses a pipeline command whose native query names an argument the command does not declare, leaves a declared argument unused, or writes ($out, $merge), and one that is not a query. The command is assigned to roles and placed in a domain like any other command.

Node draws it on the server, one process per call within the operator setting mcp.render_timeout_s; a host without Node or the built renderer refuses the call by name. generate_explore_queries answers all six query surfaces under the caller's role.

Description: A release is made only by the Release: cut workflow, run by hand on main with the version. It generates the release's notes from the previous release's tag (the UI's bundled notes, docs/releases/<version>.md, the docs navigation and CHANGELOG.md) and commits them to main before it makes the release's tag on that commit; a generation failure leaves no commit and no tag. A hand-written release page is never overwritten. The release's body is its notes page, and a tag pushed by hand gets no release.

Every file Provisa itself generates (a source's conversion caches and crawl downloads, the Calcite file adapter's working files, replicas, checker and profiler output, large results, downloaded runtimes' and bundles' per-org state, and any other file a source or engine writes by default) is written only under its org's directory in the server's default file location. Each org has its own folder under that location. [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1992, 2026-10-12 -- the folder is durable and its key is held by the org in its own vault. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] The files are ephemeral and each node keeps its own copy of an org's folder. An org setting (with its admin UI) encrypts the org's folder on each node with a random key created when the folder is mounted and held only in that node's memory; it is never stored, wrapped or derived from any persistent key, so no one, the platform admin included, can decrypt the files from stored state, and the platform admin role has no path to an org's folder. When the mount ends (restart, unmount, idle) the key is gone, the folder's ciphertext is deleted, and the files are rebuilt as needed. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] When it is on, only ciphertext reaches the underlying storage, and the components that read and write files see plain paths either way, so no adapter, engine, checker or connector needs its own encryption. No generated file is written outside an org's directory, and an operation that needs an org directory refuses, naming the org, when that directory is not available. Files a client provides (a file source in the client's own bucket or at the client's own URL) are the client's and are read with the credentials the client supplies; this requirement does not govern them. (Amended 2026-10-12, DURABLE FOLDER AND ORG-HELD KEY:) [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1992, 2026-10-12 -- a multi-node deployment shares one mount; see SHARED MOUNT below. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] Every file Provisa keeps for an org, on each node, is in that node's folder for the org, <data directory>/orgs/<org>; [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] the folder is durable: nothing in it is deleted when it is unmounted, the server restarts or goes idle, or a process crashes. Immutable artifacts that hold no org data and are shared by every org (downloaded runtimes and bundles themselves) stay where they are. Encryption is an org setting that only an org admin can read or change; the platform admin has no path to it. The setting holds a reference to one secret in the org's own secrets vault (AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault), never a key: the key is resolved from the vault when the folder is mounted, handed to the directory-encryption tool on a pipe, and never stored, logged or wrapped by any Provisa key. Mounting needs no one present, so restarts and background jobs open the folder on their own. A key the vault no longer gives (revoked) refuses the folder, naming the org; [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1992, 2026-10-12 -- a key that does not open the folder refuses it; see SHARED MOUNT below. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] a key that no longer opens the folder (lost) resets the folder and rebuilds its files, logged naming the org. [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] Turning encryption on encrypts the folder's files in place, and turning it off decrypts them out; nothing is lost either way. Rotation is: generate a new key, store it in the vault, and update the reference; the folder is re-encrypted under the new key. The admin page can generate a random 256-bit key, shown once and held nowhere (no log, store or audit row), with warnings that Provisa cannot recover it, that it must be stored in the vault now, that a second copy belongs in a separate secure place under the org's control, that few should be able to read it and it is never sent by email, chat or ticket, [SUPERSEDED by REQ-1992, 2026-10-12 -- losing it refuses the folder until a new key is set; see SHARED MOUNT below. Kept here for history; do not implement against it.] that losing it resets and rebuilds the encrypted files, [END SUPERSEDED BLOCK] and how rotation works. A node that cannot encrypt a directory (macOS run natively) refuses an encrypted folder, naming the org. (Amended 2026-10-12, SHARED MOUNT:) Maintainer ruling, through the lead: "a multi-node deployment shares a single file mount, so the org folder is not per node". Every file Provisa keeps for an org is in <data directory>/orgs/<org>; a deployment of several nodes mounts that data folder once, shared by every node (the coordinator's folder, or a shared volume, set up by Terraform or Helm), and says so by an operator setting the launcher sets on every node (org_files.shared_mount), with each node's name (org_files.node_id, its pod or host name). What belongs to one process -- a connector server's run directory, a replica spool, temporary files -- is kept in the node's own part of the org's folder, orgs/<org>/nodes/<node id>, which no other node writes; a node's start sweeps only its own spools. The embedded DuckDB materialization store has one writer and cannot serve several nodes: on a shared mount it is refused at startup, by name, and the deployment uses a server store; a single node keeps orgs/<org>/materialize.duckdb. An encrypted folder is mounted by every node from the same ciphertext with gocryptfs's -sharedstorage, each node recording that it holds a mount. A change of the folder's encryption (on, off, a new key) applies only while no other node holds a mount, and is refused naming them otherwise; the others mount it again at their next runtime build. A node releases its mount when it shuts down (a stop, SIGTERM): the last of its processes to go unmounts and removes its record, so only a node that died leaves one, and the refusal says how to clear it. Lead's rulings, quoted: "(A) Concurrent mounts with -sharedstorage: yes. (B) A per-node subtree orgs/<org>/nodes/<node-id>/ for process-bound state (pgwire run dirs, spool, tmp); the spool sweep covers only its own subtree; node id comes from a setting (pod/host name). The embedded DuckDB store is single-writer, so it can't serve a multi-node deployment. A multi-node deployment uses a server store, and the embedded DuckDB store is refused at startup in multi-node, by name. On a single node it stays orgs/<org>/materialize.duckdb. (C) Option (i): a change applies only when no other node holds a mount (mounted/<node-id> markers), otherwise it's refused naming them; the others remount at their next runtime build." KEY LOSS, restated. The earlier ruling, "a lost key resets and rebuilds the folder, logged by name", is replaced by the maintainer's choice, through the lead: "refuse, never reset: a wrong or unreadable key refuses, naming the org. A reset happens only when an org admin deliberately sets a new key." A key that does not open the folder, or that the vault will not give, refuses the folder naming the org and resets nothing; when an org admin sets a new key and the key the folder was encrypted under can no longer be read, the folder is reset under the new key, logged naming the org. The admin page's warning says that losing the key leaves the files unopenable until a new key is set, and that setting one resets them. (Amended 2026-10-13, IMMUTABLE RUNTIMES ARE NOT ORG STATE:) A downloaded runtime that is the same for every org and never changes once fetched (the Calcite file adapter's embedder model weights, like the pgwire bundles) is not an org's state: it is kept once per machine in a shared runtime cache, outside every org's directory, and holds nothing of any org. Only what such a runtime writes while serving an org is org state and goes under that org's directory. (Amended 2026-10-13, MACHINE-WIDE COORDINATION STATE IS NOT ORG STATE:) Likewise, state that coordinates every process on a machine and holds nothing of any org (the Calcite file adapter's cross-process rate-limit slots, one per external host, which keep the machine within a site's per-IP request limit) is kept once per machine, outside every org's directory; splitting it per org would let the orgs on a node together exceed that limit. (Amended 2026-10-13, THE OFFLINE ETL STAGES IN ITS DECLARED SCRATCH:) The govdata offline ETL (a machine-wide job that holds no org's data) stages its large temporary files, such as downloaded archives, raw page caches, staging batches and DuckDB spill, in the scratch directory its run declares (GOVDATA_TMPDIR), not in the operating directory. The scratch is required: an ETL run without it refuses, naming the setting, and the code never falls back to the JVM temp directory. The ETL scripts point it at the disk-backed scratch sized for the job.

Python is a source type, the Python counterpart of the Node connector (REQ-1984), on the same language-neutral worker protocol. A source holds Python code; each module-level function whose docstring carries the tag @table is offered as a table, @command as a command and @stream (a generator or async generator) as a live table; untagged functions are ignored. Parameters, columns and the types that reach every surface come from the function's type hints (a dataclass, TypedDict or annotated class becomes a named type); the docstring text is the description; a type that cannot be mapped, an unknown tag, or a @table that does not return a collection is refused by name when the code is loaded. No Provisa package or SDK is imported by the code. A source names its code as a PyPI package at an exact version (public or a private index), a Git repository at a commit or tag with a subdirectory, or an uploaded archive; the reference is pinned and the content's hash recorded. Dependencies install from the code's lockfile when the code is loaded, not per call, cached by content hash, through the org's package indexes (an organization setting with its own admin page, like REQ-1984's registries; every field resolved with the standard resolution, so it can be a secret reference). The Python runtime is fetched on demand, pinned and hashed. The code runs in its own sandboxed worker process, never inside Provisa's process: no file access beyond its code, network only to the egress allow-list. Each subscription to a @stream table starts its own generator with that subscriber's arguments.

A Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 source reads, beside mail, the calendars and To Do / Google Tasks of its accounts, and writes their events, attendees and tasks. A source states which of mail, calendar and tasks it reads; it offers the canonical tables of those (REQ-1923's canonical mail schema): calendars, events and event_attendees for calendar; task_lists and tasks for tasks. Reminders are columns, not a table: an event's reminders (Google) or is_reminder_on and reminder_minutes_before_start (Microsoft), a task's reminder_at and is_reminder_on (Microsoft; Google's Tasks API has no reminder and keeps only the day a task is due). READING: each calendar and task table is read whole, for every account, at each refresh. The events table holds single events, series masters (with their recurrence as RFC 5545 lines; Microsoft's pattern is rendered as one RRULE) and exceptions (a moved or cancelled occurrence, with series_id and original_start_at), never the expanded occurrences of a series; on Microsoft the masters come from each calendar's /events and the exceptions from each master's exceptionOccurrences. A refresh is asked for when the source's change token differs from the last: Google, each calendar's last change time and each task's update time; Microsoft, each calendar's events in a window either side of today (calendar_check_days, a setting of the source with a field on its form) by id and change key, and each task's update time. WRITING: events, event_attendees and tasks take INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE through one write path for the two source types (executor.writable WritePath.API, federation.mail_write), governed like any table write. An INSERT gives literal values; an UPDATE or DELETE names its rows by their write key (provider, account, id; an attendee by event_id and address), or one occurrence of a series by series_id and original_start_at, which a change or removal makes an exception. The rows named are found at the provider as they stand, and each is changed or removed only where the statement's whole WHERE, row rules included, holds for it. A write sets only the columns the provider keeps of the table's writable set; any other is refused by name. Recurrence is set on a series, never on one occurrence. NOTIFICATION: a write tells an event's attendees nothing unless the source's calendar_send_updates is on (a field on its form). Google takes sendUpdates=none; Microsoft Graph cannot change a meeting's attendees, or a meeting the account organizes with others attending, without telling them, so such a write is refused by name while the setting is off (the account's own reminder is changed either way). SCOPES: Google asks calendar.calendarlist.readonly, calendar.events and tasks (with userinfo.email, by which the sign-in names its account); Microsoft asks Calendars.ReadWrite and Tasks.ReadWrite delegated, and a source of the organisation's mailboxes needs Calendars.ReadWrite and Tasks.ReadWrite.All application permissions (Google: the same scopes on the service account's domain-wide delegation). The scopes a sign-in asks are the server's, from the source's settings as the form states them, never a list the form makes. The scopes the issuer says an approval grants are recorded with it; a source whose approval does not grant what it now reads is refused by name, asking its owner to sign in again.

Description: Logs is a source type that turns log files into tables. A source names a file glob (for example /var/log/system.log*) and a format; each matching file's lines become rows of one table. Built-in formats: BSD syslog (RFC 3164), RFC 5424 syslog with structured data, the macOS install-log form (ISO date with offset, host, process[pid]: message), Apache/nginx Common and Combined Log Format, JSON lines, logfmt, W3C extended, CEF and GELF; any other format is a regular expression whose named groups are the columns. Columns and their types come from the format (a JSON-lines or logfmt source types its columns from a preview, which a steward can override); a line the format cannot parse is kept with its raw text and a parse-error column, never dropped. Rotation: the glob takes in rotated files, and gzip and bzip2 files are read transparently; each file is identified by its inode plus a checksum of its first bytes, not by its name, so a renamed or compressed file is not read twice; a per-file offset lets a growing file be read from where it left off; a file found shorter than its offset was truncated and is read from the start; each row carries its file identity and line offset, which dedupe it. A logs table can be a replica refreshed on the source's schedule or a live table delivering new lines as they are written, over the surfaces that serve subscriptions. Where the files may be read is the operator's: the setting logs.allowed_roots lists the directories a glob may resolve into (by default /var/log), and a glob that resolves outside them, after following symlinks, is refused by name; on the multi-organisation SaaS plane a server-local log path is refused entirely, by name. Beyond the core formats, named presets over the shared parsers, grouped by origin in the format choice: Amazon (ALB, NLB and Classic ELB access logs, CloudFront standard logs, S3 server access logs, CloudTrail with one row per Records entry, VPC Flow Logs by version, WAF and Route 53 Resolver query logs), Microsoft (IIS, Windows Firewall, Windows DNS debug, DHCP server audit, Exchange message tracking, SQL Server ERRORLOG, Azure Storage analytics, Azure Monitor and Activity Log exports, Windows Event Log .evtx), Google (Cloud Logging LogEntry exports, Android logcat threadtime, Chrome net-export), web servers and proxies (nginx and Apache error, HAProxy HTTP, Squid access, Envoy default access, Caddy, Traefik), databases and runtimes (PostgreSQL stderr, csvlog and jsonlog, MySQL error and slow-query, MongoDB, Redis, log4j and logback default patterns, Python logging default), containers and Linux (Kubernetes CRI with partial lines joined, systemd journal JSON, auditd, dmesg) and security (Zeek, Suricata EVE, Snort fast alert). A record may span lines: a record-start pattern joins a stack trace or a slow-query entry into one row. A format whose file names its columns in a header (W3C, CloudFront, Zeek) reads them from each file's header.

Description: A file-based source (DuckDB, SQLite, CSV and Parquet: the sources whose path names a file) can be given its file by uploading it. On the source form, an upload streams the file to disk, never held in memory, into the organization's own file folder (REQ-1992) under its files area, and sets the source's path to it, written relative to the org's folder as {files}/<source>/<file>, never as the file's physical location. A file source's path may use two org-level tokens, resolved where the file is read (as ${secret:...} is): {files}, the org's files area, and {org}, the org's folder; the form, the API, every read of the source and every message name the path as written, with the token. A user may type a {files}/... or {org}/... path. A path that resolves outside the org's folder (through .. or a symbolic link) is refused, naming the path. On a server of many organizations an absolute path on the server's own disk in a file source is refused, naming the path; only a token path or a remote location is accepted. A path saved before as the absolute location of a file in the org's folder is saved as its token the next time the source is saved. Replacing the file is another upload, which takes the place of the earlier one, and the next read sees the new file; removing the source removes its uploaded file. The uploaded file is stored like every other org file: under that org's folder only, encrypted when the org has turned folder encryption on, and durable (org files are kept until what they belong to goes; nothing removes them on its own). On a deployment of several nodes the org folder is one shared mount, so an upload is seen by every node. Uploads are limited by an operator setting for the largest file accepted (sources.max_upload_bytes, by default 1 GiB), with its settings UI; a larger file is refused naming the limit. Only the org's source registrars may upload, and the path of an uploaded file is not editable as free text while the file is the upload's. Every file-based source takes every kind of location its engine can read: a local path, https, and object stores (s3, gs, az) with their credentials; a SQLite or DuckDB file in a remote location is attached read-only and offers no writes, a write to it being refused by name before it runs; on an engine that does not attach SQLite, a remote SQLite file is read through a DuckDB connection that attaches it read-only, and landed. The form says which kinds of location each file type accepts. A write to a SQLite or DuckDB file on this node takes the file's lock and never waits for it: when another process or node holds the file, the write is refused, naming the source and that its file is locked. A DuckDB file is held read-only by everything that reads it (the engine's attach, the source's own connection), so every node reads it at once, and a write opens it read-write for that statement alone. On an encrypted org folder whose mount is shared by several nodes (the operator setting org_files.shared_mount), where the encryption layer does not carry a file's lock to the other nodes, a write to a SQLite or DuckDB file in the folder is refused outright, by name. A folder shared without encryption must be mounted with locks that reach every node (an NFS mount with locking on: not nolock, not local_lock), a deployment requirement no probe checks.

A statement whose tables all belong to one Qdrant source routes DIRECT to Qdrant, as any single-source statement routes to its source: the governed statement is lowered to Qdrant's API. Payload predicates become a Qdrant filter; a key predicate becomes retrieve; a plain scan with a limit becomes scroll; ORDER BY cosine_similarity(<named vector>, <query>) DESC LIMIT k (and the GraphQL similar argument, which compiles to it) becomes query_points against that vector with the filter applied before the top-k. Single-source INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on a Qdrant collection table become upsert and delete of points. A statement holding anything the lowering cannot express exactly (another source, an aggregate, a predicate with no Qdrant filter form, a row rule that cannot be expressed as a filter) does not route DIRECT and is answered by the engine over the replica, so governance is never bypassed. A vector column written with text is embedded with the column's declared registry model; a vector given as a vector is used as given, its dimensions checked. (Amended 2026-10-12, RULINGS:) The lead's rulings, quoted: "(a) query_points as is, with grpc-fix's statement.approximate_index warning (the same rule as replica top-k). (b) A plain INSERT refuses an existing id by name (retrieve first; note the non-atomicity in the REQ). Also accept INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET … as an upsert. (c) Yes. Register Table and the table editor let a vector column name its model (filtered by dimensions), and the form carries embedding_model for it." A top-k read in Qdrant uses its own index and so is approximate, as a replica's top-k is: the answer carries the same approximate-index warning. Similarity runs DIRECT only on a collection whose distance is cosine, the one where Qdrant's score is the cosine similarity; any other distance is answered by the engine. A plain INSERT of an id the collection holds is refused naming the id: the ids are read before the points are written, and a point written by another client between the read and the write is overwritten (the check is not atomic). INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET each column = EXCLUDED.column is an upsert of every row given; any other conflict clause is refused by name. A write whose condition, with the role's row rules, has no Qdrant filter form is refused naming it, since the engine does not write to Qdrant. A write returns no rows. A vector column of a collection table names its registered model at registration and in the table editor, from the models whose dimensions are the vector's size; that declaration is what both similarity search and a written text use. (Amended 2026-10-12, LIVE-ONLY SOURCE TYPE:) The maintainer ruled that replicas cannot answer what Qdrant answers ('replicas just can't work'), that 'live-only would be a datasource type property, not an option', and that 'its reserved for scenarios where the engine cannot replicate the live db query feature.' Live-only is therefore a property of a source type, fixed by the type: no per-source setting, no form field, no operator choice. A type has it only when its defining query capability cannot be reproduced by the engine over a replica (Qdrant: its own vector index and query API); it is not a general way to avoid replication. Qdrant has it. A live-only source's table has no replica and no keyed (row_materialize) fetch. A statement on one Qdrant source runs DIRECT as above (writes, and reads lowered to scroll, retrieve or query_points with the filter applied before the top-k, the top-k reported approximate). When a statement is answered by the engine (it joins another source, or computes over a Qdrant column, as a mask does), each Qdrant collection's part of it must be expressible in Qdrant (a filter, a key set or a top-k), and is fetched live for that statement and handed to the engine as rows, as a search table's rows are; a part that is not expressible is refused naming the table and why, and is never replicated. Row rules on a Qdrant table must translate into its Qdrant filter, else the statement is refused. Search tables keep their per-statement read. (Amended 2026-10-12, COSINE SIMILARITY ON QDRANT:) The maintainer ruled: 'if cosine_similarity is used on qdrant it will lower to qdrant native - and it will always be direct-only'. ORDER BY cosine_similarity(<vector>, <query>) DESC LIMIT k over a Qdrant collection is lowered to one query_points, the filter applied before the top-k, the top-k reported approximate, and only for a vector whose distance is Cosine; it is so lowered both when the statement runs on the source and when it is the collection's part of an engine-answered statement, and is never answered over a replica. A live-only collection's part of an engine-answered statement that has no filter, no key set and no top-k is refused, since it would read the whole collection; a non-null replicate on a live-only source's table is refused at register and update.

A command can be implemented by a Provisa SQL statement with typed arguments (implementation kind statement): the statement is governed and run through the one pipeline under the caller's rights like any statement, its arguments bound as values, never spliced. An argument is written {{name}} in the statement, as a MongoDB pipeline command writes one: every placeholder is a declared argument and every declared argument is used. A statement command is a query when its statement reads and a mutation when it writes. It is invocable on every surface commands are, a scheduled trigger can run it (the trigger's SQL is one call of the command, run as the trigger's role), and every run is audited, a scheduled run under the scheduler's audit identity and bounded by the scheduler's own request timeout (limits.request_timeouts.scheduler, REQ-1905). An INSERT ... SELECT whose SELECT reads a source other than its target's, or computes embed(), is run as its governed SELECT read as any read, its rows then written into the target through that table's write route as an INSERT ... VALUES, so a command can compute rows across sources and write them to one target; an ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE on it is carried to that write, and a target whose write route has no upsert refuses it by name. The statement is the command's declaration: at registration its contract is derived from the governed statement and stored, namely its kind (a SELECT is a query, a write a mutation), writes_table (its target), the tables it reads after view expansion, its output columns (the select list's types, or the write's row count), its column lineage as REQ-1160 computes it, and the types of its {{name}} arguments. The command form shows the steward that contract (e.g. "reads support.tickets, writes kb.docs (upsert), returns a row count"). A declared kind or writes_table that contradicts the statement is refused by name. At every schema rebuild the command's contract is derived again; one that no longer resolves (a table or column it reads or writes was renamed or dropped) is marked broken with the reason, its invocation refused naming that reason and the commands page showing it; lineage and impact analysis list statement commands as they list views, so a rename or drop that would break one lists it beforehand, through its write edge. The lineage carries the write edge: the target table shows it is written by the command, from the tables and columns the command reads (e.g. kb.docs "written by command embed_tickets, from support.tickets (ticket_id, subject)"), in the lineage graph and in impact analysis, so rows a command derives into a source stay traceable as derived, not as plain source data. Those edges (its reads, its write to the target, column by column) are added to the lineage graph from the statement itself at registration, as a view's are, and derived again on a model change; a run adds none, its audit record kept apart. Each run creates one audit record for provenance, the command call's own record extended for this kind (no second log): the command and the version of its contract that ran, the caller (or the scheduled trigger's role and principal), the argument values, its start and end, its outcome, the tables it read, the target it wrote and the rows affected; the record names the command, so a derived table answers both "derived from what" (the lineage graph) and "which run, when, by whom, with what inputs" (the audit). The record lets someone prove what produced the rows: it holds the exact registered statement text with its hash and contract version, the bound argument values, and each embed() call's model (its id, provider, dimensions and version, REQ-2002), beside the caller, start and end, outcome, tables read, target and rows affected. Run records are append-only, as the audit log is.

Description: embed(model, text) is a function of Provisa SQL that returns the embedding of text by a model from the registry, its dimensions those of the model. It is evaluated by Provisa, once per distinct text in a statement, never sent to a source; a model not in the registry, or one the registry has disabled, is refused naming it. A literal text is embedded once, with the statement. A text read from rows is embedded on the rows a statement reads, so embed() of a column or expression is an item of the select list; anywhere else it is refused by name. Each registered model has a version: where the provider reports one it is taken from the provider (an Ollama model's digest, a local HuggingFace model's revision or commit hash), otherwise it is the value the operator enters (a model name such as OpenAI's carries none); it is set in the AI Models settings. The audit record of every statement that calls embed() holds each model it used: its id, provider, dimensions and version.

The documentation has a sizing guide for a customer, and the steps to run the sizing tool that produces it. The tool measures the customer's own deployment under the customer's own workload and writes a sizing and tuning guide from those measurements. The guide is for a customer: nothing about how Provisa itself is benchmarked goes in it.

provisa.dev has a live demos page with one card for each published named demo: its title, description and screenshot, and an "Open live demo" button. The button opens a cloud.provisa.dev sandbox of that demo that needs no signup, with the demo's example queries and the product tour. A named demo says whether it is published, and what its card shows, in demo/named/<name>/demo.yaml (title, description, screenshot, published: true or false); the site build generates the page from those files, as it generates the source picker, and CI fails when the page is out of step with them. Every published demo is lightweight, and its data is seeded ahead of time: never at a visitor's request, and never by a live traffic generator. Opening the page warms the cloud coordinator in the background through the front door's wake-on-hit, so that a visitor's click rarely meets the waking page. The cloud side: each published demo has a template organization on the sandbox tier, built from the demo's published bundle, whose own sources it reads live from the stores the tier's node runs (REQ-2049); only a SaaS-account source is landed, when the bundle is built. Opening the demo (cloud.provisa.dev/demos/<name>, no account) opens a sandbox: an organization of its own (id sbx<hex>) whose model is copied from the template, reading the demo's own sources live and any replica the template holds copied into its own file, so nothing is seeded at the visitor's request. The visitor is a user minted for the sandbox with the sandbox role and a personal access token the browser keeps (REQ-1035: no identity-provider sign-in). A signed-in person's "Try it Out" sandbox (POST /sandboxes/<name>) is the same organization model under their own identity, the same one from every device they use. Every sandbox runs on an in-process DuckDB engine of its own, pinned to the file in its folder (REQ-1992); real organizations stay on their own engine. Exactly one process ever opens a sandbox's file: the sandbox tier, a single-worker API of its own (PROVISA_SANDBOX_TIER), which serves only sandbox and template organizations; the UI server sends a sandbox's requests there by its address, and every other process refuses a sandbox by name (421 sandbox.wrong_tier). Inside it, concurrent requests share the one engine; a write-write conflict DuckDB raises is refused by name (engine.write_conflict), never retried, and two creates of one source id leave one created and the other refused (schema.source_id_taken). Model edits go through the model store's guards as any organization's do. Nobody else can join a sandbox of either kind: the sandbox role holds no user_management (REQ-1597), so no one can be invited into it. Limits, each an operator setting with a settings UI: sandbox.max_concurrent (past it, a visitor is asked to try again shortly, sandbox.at_capacity), sandbox.memory_limit (the sandbox engine's DuckDB memory_limit), sandbox.disk_limit (the sandbox's folder, its DuckDB file and uploads together; a write past it is refused, sandbox.disk_full), and sandbox.idle_ttl (a sandbox no request has reached for that long is deleted whole: its organization, engine, folder and token). A sandbox's sources may reach only the destinations its demo declares and public addresses, checked at registration and again at each connection, each connection made to the checked address (sources.private_destination, sources.unpinnable_destination). A named sandbox's person is told plainly that this is a lightweight version with limits, each named with its value read from the settings, in the sandbox's welcome notice and on the hosted-sandbox docs page: it runs on a single-process DuckDB engine, not the engine production organizations use; the memory cap and the disk cap (DuckDB file plus uploads); concurrent writes from several devices can be refused with a conflict, to retry; it expires after the inactivity period; its person can't invite people, or switch or manage environments; the sample sources are read-only and writes stay inside the sandbox. All of it is translated in every locale, with no requirement ids in the UI. A sandbox's AI -- Polly and every AI-model role (column and table descriptions, relationship inference, natural-language SQL, table selection) -- uses one OpenAI-wire endpoint and model the sandbox tier's operator names (sandbox.ai_base_url, sandbox.ai_model, default anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 through OpenRouter), off until the endpoint and its key are set; the key is a ${secret:...} in the deployment organization's vault, resolved there for that endpoint only, while every credential a visitor writes resolves in the sandbox's own vault. A sandbox has no embedding model. (Amended 2026-10-17, A DEMO SEEDED INTO AN ORDINARY ORG:) On a deployment of many organizations, an ordinary org created with the deployment's demo holds the demo's sources, which the operator wrote as a template's are: those sources reach the destinations the demo declares, private ones included, as a sandbox's demo sources do. Every other source of that org -- one its members add, at the demo's own host or anywhere else -- is held to public destinations, when it is saved and at each connection. (Amended 2026-10-18, TEMPLATE BUILDS A FEW AT A TIME:) The tier builds its demos' templates through a queue, sandbox.template_builds_at_once of them together (an operator setting, default 2, read when the tier starts): built all at once after a restart, a 2-vCPU tier was too busy to serve visitors. A visitor who opens a demo whose template is still waiting is told it is still being prepared (sandbox.demo_not_ready) and the demo is built next. A template that cannot be built is logged with its cause and leaves the others to build.

Description: A table Provisa reads itself for each statement (a parameterized or native-query table: a MongoDB pipeline, a Cosmos DB query, a Qdrant search, a code source's function, a live-only table's part) is kept for its TTL, which is the first one set of the table's own, its source's, and the response cache's default. A TTL of 0 is set: it means 0, never "unset", so it does not fall through to the source's TTL or the default. With a TTL above 0 the rows are landed for the engine and kept under the statement's arguments for the TTL, and the next statement asking the same reuses them (the reuse pays for the write). With a TTL of 0 the read always goes live and nothing is kept: rows up to the large-result threshold (redirect.threshold) are inlined into the statement as a VALUES CTE, with no write on any engine, and more rows are landed in a scratch table of that statement alone, dropped when it ends and never reused. An API endpoint table's TTL, and a gRPC remote query's, are likewise the first one set. A statement that lands a scratch table is answered through the pipeline terminal, which drops it, so its answer is buffered rather than streamed.

A group-by is ordered by its keys and its aggregates. The <Type>GroupBy field's order_by is a list of <Type>GroupByOrderBy entries, applied in order, that mirror the result and having: {aggregate: {count: dir}}, {aggregate: {sum|avg|stddev|variance|min|max: {<field>: dir}}} with each column under the field name the row type gives it, and {groupKey: {<key>: dir}}. groupKey offers every column the by argument can name; a key the statement does not group by is refused when it is compiled, naming it. The compiler emits ORDER BY <AGG>(<column>) or the key, before LIMIT and OFFSET, so a limit returns the top N groups. A group-by is not ordered by the table's plain columns, and the <Type>Aggregate root, which returns no rows, takes no order_by. gRPC carries the order: {Type}GroupByRequest.order_by is a list of {func, column, direction} entries (func count, sum, avg, stddev, variance, min, max or group_key; column the physical name), with limit and offset applied; the HTTP gRPC proxy takes the same body. REST's and JSON:API's group-by sort orders by group keys, and a sort on any other field is refused (400).

Description: Polly's spend is metered and, in demo sandboxes, capped. Every model call marks the repeated prefix (the tool definitions, the system prompt and the conversation so far) for the prompt cache, on Anthropic's API and, for an Anthropic model, through an OpenAI-wire gateway such as OpenRouter; other vendors cache a repeated prefix by themselves. Each turn ends with a usage event: its fresh input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens summed over every call, tool round trips included, and its cost at the model's price in polly.model_prices, an operator setting holding a price table the operator sees and edits (USD per million tokens, one entry a model; an entry that does not read is refused when it is saved). When the gateway is OpenRouter the event also carries what OpenRouter billed. A model with no price reports tokens and no cost. In a demo sandbox org, Polly runs the model polly.sandbox_model (default claude-haiku-5-5), its spend is metered from that cost, and it refuses by name when the sandbox's budget (polly.sandbox_budget_usd, default $0.50) or the daily budget of every sandbox together (polly.daily_budget_usd, default $10) is used up: "this demo's assistant budget is used up" or "... for today"; the rest of the sandbox keeps working, and there is no fallback model. Polly's panel in a sandbox shows what is left. A tour step that asks Polly a fixed question is answered once, when the demo's bundle is built (Polly asked through OpenRouter on the sandbox's model, the build given OPENROUTER_API_KEY; scripts/demo_bundle.py), and the stored answer is served to visitors at no cost; a question it does not answer fails the build. A tour step's question is one of its own demo's bake-off questions, each graded by SQL over that demo's tables. A bake-off (.github/workflows/polly-bakeoff.yml, manual dispatch) asks a list of models eleven weblogs questions with known answers, the weblogs demo's own question among them, and reports accuracy, cost per question (median and p90), questions per $0.50 and latency.

The control plane is PostgreSQL only, in every tier and every test: embedded PostgreSQL (pgserver) where no control-plane URL is given -- demo, native, desktop, an ephemeral profile (in a throwaway data directory removed when the process ends), the UI e2e lanes and the unit tests -- and an external PostgreSQL server otherwise. No other control-plane store exists: SQLite, DuckDB, MySQL, MariaDB, SingleStore, SQL Server and Oracle are removed, and a PLATFORM_DATABASE_URL or TENANT_DATABASE_URL naming any of them is refused by name. The DuckDB engine reads provisa_admin live through its postgres extension; no snapshot of the control plane is taken. schema_org.py stays as the query metadata the repositories build their statements from, guarded against schema.sql by the parity test. It builds no DDL; schema.sql does. Native Linux arm64, for which pgserver ships no wheel, refuses by name to start without an external PostgreSQL URL; Docker installs and every other platform are unaffected.

A replica is indexed as its table is used: its declared primary key, enforced as the key, and the columns its declared relationships join on: the foreign key of each relationship whose source is the table, the target column of one whose target it is when that column is not the key, and both foreign keys of a junction table a relationship traverses. The indexes are built after the replica lands, never in its landing: the replica is read from its swap, and its indexes follow, built by the replica runner under a per-replica index lock that a landing never waits on. PostgreSQL stores build each with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside the swap, the key as a unique index made the primary key (ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX); other SQLAlchemy stores by the dialect's DDL; the embedded DuckDB store file through its broker. ClickHouse keeps its sorting key (the declared key) and warehouse stores build none. What a landing asked for, what was built and what failed is kept by name on the replica's record (replica_state.index_state); a failed index is logged with its cause and asked for again by the next landing, never failing the landing. Rows that repeat a declared key are a named failure carrying the key's columns. A landing that replaces the table while the last one's indexes are being built leaves them behind (a PostgreSQL swap cancels a build still running on the table it replaces), and the new table gets its own. Index names are fixed by the replica and the columns.

Description: A table on an Elasticsearch source can be registered from a native search instead of an index: one JSON document, {"index": ..., "query": {...}}, the Query DSL of a _search request, optionally with aggs, sort and highlight. The table stores it in query_template. Each "{{name}}" placeholder string anywhere in the request is a parameter of the table (query_arg, REQ-1986) with an IR type, optional unless a steward makes it required; a caller passes it as a GraphQL field argument or an equality condition on the parameter column in SQL. Each value is checked against its type and bound by replacing the placeholder node of the parsed request with the value, never written into the request text. The request is sent to _search and nowhere else: an index that names another endpoint, and any key that is not part of a search or that pages it (from, search_after, pit, scroll), is refused by name. A search with aggregations answers one row per bucket, nested buckets flattened with one column per key, doc count and metric; otherwise one row per hit, read in a point in time with search_after, with the hit's id, score and highlighted fragments beside its fields. Output columns are fixed at registration, from the index mapping restricted to the fields the hits hold, or from the aggregations for a bucket search, found by one preview run with sample arguments, and every row is checked against them. Like a MongoDB pipeline table (REQ-1980), it is read per statement by Provisa itself on every federation engine and landed for the engine; with no arguments it behaves as a view. It is registered on the Register Table form as a pipeline table is, and joins and is governed like any registered table.

The reviews named demo: an electronics shop's three NoSQL stores, read live and joined on the product id they share. MongoDB holds the catalog (about 200 product documents, specs nested) and the star ratings; ratings_by_product is an aggregation-pipeline table over the ratings (REQ-1980), a row a product. Elasticsearch holds about 5,000 reviews; reviews_matching is a native search table (REQ-2017) whose phrase is its parameter, each row a review whose text holds the phrase, the phrase highlighted. Neo4j holds about 2,000 customers and (:Customer)-[:BOUGHT]->(:Product); bought_together is a Cypher table, for each product each other product its buyers bought and how many did. Relationships join reviews, ratings and purchases to the catalog's products, and reviews and purchases to the customers. Every value is invented by the demo's seeder from a fixed seed (no licensed data): a few battery products have reviews that say the battery dies, lower ratings, and buyers who also bought power banks. The demo ships 4-6 example queries, and its tour follows the named-demo shape: the scenario and its three stores; the pipeline, search and Cypher tables and the relationships; then the shop's question answered over several surfaces -- the battery complaints by product in SQL, what the buyers of the lowest-rated products also bought in Cypher, the search over REST and in GraphQL -- and a recap. Its tour's words are in every language the UI speaks.

A TTL of -1 means never expires: the table lands once and its replica is never stale after that. -1 can be set on a source, which its tables inherit as they inherit any TTL, or on a table. A read of a TTL -1 table is always answered from its replica; with no replica yet, a read is refused by name, never sent to the source. The UI shows the replica's landing time ("as of") where freshness would show. Provisa contacts a source only to land a table that needs landing: a source whose tables are all TTL -1 and landed is never attached, probed, reconciled or landed, at boot or later, and needs no credential to be read. Other negative TTLs are refused. A TTL of 0 keeps its REQ-2003 meaning. -1 means never expires everywhere a TTL applies (amended 2026-10-15, lead ruling): rows a per-statement table keeps under their arguments (REQ-2003), and a response-cache entry reading only such tables, are kept for good. A per-statement table avoids contacting its source only for argument sets it has already kept; a new argument set still reads the source.

The sonnets named demo: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets in Postgres, embedded into Qdrant, searched by meaning, grown into a graph. Its database holds a row a sonnet (number, first line, sequence: Fair Youth for 1 to 126, Dark Lady for 127 to 154), a row a line (loaded from the text of Project Gutenberg eBook #1041, committed with the demo), the five themes it searches for, and an echo table. The statement command embed_lines writes every line's embedding (sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a local model) to the Qdrant collection sonnet_lines through embed() and the collection's write route. The search table lines_like is read live in Qdrant under its arguments (a phrase, a count). Five materialized views each store one fixed search joined back to the lines it found, with its score. The python command link_echoes asks the vector store, for each line, for its three nearest lines in other sonnets and writes them, with their similarity, to the echo table through Provisa as the caller. Relationships make a graph: Line IN Sonnet, Line EVOKES Theme (through the theme views), Line ECHOES Line (through the echo table, with its score). Its tour opens on what the demo is and the question it asks -- which themes run through the sonnets, and where Shakespeare echoes himself -- says in each step what Provisa does, leads with the echo network (sonnets 36 and 96 end on the same couplet) and then the themes, and asks the question on two or three surfaces, Cypher for the echo network, before the stored Polly answer. (SETUP:) A named demo may ship setup.yaml, an ordered list of its own commands (command: <name>, called as org_admin with no arguments) and materialized-view builds (refresh: <view>), run once per control plane through the API after the server is healthy, by scripts/run_demo_setup.py: start-ui-install.sh runs it, and a demo's template build runs the same list. A demo whose name is in the operator setting demo.setup_completed is not set up again; the name is added when every step has succeeded, and removing it sets the demo up again on its next start. The first step that fails stops the run, naming the step; nothing is retried. (EXTRAS:) A named demo names in its demo.yaml the optional dependency groups it needs (extras: [vector]); start-ui-install.sh installs them for that demo alone, and every other start installs nothing more.
