Description: A zoned timestamp is an instant, and the model has a type for it: timestamptz, carried as UTC with its zone marked, beside timestamp, a date and time with no zone. Registration types a source's zoned timestamp as timestamptz: PostgreSQL timestamptz and timestamp with time zone, Oracle TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE and WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE, SQL Server datetimeoffset, Snowflake TIMESTAMP_TZ and TIMESTAMP_LTZ, Trino and DuckDB timestamp with time zone, BigQuery TIMESTAMP, the MySQL family's TIMESTAMP and an Elasticsearch date. Each source's reader hands on the instant: the Oracle and SQL Server readers take the value to UTC with its offset, which their drivers would otherwise lose, and the MySQL family is read in a UTC session. Every engine and store holds the instant as its zoned type (timestamptz on PostgreSQL, TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE on DuckDB, timestamp with time zone on Trino, an Arrow timestamp in UTC), the engines read in UTC, and every surface gives the instant with its zone: ISO 8601 with its offset in JSON and GraphQL, google.protobuf.Timestamp in gRPC, timestamp with time zone in the pgwire and Flight catalogs. A literal compared to a timestamptz column is read at its own offset, or as UTC when it has none.

Each published named demo is its own bundle, built and published on its own and never part of a release or the app image. A bundle holds the demo's model (config.yaml), its data landed once at build (the seed the sandbox tier lands its template from, the files its traffic generator wrote, and a dump of each of its databases a run-time compose file loads), its tour and example queries, and the oldest Provisa version it runs on (requires_provisa in demo.yaml). The Demo bundles workflow builds a demo when a push to main changes demo/named/<name>/, or on a dispatch naming it, and publishes it as an OCI artifact to one package every demo shares, ghcr.io/<owner>/provisa-demos, tagged <name>-<version> and <name>-latest; the version is the build's UTC minute and commit, and a version is never published twice. Whoever runs a demo pulls its bundle and runs its own stores, which it reads live, as the demo defines them; only an external SaaS-account source is landed at build (TTL -1, REQ-2031) and served from replicas. On the sandbox tier's node a sync (scripts/demo_stores_sync.sh, run at boot, on a timer and whenever the tier asks) pulls each offered demo's version (PROVISA_DEMO_BUNDLES), brings up the bundle's run-time stores as a compose project of that version, shared read-only by its sandboxes, writes where they are into the bundle's stores.env, and marks the version ready; it takes down the stores of versions nothing reads any more. The tier serves the ready version; when a sandbox is opened it looks for a newer published version and asks the node for it, serving the ready one meanwhile, so a newly published version reaches the next sandbox opened after it is ready, with no release and no redeploy; the demo's template is replaced from it, and a sandbox already open keeps reading its own version. A sandbox's visitor sees what the demo shows its admin and holds the demo's own roles, never a right the sandbox role withholds (REQ-1597), and is shown the example queries and tour of the version it was opened from. A demo's log files are read live from its bundle, by its template and sandboxes only, inside that demo's directory. start-ui-install.sh --demo <name> pulls <name>-latest, --demo <name>@<version> that version, and runs it with only what reading it needs (the weblogs demo: its shop database, loaded from the bundle's dump; no shop, web server or traffic generator), while --from-source runs a demo from the checkout's own directory for development. A bundle that needs a newer Provisa than the one pulling it is refused by name, and so is one in an older demo format than it reads (the format its manifest names, bumped when a demo's files gain something a reader requires), when it is pulled or loaded, naming the bundle and saying to pull its latest. Only the OCI distribution API is spoken, so no registry client is needed where a demo runs.

A feature demo, data quality (quality): a medallion over the demo's own Postgres, every layer after bronze a materialized view kept current by the product's own cascade, driven by landing alone. A chain of shops sends its sales as a feed, a batch a day; the database's sales.land_batch lands a batch into bronze, append-only, each row stamped with its batch and when it landed. Bronze types its well-formed fields on landing (sale id, sold at, quantity) and keeps the messy ones raw (shop code, product, price). Bronze is read live and declares change_signal probe on its landed_at watermark (REQ-2055), so a landing refreshes dq_results -- a view computing the checks in SQL per batch (shop known, quantity above zero, price a number, sale id present): failing rows, pass or fail, under the batch's run id -- then silver, then gold. Silver is bronze joined to dq_results, from the batches whose checks all passed only, with the run id on every row, and visibly cleaned: codes trimmed and upper-cased, product spellings mapped to one, the price cast to a number, the sale day derived, a resent sale deduplicated on its id keeping the latest line. Gold is one GROUP BY over silver (sales, items, revenue and price range by day and product). A batch that fails a check shows failed in dq_results and never reaches silver or gold; earlier good batches stay. A relationship from silver.run_id to dq_results answers "which checks admitted this version of silver", and dq_results' failed rows "what the bad batch failed on". The seeder lands the batches at bundle build; history is in bronze, which ships in the Postgres dump, read only in every sandbox, whose views build from it. Description: A trigger says when something runs, and what runs is an ordinary command (python or statement), a SQL statement or a webhook. Besides a cron schedule, a trigger can be on a registered table (named source_id.schema.table) for its change, or for the event loop's error or quarantine event for it. A change fires once per burst of changes its change signal reports: native (PostgreSQL logical replication, MongoDB and Cosmos DB change streams), debezium, kafka, the signal webhook, or a write made through Provisa. A table read from its whole-table replica changes when a build of the replica lands rows that differ from the last; a table read live changes when it is written or signalled. The trigger gives the command what fired it as arguments: on change, the table and, where the signal carries it (Kafka, Debezium), the landed batch (changes); on an event, the table, the event, its reason and its error. A trigger whose command declares an argument it does not give is refused at save. The command runs as the trigger's role through the command's normal governed dispatch, and stays runnable by hand or from a schedule. A command's own write is itself a change, so triggers chain. Each run, scheduled or not, is recorded on the trigger: when it ran, whether it succeeded, was refused or failed, why, and what fired it; a refused or failed run wrote nothing and fires nothing downstream. Only an org's prod triggers fire. No trigger is installed in any source database. The admin API lists each trigger with what fires it, its target, role, enabled, last run and a schedule's next firing.

Description: A table read where it lies (not replicated) that declares a probing change signal -- probe or ttl_probe, its own else its source's -- is a signal-only node of the event loop: its probe (MAX of its watermark column, a count, or its probe_query) runs on its cache TTL, and a change is posted to the materialized views that read it, which recompute and ripple on to theirs. A capability demo, insider review at an investment bank: Is anyone sending deal-sensitive or customer data out of the bank? Generated private data only: the control room's watch list (each deal: entity legal name, aliases, ticker, project code name, deal type -- merger, acquisition, loan or underwriting -- a short description, the deal team and when each member was brought over the wall, and the public announcement date if any), employees, and an employee mailbox (messages with sender, recipients, sent time and body) whose tables would sit equally over a real mail source. Every outbound message is scored against every watch-list deal: entity match (legal name and aliases fuzzily, ticker, project code name) and semantic similarity of the message to the deal's description through the demo's own local embedding model, so a paraphrase that avoids every name still scores; the score is weighted by context: a sender not on that deal's team, a recipient outside the bank's domains or a personal address, and a message sent before the deal's announcement each raise it; a deal-team member writing to the deal's own counterparties lowers it. The same messages are checked for customer PII by SQL pattern checks, joined to the bank's customer-data access log (who read customer data, and when) so a sender who read customer data that week and then mailed it out ranks high. One materialized view is the review queue: per message and deal, the score and which signals fired. Governance is half the demo: the watch list is the most restricted table, so a first-level reviewer's role sees only the flagged entity of their own cases through row rules and masking, never the list; the control room sees all; a deal team sees only its own deal; every read of the watch list and every review is in the audit record and queryable. The tour names its limits: it is post-review analytics after real-time controls, not a data-loss-prevention replacement; attachments, images, encoded text and personal channels are outside it; employee monitoring needs disclosure and, in places, works-council agreement. Its tour follows the settled demo tour shape. Its business question: "Is anyone sending deal-sensitive or customer data out of the bank?" The bank's own customer-data access log (employee, customer table, read at) is a generated table of the demo, since the employees are not Provisa users; the tour shows ops.pii_access live as the record of the visitor's own reads. A visitor's demo sandbox is released soon after its tab closes. The load management window (REQ-1141's off-peak window) also applies to a materialized view, meaning: outside the window the view may not be read by a user's workload. Description: Per-table write grants. What a role may write to a table is stated per operation, as a write grant: role, operation (insert, update or delete), the columns an INSERT may list or an UPDATE may set, the rows an UPDATE or DELETE may touch (a SQL predicate), the check every row an INSERT writes or an UPDATE leaves must satisfy (a SQL predicate), and presets: columns the grant sets itself from a session variable, a literal or the time of the write, which the statement may not supply. A table holds at most one grant per role and operation. A grant that states no rows or no check takes the role's read row filter on the table, by design: a role writes the rows it reads unless its grant says otherwise; TRUE is every row. The one write admission (REQ-1925) admits a write on every surface by the write right (REQ-868) and the grant: an operation without its grant is refused naming the table, role and operation; a column outside the grant, or a preset column the statement supplies, is refused; the presets are added to the statement; the rows predicate is ANDed into an UPDATE or DELETE; the check is evaluated on the new rows before anything is written, and what cannot be decided is refused. A TRUNCATE needs a delete grant over every row; a MERGE an insert and an update grant over every row; an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE an update grant over every row with no presets; a COPY an insert grant with no presets. Mutation fields, gRPC insert routes and their inputs are offered per role for exactly the operations it holds grants for, with the grants' columns. A child role takes, per table and operation, the grant of the nearest role in its chain holding one; a meta role the first member's. Grants are stored with their table (rows and check encrypted at rest as row filters are), carried by environments, exported with the model, block deleting the role they name and are taken off by revoking the role from the table. A column's writable_by and a table's column_presets are refused by name. A Hasura v2 import carries each insert, update and delete permission as the role's grant (columns, filter, check, set), and Hasura's admin as org_admin's grants over every column.

Description: An MCP agent never acts beyond the roles it was given. Over the local stdio transport (and a loopback HTTP call that carries no bearer), the roles are the set the operator pinned in mcp.role (PROVISA_MCP_ROLE): a tool call that names a role, or a comma-separated set, acts as it only when every named role is within that pin, and is otherwise refused with a PermissionError naming the first role beyond it. A call that names no role acts as the pinned set. A remote call is governed by its bearer token's principal (REQ-1105).

Naming a role the caller does not hold is a high-severity security event, detected on every transport (the HTTP API, MCP, pgwire, Bolt, Arrow Flight, the airport Flight service and gRPC). The caller is refused and, except a signed-in session on the HTTP API, told only 'not permitted', nothing about whether the role exists; the connection or session ends where there is one (pgwire, Bolt, the gRPC call, the MCP session). A personal access token that does it is suspended on any transport. A token an external identity provider signed (firebase, oauth, keycloak) suspends that principal's token access to the org when presented over MCP or a transport that is never a browser session (pgwire, Bolt, Flight, gRPC); on the HTTP API it is refused and recorded, not suspended, because the browser presents the same bearer and a tab still naming a role since lost is routine. A local MCP session (no bearer, the pinned posture) is refused, its session ended, and the event written to the operator's log. Only an administrator lifts a suspension; nothing lifts it on a timer. Each event is written to the org's admin trail (admin_audit_log, action security.role_probe, severity high: principal, credential id, client, transport, endpoint or tool, requested role, held roles, time, and the ids of the principal's most recent audited statements, whose text stays in the query audit log under its own right). The org's administrators are emailed where the deployment sends mail, and the event is posted to the operator's security webhook (security.webhook_url) where one is set; what leaves the org names the principal, credential id, transport, endpoint, requested role, time and severity with a link to the admin view, and no statement and no held role. Administrators see each suspension and its event, and lift it, on the team page (GET /admin/orgs/{org}/suspensions, POST /admin/orgs/{org}/suspensions/lift). Description: A role grant Provisa holds (a user_role_assignments row) may be time-limited, and a role may remove its grants once they go unused. A grant may carry an expiry (expires_at): from that instant it is absent from the user's held roles on every request, however the request arrives, and an expired org_admin or platform_admin grant counts as no administrator. A role may state inactivity_days: a grant of it that no request has depended on for longer than that, counted from the later of the grant's last use and its creation, is removed. A request depended on a role when that role served it as the single acting role, or, acting as several roles (a named set or All), when the role is granted a table the governed statement read; acting as All does not count every held role as used. The grant's last use (last_used_at) is recorded at most once a day per grant, after the statement's audit row lands. A sweep on the scheduler, every 15 minutes per org, deletes the expired grants and the unused ones and records each in the org's administrative trail as role.expired or role.removed_inactive. Wherever mail is configured (mail.provider), a self-hosted single-org deployment included, the holder and the org's administrators are emailed auth.role_grant_notice_days days (an operator setting, default 7) before a grant expires or is removed for going unused, once per coming end (again after a grant is used and falls idle again, or is given a new expiry), and the administrators are emailed when a grant is removed; where no mail is configured the trail entry is the record. Security notices are sent whatever a user's email opt-in says. A grant given again states its expiry anew. Roles from an identity provider's claims or role mappings are the provider's to time-limit, and derived roles and meta-roles never expire. The grant form takes an optional until date (the grant ends at the close of that day), the role form takes remove after N days unused, and the grant list shows each grant's end and last use.

Description: A role constant (session_vars) may be a ${env:NAME} or ${secret:NAME} reference, resolved through the same resolver as every other reference (provisa.core.secrets.resolve_secrets), at use: when a request's session variables are formed, when the regional administrator's are, and when a meta-role inlines a member's constant. The model keeps the reference, never what it resolved to; it is saved as written. A reference that resolves to nothing fails, naming the constant and the reference; there is no default. A resolved constant takes part in the query: Provisa's own records of it are covered by central redaction, and a federated source's own logs are out of Provisa's reach. docs/security.md and the role editor's help say so.

Central redaction: one list of rules is applied to text before it leaves Provisa. The list holds the built-in patterns (a starter set: card numbers passing the Luhn check, US SSNs, bearer tokens, Provisa access tokens, AWS, GCP, Azure, GitHub and Slack keys, private keys), the deployment's rules (platform_settings), each org's own rules (org_settings), and an automatic rule over the org's secrets: the values Provisa's vault holds for the org, every ${secret:NAME} the org's stored model and settings name on any backend, and each ${secret:} or ${user:} value as it resolves. A rule is a named regular expression or a named ${secret:NAME} / ${env:NAME} reference resolved at load; a reference that does not resolve is logged at ERROR by name and shown unresolved, and the other rules stand. Matched text becomes [REDACTED:<rule>]. It applies to every exported span (one redacted copy handed to every channel) and the recent-spans view, to the OTel log pipeline and every logging handler (stdout included), to audit query text before it is hashed and encrypted, to the admin trail's detail, and to error messages sent on HTTP (bodies of status 400 and above, up to 1 MiB), pgwire, gRPC, Flight and MCP. Telemetry and errors, which carry no org, are redacted by every org's rules together. Rules reload on start, when an org's runtime is built, on a model or settings reload, and when an org secret is stored or removed. The Secrets page shows and edits the rules; the automatic rule's secrets are shown by name only, never a value. Redaction is best effort: the org adds patterns for its own sensitive formats, and a source's own logs are out of Provisa's reach. docs/security.md and the page say so.

The MCP server offers five statistics tools over a dataset the caller defines in SQL: describe (per column count, missing, distinct, mean, sd, quantiles and top values), correlate (pearson or spearman matrix and n), regress (linear: coefficients, standard errors, p-values, R²; logistic: the same with pseudo R² and AUC), compare (Welch's t-test for two groups, one-way ANOVA for more, with Cohen's d or eta squared) and forecast (exponential smoothing, ETS, with prediction intervals). Each runs the SQL through the one governed pipeline as the caller's resolved role, as run_sql does: row rules, masks and redaction apply, SQL the pipeline refuses fails as it fails for run_sql, and a role the caller does not hold is refused. Each returns only results, stating the method and n. Counts, distinct counts, means, standard deviations and each group's n, mean and variance are computed by the engine over every row the role reads; a fitted model, quantiles and top values read at most mcp.stats_max_rows rows (an operator setting on the Limits card), and the answer gives rows_read, row_cap and truncated. The models are fitted with numpy, pandas, scipy and statsmodels, the packages the Python sandboxes ship. docs say the rows behind an analysis never enter the model's context (data minimization by default), and that access control limits what an agent can learn: to keep identities out of an agent's reach, grant its role only the columns that identify no one, since a role that can read a column can aggregate it and aggregates over small groups can still identify individuals.

A table or a view is bitemporal by mapping three values to its columns: business_key (what identifies the same thing across versions), valid_time (the date the business gives the record: when it was agreed, booked or took effect) and recorded_time (when this version was entered or changed). Recorded time is called transaction time in the temporal-database literature and system time in SQL:2011; valid time is called application time in SQL:2011 or effective date. All three or none; each names a column. as_of filters valid time (valid_time <= X, latest version per business key) and as_recorded filters recorded time (recorded_time <= Y). Provisa picks the mechanism: a table whose business key is not its primary key keeps every version as a row, so a read filters and keeps the latest version per key, pushed down with the query; a table whose business key is its primary key is updated in place, so Provisa keeps its version log in the table's home region's store, captured incrementally on recorded time (re-reading a window of allowed_lateness so a late commit is not missed). A plain read returns the latest version per business key. A materialized view over a bitemporal input inherits its temporality with no settings of its own: each refresh reads the input rows recorded since the last refresh, recomputes only the valid-time dates they touch, appends versions for those dates (removals confined to them) and advances its watermark only after the append. A row moved between valid-time dates, or a source that deletes rows, needs a full refresh, which is offered on demand.

A calendar can declare the local time its day closes at, in its time zone (an 18:00 close of business in Europe/London); a day then runs from the previous day's close to its own, every grain's boundary moves with it, and a daily view refreshes at the close. With no close declared a day ends at local midnight.

A pgwire session sets its time travel with SET provisa.as_of and SET provisa.as_recorded (RESET either, or set it TO DEFAULT); every statement the session then runs, COPY included, reads as a request carrying the matching X-Provisa-As-Of / X-Provisa-As-Recorded headers does. A value that cannot be read is refused naming the setting; a statement prepared under other settings is governed again.

A materialized view's build takes the same route decision a query with its definition takes: a definition one source reads whole runs at that source, on any engine kind, and only its result rows come back; they are staged beside the view's table and every build step reads them there. The size guard counts the staged rows, so the source is read once.

Request deadlines are watched by one shared watchdog thread per process instead of a threading.Timer per request; a request that passes its deadline is cancelled as before, on every transport that registers a cancel.

A meta-domain view, sensitive_coverage, lists every sensitive column of the org (any tag with the Sensitive data option, pii included), one row each, read through the same statement that decides a Test (fake) environment's uncovered columns (provisa.security.sensitive.sensitive_assignments): its tags; has_fake and has_synthetic_rule; the fake as declared, its kind, that it is deterministic, whether it is stable across engines and whether it is computed from the real value; the synthetic rule as declared; and a status of covered, no_fake or inadequate with the reason. The fake and synthetic_rule columns are governance columns, read with view_governance as masks are. Provisa runs three adequacy checks on each sensitive column's fake and synthetic rule, daily per org and on demand (POST /admin/fakes/adequacy, sensitive_data right), and stores each run's result with its time; the view reads each check's latest: leak_rate (over a sample of up to 1,000 real values read as the org admin, the share whose fake equals the real value and, for truncate, prefix and bucket, the share keeping the part they keep; failed above the fakes.leak_rate_threshold setting, default 0.001; a fake computed from measurement or other columns is not sampled), kind_mismatch (an identifying fake kind other than the one the column's latest profile run proposes for a confident plausible type) and copies_real (a fake or synthetic rule naming a sensitive column with no fake, which it reads real). A column with a failed check is inadequate. Results are shares, flags and reasons, never values. The checks refuse nothing. docs say where coverage is reported (each environment's detail for the steward, the view for audits and evidence) and that a Test (fake) environment refuses to serve data until every sensitive column has a fake.

Description: A Node or Python code source runs in one of two modes. DEV: its code on the Provisa server, in today's sandboxed worker (REQ-1984, REQ-1993), unchanged. BUILT: from an image on a remote host. Switching modes keeps the source's tables and grants, since its exports and code hash are the same. HANDSHAKE: every host's hello names the protocol version it speaks, the content hash of the code it runs and its exports; a host speaking another protocol, running other code than the source is pinned to, or offering other exports is refused by name, and told why before its connection closes. BUILD IMAGE (the UI, on a dev-mode source): Provisa generates the boilerplate, installs the dependencies from the code's lockfile through the org's package registries (wheels only, npm --ignore-scripts), and builds a Linux image with a daemonless rootless builder in a sandbox, never a Docker daemon beside the server. The image is pushed to one of the org's container registries (an admin setting, Container Registries, beside Package Registries) or downloaded as a tarball for docker load; its tag carries the code hash and Provisa's version, and its OCI labels are dev.provisa.codehost=1, the protocol version, the runtime, the code hash and the exports. PORT: the container always listens on one fixed internal port, 7443, baked into the image with no variable; the host port is the operator's. The compose snippet the UI shows after a build, and the docs, map it with Compose's required-variable syntax ("${PROVISA_HOST_PORT:?set PROVISA_HOST_PORT to a free port on this host}:7443"), so a missing port fails before anything starts, with no default. On a shared Docker network or in Kubernetes the address is the container or Service name and 7443, nothing published. CONNECT: Provisa installs nothing on the remote host; the operator deploys the image their own way and enters the host and port on the source (the port field names it as the host port published, PROVISA_HOST_PORT in the snippet shown beside it, with a hint for the no-port case), plus the one-time pairing code the container prints on first start, which establishes the mutual-TLS trust both ways. Provisa dials, verifies the handshake and switches the source to built mode; a container with no published port fails the connection test naming host:port. Every Provisa process (each worker process, on every node) dials the host itself and keeps its own connection in its worker pool, keyed by source and content hash; it redials with backoff, a host that stops answering is shown on the source, and its reads fail naming the host. REDEPLOY: a host that comes back with other code has its reads refused naming the pinned and reported hashes until a steward re-pins after reviewing its exports. ROWS AS ARROW: anything that returns rows -- a @table, a @stream, and a @command that declares a row-set return_schema -- sends them as Arrow IPC record batches, built by the host program from the discovered column types with no change to the code; a @stream sends small batches. Arrow is the only rows encoding, never negotiated: the JSON rows message is gone, and the protocol version changes with it. Control messages (hello, call, cancel, error, end) stay JSON, and a @command returning a single value (a scalar or an object) sends it in its JSON value message. Provisa lands the batches directly (DuckDB natively; PostgreSQL through its Arrow or binary path). This holds for the local worker and the remote host alike; pyarrow and apache-arrow are in the host runtimes. In Docker the container's network policy is the code's egress boundary. UI: mode, host status, re-pin, build and push or download. LATER PHASE, Registered Remote Hosts: an administrator registers a remote host once under Admin with its SSH address, user, private key (in the secret store) and pinned host key; registration checks that the login runs Docker with no interactive sudo prompt and is refused naming what is missing; source authors then pull and run a built image on it without seeing the key. A registered remote host carries no Python/Node classification: the runtime is in each source's image, and a host needs only Docker.
